News.title: At least 4 dead and thousands left without power after devastating hurricane Isaias rips through US Gulf Coast
News.content:
Next

AT least four people have been killed and thousands left without power after a violent hurricane ripped through the Gulf Coast.

Florida has been drenched in heavy rains and battered by gusts of up to 105mph as Hurricane Isaias barrelled along the coast near Destin.



The monster storm slammed into the sunshine state at around 8.30pm on Friday and has continued to wreak havoc along the coastline.

Trees have been ripped from their roots and cars hurled through the air in a weekend of weather hell.





One woman was crushed to death after a tree collapsed onto her home on Saturday morning, confirmed Escambia County Sheriff’s Office.

Her husband Joey Williams told NewsNation the pair had gne outside to take photos of the damage but when they went back inside the tree smashed through their roof and trapped them.

He said: “I was able to squeeze out. My wife didn’t make it.”

Another was found dead from carbon monoxide poisoning after operating a generator indoors – with four others hospitalised in the same home.



At least 440,000 people were left without power in Florida on Saturday night as the hurricane knocked out power cables.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis warned residents to “be careful out there”.

He said: “Downed power lines, standing water, any of that can be very, very hazardous.



“Don’t run any generators inside your home or inside your garage.”

In Birmingham, Alabama, a second woman was trapped under a tree and a further two people were killed in the storms.

Governor Kay Ivey said: “This storm brought in heavy winds throughout Alabama, taking down trees, knocking out power and doing some damage.”

On Friday a flying tree struck a deputy with the Dale County Sheriff’s Department on Friday – leaving him with minor injuries.

Terrifying video footage shows emergency responders speeding to a wrecked vehicle – before a rogue tree crushes the vehicle, striking the deputy.



Forecasters feared the hurricane would reach a Category 3 “danger” level – but it stayed at a lower level Category 2.

There remain major flash flooding and landslide risks, said the National Hurricane Center (NHC).

The weather body warned that some areas could see up to 10 inches of rainfall, sparking floods and possible landslides.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Across the country, California has been ravaged by tropical Storm Rachel.

Waves towered to nine feet and crashed into homes along the West Coast including Malibu and San Diego, leaving a trail of destruction.

News.title: M62 closed after ‘serious multi-vehicle crash’ as drivers warned of long delays lasting hours
News.content:
ROAD CARNAGE M62 closed after ‘serious multi-vehicle crash’ as drivers warned of long delays lasting hours







Next

A MAJOR motorway is currently closed following reports of a serious collision, with motorists warned of hours long delays.

The M62 “multi-vehicle” crash happened just before 11pm last night between Denshaw and Rochdale.

As of this morning the carriageway between J21 and J22 is still fully closed, with reports of debris strewn across the road.

A full diversion is in place as recovery work is underway, and drivers can expect delays.





Motorists have been urged to avoid the area while a police investigation remains ongoing.

In a statement, National Highways said: “The M62 westbound is closed in Greater Manchester, between J22 (Denshaw) and J21 (Rochdale) due to a serious collision involving several vehicles.

“Greater Manchester Police and National Highways Traffic Officers are on scene. There is currently a large amount of debris in the carriageway which will need to be cleared once vehicles have been recovered.

“Police investigations remain ongoing. The closure is likely to remain in place for several hours.”



More to follow… For the latest news on this story keep checking back at The Sun Online

News.title: Cops probing murder of celebrity plastic surgeon in Marbella identify woman suspected of ordering hit
News.content:
DOCTOR HIT Cops probing murder of celebrity plastic surgeon in Marbella identify woman suspected of ordering hit







Next

COPS investigating the murder of a celebrity plastic surgeon have identified a woman they suspect of ordering his execution.

Dr Alexander Aslani, 57, whose clients included Towie’s Chloe Sims, was gunned down at his Marbella clinic on Wednesday.

Detectives believe a furious patient may have hired a hitman after a row over cosmetic surgery.

An 18-year-old Swede arrested on Thursday has admitted shooting the surgeon, according to Spanish sources.



Police are now trying to find out who hired him and how much he was paid.

A woman is said to have sent Aslani angry messages demanding a refund and threatening him just hours before he was killed.

Her partner had also allegedly threatened staff at the clinic days earlier.

Aslani’s clinic claimed to have carried out more than 14,000 operations, but the surgeon also faced complaints from former patients, including one who accused him of botching three procedures.

Cops have ruled out an earlier theory that Aslani was killed in revenge for a patient dying during surgery, after finding no evidence of any such death.

The Swedish teenager was arrested at a holiday apartment in Benalmádena as he prepared to flee Spain.

Aslani, known for his Brazilian butt lift operations, was shot several times by a masked gunman who walked into his office.

News.title: My pal Ranulph Fiennes ‘shouldn’t be in a care home’ Jeremy Clarkson blasts, saying the idea ‘fills me with despair’
News.content:
TOP GEAR PAL My pal Ranulph Fiennes ‘shouldn’t be in a care home’ Jeremy Clarkson blasts, saying the idea ‘fills me with despair’







Next

JEREMY Clarkson has said his life-long pal Sir Ranulph Fiennes shouldn’t be in a care home and the idea fills him with “despair”.

The 82-year-old world famous explorer has not been seen in public for two years and reportedly even his actor cousin Joseph Fiennes had to sneak secretly in to see him.



The former presenter of Top Gear, 66, said “Ran” was “by far the most memorable“ guest on the motoring show.

Normally on the show, guests were given a slot lasting eight to 10 minutes, Sir Ranulph’s interview ran for 17.



Even the audience were asked what they wanted to see, a road test of the Renault Clio or the interview. Sir Ranulph won the day.

Along with extraordinary tales of how he’d sawn off his own fingers and how he lost his toes, he also told about his days in the SAS.

He had stolen some explosives so that he could blow up a dam that had been built by Twentieth Century Fox in order to make Doctor Dolittle.

Jeremy added that Sir Ranulph had become a family friend when his mum had made a soft toy incarnation of his dog Bothie.



The presenter of Clarkson’s Farm wrote in The Times: “That’s why I’ve been sad over the last few weeks to learn of his current problems.

“But there’s more to it than that. A man like that should not be in a bloody care home.

“The idea of him sitting there doing beetle drives and eating fish fingers fills me with despair.”

Sir Ranulph is being illegally kept in care homes under fake names by his wife, it is claimed.

Earlier this year a care watchdog found Sir Ranulph – who was diagnosed with Parkinson’s – was being deprived of his liberty unlawfully.



Several friends and family members are now contemplating a legal challenge to Ms Millington-Cotes’ guardianship, the Telegraph reports.

Concerns over his whereabouts emerged after the former explorer failed to attend a Royal Geographical Society gala evening celebrating his life on October 23, 2024.

He instead appeared in a brief pre-recorded video – and has not been seen in public since.

It’s alleged Sir Ranulph spent time at a care home in London last year where his wife allegedly asked visitors to sign non-disclosure agreements before they could see him.

He was later moved to care facilities in Wales and Cheshire.

News.title: Two Ole Miss students found dead on same day ‘bought Kratom pills days before’
News.content:
DEADLY DRUG Two Ole Miss students found dead on same day ‘bought Kratom pills days before’







Next

TWO students found dead in separate incidents at the University of Mississippi had bought Kratom pills days before, investigators believe.

It comes as their cause of death was revealed in court on Friday during a court hearing involving two men accused of selling drugs at a smoke shop near the college’s campus.



The college’s student newspaper identified the undergraduate students as Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20.

Both were found dead in separate incidents at the University of Mississippi on September 21.



A defence lawyer for one of the two men accused of selling narcotics told the court one of the students died from a combination of substances, including cough syrup, Action5 News reported.

The other student died from inhalation asphyxiation, meaning breathing in toxic gases, the attorney said.

Aidan was a freshman from Englewood, Colorado, and Robert a junior from Atlanta, Georgia.

Investigators say both students had three kratom-related substances in their systems.

They included mitragynine, MGM-15 and MGPI.

Kratom is a supplement sold at gas stations that’s advertised as an energy booster and mood lifter but has no legitimate medical use.



Investigators think Aidan bought pills from Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford in the days before his death, according to court records.

Robert reportedly bought similar pills from another shop around 20 miles away.

An undercover informant visited the first store, cops said.

A worker there confirmed the store sold the pills and warned them to be careful because people were dying from them, according to an arrest affidavit.

Cops later raided the store and seized around 500 units of kratom and kratom-like products.



They also seized suspected THC products.

A narcotics agent told the court that one of the students had been found dead in a dorm with white foam around his mouth.

They said the second student, found off campus just an hour later, had the same white foam.

Two drug store workers have been hit with federal drug charges linked to the investigation.

The Lafayette County Metro Narcotics team previously stressed they were conducting two separate death investigations, adding “we have no confirmed evidence indicating that the two deaths are connected.”



Authorities said they did “not have confirmed information indicating that kratom or any other substance was a contributing factor in either death.”

Local coroner Glenn Coleman told the Clarion Ledger that autopsies and toxicology tests have been ordered for Hamilton and Strang, and results are expected in two to three weeks.

Kratom, an addictive herbal extract that comes from the leaves of an evergreen tree called Mitragyna speciosa, is legal in parts of Mississippi, but is restricted in Lafayette County.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

There have been several reported cases of deaths involving kratom, as it is possible to overdose on it, but typically an overdose happens when it is mixed with other drugs or substances.

Healthcare providers have raised concerns over the use of kratom in recent years as the supplement is not standardized, and therefore the potency can vary between brands and batches.

News.title: Green Party may have been captured by ‘extremists and racists’, warns top party MP after Polanski skips crucial vote
News.content:
Next

THE GREENS may have been captured by “extremists and racists”, a senior party MP has warned.

Zack Polanski’s party has been plunged into civil war after they passed a motion saying “Zionism is racism” – effectively demanding the end of the Israeli state.



Mr Polanski is facing questions over his leadership after he skipped the crucial vote – and then failed to win the Kings Cross St Pancras by-election.

Green MP Ellie Chowns slammed Mr Polanski’s “lack of leadership” in an interview with the BBC.



Asked repeatedly if the party had been taken over by racists , she said: “I don’t know if there are extremists and racists in my party, but I want to make sure that my party isn’t vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists.

“I want to make sure that my party’s policies represent the views of the majority of members of the Green Party who absolutely are not that sort of person at all.”

Mr Polanski has repeatedly refused to say he would have voted against the motion and said it is up to members if he stays as leader.

“What I’m experiencing, though, is an immense amount of people who are saying actually they’ve never been prouder to be a Green Party member.”

Meanwhile, Lib Dem leader Ed Davey is also facing a plot to oust him after frontbencher Charlie Maynard quit as Treasury spokesman in a bid to launch a leadership challenge.

A Lib Dem insider said: “Ed may see this challenge off but it is probably the beginning of the end.



“He is on a clock now. If someone better challenged him they would win in a second.

But an ally of Sir Ed insisted he is going nowhere saying: “Ed is fired up and focused on the next General Election.”

The party civil wars mean both the Greens and Lib Dems could face leadership contests before the next election.

News.title: Three joyriders who killed two police officers in crash racked up £20k in taxpayer-funded legal aid since they were kids
News.content:
Next

WRONG-WAY joyriders who died ploughing into a police car killing two officers racked up £20,000 in tax-funded legal aid since they were kids, The Sun on Sunday can reveal.

Three of the five who died with PCs Tom Clough, 38, and Matthew Blades, 37, near Middlesbrough in August had cash help since aged 12.



Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Worthy drew legal aid from 2021.

Saddington had £1,460 in 2025 and 2026 including £284 over “offences against the person”.



Rae racked up £5,545 including £170 relating to taking a car at 12 — and hundreds more from 2022 to 2024 for offences including theft and drugs.

Worthy had £13,774, our Freedom of Information request shows.



The total legal aid bills for the three comes in at £20,780.46.

Police have previously confirmed all five of the youths had links to organised crime with four of those killed having clocked up extensive criminal records with 37 convictions among them including for drug offences, assault, and robbery.

Last week it was revealed Cole Worthy’s father, Gye Worthy, was facing jail for attacking the celebrant at his son’s funeral.

The 40-year-old flew into a rage when Paul Maull failed to mention him in the eulogy to son Cole Worthy but did reference the teen’s stepdad.



He hurled insults and then attacked him as shocked mourners looked on.

The Legal Aid Agency was unable to locate any legal aid payments for Michael Robert Cahill, 23, or Jacob Matusiak, 23, the two other men killed in the crash.

The Ministry of Justice said: “Legal aid is not paid directly to individuals.”

News.title: ‘Significant concerns’ were raised about sick nursery worker 3 years before he was arrested for abusing sleeping kids
News.content:
Next

“SIGNIFICANT concerns” were raised about a sick paedophile nursery worker three years before he was arrested, according to reports.

Vincent Chan was jailed in February having pleaded guilty to 56 offences on three-year-old girls in his care at Bright Horizons nursery in north-west London.



Following his conviction, prosecutors describe Chan as a “prolific sexual predator”.

It has now been revealed Chan was the subject of a previous safeguarding investigation, carried out by Bright Horizons, with the oversight of Camden council, The Guardian reports.



It came after “significant concerns” were raised with the nursery in 2021 about Chan’s conduct and behaviours by the parent of a young girl, including concerns about what her daughter was saying to her about Chan.

The nursery referred the matter to Camden council, which advised it to investigate.



While the investigation was carried out, Chan was put on duties that involved no contact with children.

He was cleared to return to his role caring for young children at the nursery.



Just a year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself sexually abusing three-year-old girls at the Bright Horizons nursery.

In June 2024, he was arrested, initially on suspicion of child cruelty, after videos were discovered by nursery staff that Chan had filmed of distressed children in his care.

Cops then searched his devices and discovered he was a prolific sexual offender with tens of thousands of child abuse images on his computer.

It was also revealed he had committed sexual offences in his previous job as a teaching assistant at St Mary’s Church of England primary school in Dollis Park, North London, including upskirting female pupils.

He was sentenced to 18 years in prison in February this year.



The case raises serious concerns about whether existing safeguarding measures for nurseries are adequate.

Before Chan was arrested, other parents claim they raised concerns with Bright Horizons about Chan’s conduct at work.

They say concerns were raised with the nursery that their children were telling them that Chan shouted at them, was “angry” and a “bad man”.

The parents say their concerns were dismissed.

The Bright Horizons nursery on the Finchley Road closed in June 2025.



When there are concerns that a nursery work has been accused of harming or posing a risk of harm to children, may be guilty of criminal conduct or has exhibited behaviour that makes them unsuitable to work with children, nurseries have a responsibility to refer to local authority designated officers (LADOs)

The ultimate responsibility for managing allegations raised that relate to adults who work with children lies with the local authority.

If the concerns meet a criminal threshold, LADOs can recommend the matter is referred to the cops.

It is understood the Met Police didn’t receive a referral in 2021 regarding Chan and were only later told of the concerns.

Once Chan’s sexual offending came to light, Camden council carried out a rapid review of the decision to clear him to return to work, following the Bright Horizons investigation.



That review ended in November 2025 and Camden council then commissioned a local child safeguarding practice review to look at how Chan was able to abuse children at the nursery as well as offences committed in his previous job.

The review, which has been repeatedly pushed back, is now likely to be published in early 2027, according to Camden council.

It is expected to be critical of the safeguarding culture within Bright Horizons.

However, Camden council has said it cannot investigate Bright Horizons under health and safety laws because it is conflicted due to its participation in the safeguarding review.

Local authorities have the power to prosecute businesses that do not comply with health and safety legislation.



A letter sent to the parent of a child at the nursery, Camden council said the purpose of the safeguarding review was “not conducted to hold individuals, organisations, or agencies to account,” The Guadian says.

The parents of Chan’s victims are unlikely to be satisfied by the review as it is unlikely to apportion blame to executives at Bright Horizons.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The review was first due in the summer this year.

There has been no explanation as to why it was delayed.

News.title: Man dies after tiger attack at wildlife park
News.content:
A man has died after being attacked by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, police have confirmed.

The man was seen entering the tiger enclosure at the park near Doncaster just before police were called at 13:35 BST on Saturday.

South Yorkshire Police said the tiger then attacked the man and he died at the scene. The animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident - but the park was closed and will remain shut for the rest of the weekend.

Foreign Secretary and MP for Doncaster North Ed Miliband said he was "deeply saddened" to hear of the incident and sent his "thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died."

He added he was "very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded."

Yorkshire Wildlife Park said in a statement: "Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies are with the family and loved ones of the person who has lost their life."

Police said the man's family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said in a statement.

It added: "We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this footage."

Earlier on Saturday, in a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".

News.title: MPs seek to overturn ruling that stops police being sued for failings
News.content:
Backbench MPs are seeking to roll back a court ruling they say will have "devastating consequences" for victims of crime by preventing them taking legal action against the police, even when there have been grave investigative failings.

The 2025 Court of Appeal judgment, which applies to England and Wales, held that police officers are immune from civil litigation both in their role as witnesses, and for conduct or statements they make when carrying out criminal investigations.

Conservative Andrew Mitchell and Labour's Jess Phillips have submitted an amendment to a bill being debated in Parliament next week seeking to counteract the ruling.

Separately, the judgment could also be overturned at a Supreme Court appeal this month.

The MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying, including in cases where police have fabricated evidence, been dishonest or negligent, and where there has been a reckless disclosure of confidential information relating to victims.

The ruling came in a case brought by a victim of serious domestic violence who fled her abuser for a secret refuge, but Sussex Police included her new address in a file sent to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) without sufficiently flagging its confidentiality.

A CPS lawyer subsequently disclosed her address in court during a bail hearing, thereby revealing it to her abuser. As a result, she had to flee again.

The woman said the disclosure of her address had meant the place she was supposed to be safe "no longer felt safe at all" and she was still living with the impact of what happened and that loss of security.

She brought claims against both the police and CPS, arguing their failure placed her in fear for her life, compelled her to leave her home, caused her to suffer loss of earnings, and resulted in her developing a psychiatric injury. Her claims were initially rejected, reinstated on appeal, then struck out again.

The key issue was who could be held legally responsible for what happened, and who would benefit from legal immunity. Witnesses and lawyers have what is known as "core immunity" for things they say in court, so that they can speak freely there.

The Court of Appeal ruling further expanded such immunity, holding that it extends to an extremely broad range of police activity, including conduct or statements which are part of an investigation leading to a potential prosecution

Most types of legal claim are thus blocked by this immunity, including cases about serious human rights abuses and data breaches, and there are no exemptions for unjustifiable conduct.

Officers can still be prosecuted in the criminal courts and held accountable by police misconduct processes.

News.title: UK launches flood taskforce to prepare for extreme winter weather
News.content:
The government has launched a new taskforce to respond to extreme weather, including the risk of flooding this winter.

After a summer of record-breaking temperatures, the group will meet this week to assess how prepared the UK is for what the Met Office described as the "heightened potential" for wet, windy, stormy weather in the coming months.

"We're facing extreme weather, with flood and drought intertwined but the government is taking decisive action," Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Minister Emma Hardy said in a statement ahead of the meeting.

The Environment Agency has warned approximately 6.3 million homes and businesses in England remain at risk of flooding.

Defra will host the first meeting on Wednesday, bringing together the Met Office, Environment Agency and mayoral authorities as well as the farming, water and insurance industries.

Hardy said: "This will put communities and businesses at the heart of our work and will make sure the UK is ready for whatever the weather brings next."

The government has committed at least Â£10.5bn until 2036 to protect homes, businesses and critical infrastructure from the growing threat of flooding.

The Met Office has said the current seasonal outlook suggests an increased likelihood of wetter than average conditions during autumn, in part due to the El NiÃ±o weather event.

It has warned that this year's iteration of the climate phenomenon is likely to be the strongest in living memory, with the peak not expected until the end of the year.

The Environment Agency has said that while flooding is not guaranteed, the odds of repeated storms, prolonged rain and saturated catchments are higher than average this winter.

It has urged households to check their flood risk, sign up to alerts and make a flood plan to prepare for any emergencies.

The warnings follow 12 months of extreme weather across the UK, with the summer of 2026 the country's hottest on record.

Last winter brought four named storms to the UK - Bram, Goretti, Ingrid and Chandra - and several significant flooding events, with the Met Office reporting that England received 42% more rainfall than its winter average.

News.title: Northern Lights stun UK down to England's south coast
News.content:
Residents across the UK were left stunned as the sky was illuminated by the spectacular colours of the Northern Lights on Friday and Saturday evenings.

The natural phenomenon, known as the Aurora Borealis, is the result of increased solar activity.

Such occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland, but particularly strong activity levels meant they could be seen as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent on Saturday night.

The Met Office has said sightings could continue to be possible during clear skies until Tuesday.

News.title: Three friends on their student debt: One paid off, one chipping away and one creeping up
News.content:
When Lizzy, Libby and Charlotte met as freshers in 2012, their main responsibility was making it to lectures on time after early morning sports practice.

Their student debt, growing with interest from the day they took out their loans, was the last thing on their minds.

"The conversation was just so much less relevant at that time," says Charlotte. "As our careers have gone on and our paths have diverged more and more... those conversations start to come more to the forefront."

The friends, now in their early 30s, went to the University of Newcastle in the same year tuition fees tripled to Â£9,000 a year in England and Wales, and new loans called Plan 2 were introduced. Each borrowed about Â£37,500 to cover three years of tuition and living costs.

This year marks a decade since the first students in their year started repaying.

They may have started out in the same position, but over that time their career trajectories, life choices and earnings have shaped how much they've repaid, how much interest they've racked up, and how much they owe - with very different outcomes.

Student loans have come under scrutiny this year and there's been a particular backlash over Plan 2 loans. The government has said it wants to make the whole system fairer and campaigners are waiting to see what, if anything, changes in this month's Budget.

News.title: Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
News.content:
What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?

That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal â one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.

The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.

The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.

The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.

Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.

With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.

"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.

The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".

Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.

"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.

Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".

Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.

"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.

"But I did wrong."

It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).

Kim says Lisaâs in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.

"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.

"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.

"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."

News.title: AI is creating a 'human premium' for art made by people, but will it hold?
News.content:
The music platform Deezer says 44% of tracks uploaded to it are AI-generated. Its research also found that 97% of listeners couldn't tell what was AI-generated and what wasn't. But here's a third statistic: more than half of those surveyed said they did care if it was made by AI. They want humans to be involved.

Daniel Susskind, an economics professor at King's College London, says many of us place huge value on the human role in making art. It's what makes the creative process different from more functional, practical tasks, he thinks.

"I was once in a room of accountants, and one of them stood up and said, 'My clients come to me for the personal touch, the human process'," he remembers. "And I said, 'That isn't why they come to you, they come because they want their taxes done properly'."

But it's different with art, he says. "If I walk into the Sistine Chapel and look at the ceiling, I think not only is that extraordinarily beautiful, but isn't it amazing that a human hand, flesh and blood like my own, came up with that. A mind like mine dreamt that up," he says.

As Susskind describes it, what we value isn't just the destination, it's the knowledge that a human - one of us - got us there. We can wonder at that achievement.

News.title: Toxicity and uncertainty await Man City as they prepare to take on Liverpool
News.content:
Manchester City will face an atmosphere of toxicity and hostility they have never experienced before when they walk out to face Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

If City made a list of clubs they would prefer not to visit immediately after being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, Liverpool would be at the top ringed in red.

The relationship between the clubs has often been fractious for more than a decade, tensions fuelled by a sense of injustice felt by Liverpool fans who believe more Premier League titles should have been theirs instead of City's.

In 2013-14, 2018-19 and 2021-22, Liverpool finished second behind City â on the last two occasions by a single point - in what became, especially with Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp in charge, the defining domestic rivalry in recent years.

Liverpool supporters have long been convinced they would have won those titles had City not wielded the vast financial firepower that brought them under investigation, while those of a sky blue persuasion counter by simply highlighting the enduring brilliance and beauty of the teams Guardiola produced.

City, under new head coach Enzo Maresca, arrive at Anfield continuing to maintain their innocence after launching an appeal against the decision of an independent commission to deliver a guilty verdict.

And they arrive top of the table â but with a shadow cast over the entire season and its potential outcomes as the Premier League weighs up City's punishment, with their appeal running alongside.

As the cloud of City's guilty verdict hangs over the Premier League, each victory will carry a qualification, each league table will contain an unseen asterisk, each achievement viewed through the prism of potential future penalties and the fallout at each end of the top tier.

It has even led to the unheard of suggestion that the entire Premier League season could be rendered meaningless, given the potential scale of the consequences facing City, with talk of expulsion and relegation as well as record points deductions.

This must wait for what is likely to be a lengthy legal process, but it is against this backdrop of bitterness that City play their first league match since the verdict, in an Anfield arena that barely disguised its contempt for their fierce rivals even before that guilty verdict was handed down.

The Kop will be in no mood to await legal finalities or the outcome of an appeal. There will be sound. There will be fury. There will be resentment.

News.title: King warns malicious online actors are evolving tactics
News.content:
King Charles III has warned of the challenges disinformation and other "hostile online activity" pose to trust and security in the digital age.

The comments, made in a letter to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to mark its 10th anniversary, spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics by using automated technologies".

"From threats to our international order, to the need to balance the risks and opportunities of powerful new technologies, strong cyber security is fundamental to making the online environment safer and more resilient," he wrote.

Last month, the King warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

In the letter published on Saturday by NCSC, the King praised the government agency. He said its achievements over the past decade have included defending the country against cyber attacks, safeguarding democratic institutions and protecting "the critical infrastructure upon which daily life depends".

"You have built resilience across our public services, businesses and communities, equipping us all to prosper in our ever-evolving digital world," the monarch added.

The King said he was "acutely aware" that much of the work done by the NCSC cannot be praised publicly and that he was filled with "profound gratitude".

The NCSC was established in 2016 as part of the Government Communications Headquarters to protect the UK against cyber threats.

Earlier this week, the NCSC offered assistance to online shopping store Asos after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers, the BBC understands.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Asos said it was investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms. The company told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the company's users - including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

The letter from the King to NCSC came after he spoke to AI executives at Dumfries House in Ayrshire last month on how the tech can be used to benefit security.

News.title: Head of Met's volunteer force fired after AI tool found deleted intimate images on work phone
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has fired the head of its Special Constabulary after Palantir's AI monitoring uncovered that he had used his work phone to copy intimate images of a woman.

Special chief officer James Deller, who led the force's volunteer officers, was dismissed following a misconduct hearing on Friday.

The Met said investigators used lawful business monitoring and Palantir's Foundry system, which uses artificial intelligence (AI), to find the misconduct by Deller.

Cdr Pete Stevens said: "SCO Deller failed to meet that bar. His actions were an abuse of the trust put in him and it is right that he is no longer able to serve in policing."

Investigators found that in July and August 2025, Deller used his police-issued phone to take photos of two intimate images that had been sent to his personal phone.

The pictures had been sent using WhatsApp's "view once" feature, which makes them disappear after they are opened.

He then sent the copied images back to his personal device before deleting them from his work phone.

The misconduct was discovered during a week-long operation called Project Galatasaray, which used the AI technology in a bid to identify corruption and professional misconduct within the Met.

Deller will be added to the College of Policing's barred list, meaning he will not be able to serve in policing again.

Stevens added: "The vast majority of Met officers and staff serve London with dedication and integrity, and they rightly expect robust action against the small minority who abuse their position and undermine public trust.

"That is particularly true of those who serve in the Special Constabulary. They are volunteers who selflessly give up their time to keep London safe.

"They deserve to be led by people who demonstrate the highest standards in all parts of their lives."

News.title: Green Party MP wants to make sure it is 'not vulnerable to extremists'
News.content:
A Green Party MP has said her party needs to make sure it is not "vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists" after members voted for a motion that claimed Zionism was racism.

The motion put forward by activists, which became formal policy after it was approved at the Green's conference earlier this month, has divided senior party figures and been criticised by Jewish groups.

Westminster leader Ellie Chowns told the BBC it was a "significant and damaging policy" and she would work to reform the Green Party.

It comes after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said it was not being protected from entryism - where people sign up to a party to try to change it.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Saturday, Chowns said: "I don't know if there are extremists and racists in my party. But I want to make sure that my party isn't vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists."

The MP described Zionism as a "contested concept" and said the motion did not represent the views of the large majority of Green Party members, "nor of people in the country".

Chowns said the motion would be a "distraction from the very important work" the party has been doing campaigning for Palestinian rights.

She added: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The policy also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said: "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."

News.title: Drumcree parade ban was in 'best interests of peace', says Bryant
News.content:
The Northern Ireland secretary of state has said his decision to ban the contentious Orange Order Drumcree parade "was in the best interests of peace".

The decision on Friday came after agreement couldn't be reached between the Portadown District Lodge and the Garvaghy Road residents over whether the march would be allowed down the predominantly nationalist road.

Sir Chris Bryant said he received advice from the PSNI chief constable that allowing the procession to go ahead could lead to serious injury, disorder and wider unrest.

On Saturday, a legal challenge by Orangemen against the decision to ban the parade was adjourned until Monday after the judge said it was not an "emergency" case.

The stalemate has reopened what was once the most bitter parading dispute in Northern Ireland, with stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

The Parades Commission was established in 1998 to regulate contentious processions.

Its decisions restricting the Drumcree march have been challenged by the Orange Order for decades.

Earlier this year, a court overturned the commission's original decision to stop the parade, ruling it could go ahead, with restrictions on 27 September.

But Garvaghy Road residents blocked the road that morning, preventing the Orangemen from marching, and a stand-off has continued for almost two weeks.

The Court of Appeal has reserved judgment on a legal challenge brought by Garvaghy Road residents against the decision to allow the march.

Sir Chris said he had spent almost two weeks trying to broker a deal and believed the two sides had come close to an agreement.

He said two outcomes were discussed. One would have allowed the Orangemen to complete one final march along the Garvaghy Road, on the condition it would not apply to march the route again.

The other would have seen the group accept that it had won the right to march, but agree not to exercise that right, but neither proposal secured agreement from both sides.

News.title: Sara Sharif's grandfather granted guardianship of her siblings in Pakistan
News.content:
Sara Sharif's paternal grandfather has been granted guardianship of her siblings by a court in Pakistan.

The decision comes after years of legal limbo following the murder of 10-year-old Sara by her father and stepmother in 2023.

All five children, who are now aged between 16 and four, have been living in Pakistan since 2023. They were asked to speak to the judge in court, where the eldest said they were comfortable and the siblings were settled.

Sara's grandfather, Muhammed Sharif, told the BBC he was relieved to be granted guardianship after three years of legal battles, saying his hope is that the children "stay healthy" and receive "a good education".

"It is my responsibility to ensure they get the best possible education and care," he said.

When told by the judge that the grandfather would become their guardian, the eldest child responded saying "that's all good".

The five children have been in Pakistan since August 2023, when they were brought to the country by Sara's father, stepmother and uncle after Sara was killed.

The family was in hiding for weeks before the children were discovered by police at the grandfather's house. They were initially put into state childcare.

The adults flew back to the UK and were arrested at the airport. Sara's father Urfan Sharif and stepmother Beinash Batool were found guilty of Sara's murder. Sharif was sentenced to a minimum of 40 years in prison and Batool received a minimum of 33 years.

Her uncle, Faisal Malik, was found guilty of causing or allowing her death and given a 16-year sentence.

Sara had been hooded, burned and beaten during a "campaign of torture" that lasted two years before her body was found at the family home in Woking, Surrey.

News.title: Ceremony marks return home of kiwi feather cloak
News.content:
A ceremony has been held to mark the return of a MÄori kiwi feather cloak to New Zealand by a British museum.

The kahu kiwi was one of the farewell gifts presented by MÄori leaders in 1900 to Dr George Cleghorn, a medical doctor who had been working in New Zealand.

It was loaned to the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford by Cleghorn's widow in 1913.

The return was organised by the charity the Homebound Project which specialises in reuniting indigenous artefacts with their country of origin.

Dr Lorraine Eade, chair of NgÄti RÄrua o Te Wairau Society, which now owns the item, said the cloak was "crying to come home".

News.title: Eight men arrested by Greater Manchester Police days after early release from jail
News.content:
Eight men have been arrested by Greater Manchester Police days after leaving prison under the government's early release scheme.

About 700 prisoners from across the country were released early on 1 October in a bid to tackle overcrowding, with about 50 of them being from Greater Manchester.

GMP confirmed that five men had been arrested for breaches of criminal orders, including a domestic abuse prevention order, and others were held on suspicion of robbery, drug offences and domestic violence.

In response, the Ministry of justice (MOJ) said: "We inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse. If we had failed to act, the police would have been forced to halt arrests."

News.title: Rail disruption after overhead line fault
News.content:
Rail passengers are being urged to check before they travel due to overhead line problems on the West Coast Main Line in Staffordshire.

Work was ongoing to fix a fault with the 25,000-volt wires which power trains near Penkridge, causing disruption between Stafford and Wolverhampton.

At 12:00 BST, National Rail confirmed that lines have reopened between Stafford and Birmingham New Street, but residual disruption can still be expected until 16:00 BST on Saturday.

Adam Checkley from Network Rail, said: "Our teams have now cleared the issue allowing the route to reopen, but with trains and their crew out of position, delays and cancellations will continue throughout the day."

Rail replacement buses are in place at Birmingham, Stafford and Wolverhampton.

Checkley added: "We're sorry to passengers impacted by the overhead line problems at Four Ashes near Penkridge.

"With disruption to train services likely throughout the day, I'd urge people to check National Rail Enquiries before they set off on their journey."

Ticket acceptance is in place on alternative routes including the East Coast Main Line, and Midland Main Line via Sheffield.

News.title: Nepal issues evacuation orders after flash floods leave four people missing
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Authorities in Nepal urged people to move away from riverbanks in the mountainous north after flash floods swept away homes and bridges, leaving at least four people missing.

The flooding struck the Budhi Gandaki river in Gorkha district, about 100km west of the capital Kathmandu, early on Sunday.

Residents and tourists fled to safety as the river surged and officials issued evacuation warnings along its banks and downstream stretches of the Trishuli river.

The four missing people had been living in a shed on the banks of the Ungilung river, a tributary of the Budhi Gandaki, according to The Kathmandu Post. The shed was among four livestock shelters swept away by the floods, which also carried away 15 yaks.

The flooding was reportedly triggered by a landslide, which blocked a tributary before suddenly releasing the water downstream, the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology said.

open image in gallery Budhi Gandaki river in Nepal in spate on Sunday ( AP )

Authorities said they had identified a large landslide near Chumchet village in satellite images, but were yet to confirm the precise cause.

Residents reported hearing loud roaring sounds from nearby streams from about 4am, while officials said the river’s flow continued to fluctuate.

The floods swept away three bridges and dozens of houses, according to local media. The Himalayan Times said 35 houses were washed away while police confirmed that two suspension footbridges and one steel bridge had been destroyed.

A camp for workers and construction equipment at a hydropower project were damaged as well. At least 18 workers who were in the camp escaped to safety.

The full extent of the damage remains unclear, however, as assessments continue.

The Flood Forecasting Division urged people to stay away from riverbanks and move to safer ground.

Its warnings extended along the Trishuli river corridor towards Mugling and further downstream into Chitwan and Nawalparasi districts, where authorities said the flood risk remained high.

The army rescued six people who were at risk from a landslide, prime minister Balendra Shah said in a post on X.

“Following the flood in the Budhi Gandaki river, a contingent of the Nepali army has been deployed via air and land routes for search and rescue operations, and six individuals have been airlifted from the Jagat area, which is at risk of landslides. The composite quick reaction team stationed in Kathmandu has also been deployed to the aforementioned area via air transport,” he said.

open image in gallery Aftermath of deadly flash floods and mudslides along the Likhu river in Nepal in August ( Reuters )

Nepal is still recovering from catastrophic flash floods in August, when a sudden surge of water hit the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems, devastating entire communities near the border with China. The floods were likely caused by an ice avalanche and the temporary blockage of a river upstream, although assessments were ongoing.

At least 1,455 people were confirmed dead and 5,285 remained missing when the government ended its search-and-rescue operation earlier this month.

The disaster affected nearly 33,000 people and damaged or destroyed about 7,500 homes as well as 13 hydropower projects.

The government estimates that reconstruction will cost $4.7bn, with damage to roads, bridges and other infrastructure leaving some remote communities cut off and complicating relief and recovery efforts.

News.title: Trump may join Saudi strikes after major Houthi attack on Riyadh airport kills 12
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

At least 12 people were killed and over 300 injured following a strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday – the third attack this week – as Yemen’s Houthi forces stepped up their campaign against the kingdom.

The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the casualties, saying four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and a person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan, and Egypt were killed.

At the latest count, officials said 309 people were injured.

Hospitals were overwhelmed with casualties brought in by ambulance and helicopter, according to people briefed on the situation. Some of the injured were reported to be in critical condition.

The attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in almost a decade, struck without warning, as no alert was issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. Two earlier attacks this week targeting King Khalid international airport left four people dead and severely damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft parked on the tarmac.

open image in gallery Thick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh ( AP )

The fatal strikes highlight vulnerabilities in the country’s defence capabilities while it conducts an air campaign against the Houthis in Yemen. A Saudi-led military coalition promised to retaliate.

Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni forces backed by it claim to have launched hundreds of strikes against targets in Houthi areas in recent weeks. The Houthis say the air raids have killed civilians, including women and children.

The Saudi civil aviation authority said operations at the Riyadh airport were temporarily suspended on Saturday and all flights were diverted. The airport serves a city of about eight million.

Following the strike, the head of the Houthi media office posted on X that the movement had "shut down Riyadh international airport".

The Houthis warned commercial airliners to avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a military operations zone after the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launched an offensive on Monday.

In the US, president Donald Trump was asked by reporters if Washington intended to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen.

open image in gallery A security force member stands guard during a protest against Saudi intervention in Yemen, in Sanaa ( AFP/Getty )

"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.

US secretary of state Marco Rubio condemned the raids, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life”.

An eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then several casualties lying injured on the ground inside the facility. More than a dozen ambulances were seen heading towards the building, with video verified by Reuters showing emergency vehicles at the scene.

An injured passenger told Reuters they saw an object flying through the sky outside the terminal before part of the ceiling collapsed near a departure gate.

Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015, leading an Arab coalition to attempt to drive the Houthis from the capital Sanaa after the rebels had seized the city the previous year.

The war resulted in a devastating stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and starvation.

Saudi Arabia subsequently signed a 2022 agreement with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.

That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a rapid Houthi advance that seized the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el Mandeb from Saudi-backed forces. The Saudi-supported forces launched a new offensive this week to reclaim that territory, making slow progress even as Houthi forces placed Taiz, the country's third-largest city, under siege.

Flight-tracking service flightradar24 showed that all incoming flights to Riyadh were redirected or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one stage.

Houthi strikes earlier in the week had already driven several airlines to suspend or cancel flights to the Saudi capital, shortly before it was scheduled to host major energy and investment conferences.

Organisers of those events stated prior to Saturday's attack that they would proceed as planned.

News.title: Missile attack on airport in Saudi Arabia's capital kills 12 people and injures over 300
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Saudi Arabia on Sunday extended the closure of the country’s main international airport, according to an online flight tracker, a day after a missile attack on the facility killed 12 people from several countries and left more than 300 injured in a major escalation of the war between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom.

A Saudi-led coalition blamed Saturday afternoon's attack on the Houthis. It was the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh and marked the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.

Following the attack, U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday he was weighing whether the United States would join Saudi strikes against the rebels.

Airport operations were suspended Saturday. Authorities later extended the closure until at least 9 p.m. Sunday, according to Flightradar 24.

Also Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 91 Yemenis were killed and 168 injured by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks. It said 60% of those killed were women and children.

Mix of nationalities killed at Saudi airport

The attack struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media.

The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged in a social media post that an American citizen had been killed in the attack, which he condemned.

The Egyptian man was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, working for a Saudi airliner Flybas, according to the Egyptian state-run Al-Qahera New television.

Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebels

The attack is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom, which has seemingly tried to avoid all-out war with the Houthis.

Shortly after the attack, U.S. President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” he said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

Trump later Saturday said he planned to speak to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Asked if the U.S. might get involved, Trump responded, “We’ll find out.”

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the attack, calling it a “fully-fledged war crime” and vowing a firm response. The airport has no military facilities.

There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.

The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.

For Iran, the fighting puts pressure on a key US ally

The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region.

Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war. Now the rebels are a way for Tehran to apply pressure on a key U.S. ally.

The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government.

Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.

Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

The Houthis this week warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.

Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.

___

Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

News.title: 'Do not eat': Warning issued after Salmonella identified in imported eggs
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A "do not eat" warning has been issued to consumers and businesses after Salmonella was identified in certain eggs imported from Ukraine.

Food Standards Scotland (FSS) and the Food Standards Agency (FSA) said the eggs originate from Yasensvit Ltd, Kyiv, Ukraine, and are stamped with the code 3UA1012066, which is printed directly onto the shell.

The eggs may have been supplied to catering businesses or sold through smaller retail outlets.

The eggs may have been repacked by UK businesses and sold under different business names or packing centre details on the outer packaging, making the egg stamp code the most reliable way to identify affected products, FSS said.

“The FSA’s advice is that if people have bought any of the affected products, do not eat them and instead, dispose of them at home, as they may be unsafe,” it said.

What are the symptoms of salmonella? NHS Symptoms of food poisoning include: feeling sick or being sick

diarrhoea

tummy pain

a high temperature

feeling generally unwell The symptoms usually start within a few hours or a few days of eating food that caused the infection.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) detected Salmonella Enteritidis in samples of eggs and carried out whole-genome sequencing, which showed that the strain did not match the outbreak strains currently under investigation.

Salmonella infection can cause symptoms including fever, diarrhoea and abdominal cramps, which usually resolve without treatment after a few days. However, the infection can occasionally cause more serious illness, including sepsis.

Anyone experiencing symptoms should avoid attending work, school or nursery until they have been symptom-free for at least 48 hours to help prevent the spread of infection.

Food businesses that have received eggs stamped 3UA1012066 should immediately stop selling or using them, withdraw affected stock from sale and, where products have been sold directly to consumers, undertake a recall, FSS said.

FSS added that while most affected eggs are believed to have been supplied through the catering sector, some may also have been available through smaller independent retailers and convenience stores. They are not sold through major supermarket chains.

Eggs that are thoroughly cooked and handled hygienically should not present a food safety risk. Infants, young children, pregnant people and older adults should continue to only eat raw or lightly cooked eggs if they are produced in the UK and are part of a recognised assurance scheme, FSS said.

News.title: WHO issues update on investigation into Russian plague lab worker’s death
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The World Health Organisation (WHO) has said it still does not know what caused the pneumonia that killed a Russian lab worker at an anti-plague research centre in Siberia this month.

On Saturday, the UN health agency said no case of plague has been registered.

The lab worker fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on October 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people.

The WHO said the Russian state regulator reported that tests of the lab worker and those who came in contact with her were negative for the high-threat pathogens tested, that her contacts still showed no symptoms, and that no further linked cases of severe pneumonia had been identified.

"Based on the information provided ... (the) WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker," it said.

The WHO, in its first full Disease Outbreak News (DONs) update since the case emerged earlier this month, called for a continued investigation.

The lab worker fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on October 2 ( The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East )

“Additional clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information, including confirmation of the diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker, is required to improve confidence in the assessment,” it added.

It did cite initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting the death was linked to the pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. Pneumonic plague spreads from person to person, causing a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time.

Global health officials have been extra alert to fatal pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China. The cause of individual pneumonia cases can often not be determined.

Russian authorities have said the lab worker was appropriately vaccinated and that they found no microorganisms linked to her work in her body.

On Thursday, Russia also said it had completed health checks on all the worker's contacts. It says it had provided full information to the WHO, in line with established procedures.

News.title: Three tasks to get your home ready for autumn, according to a professional cleaner
News.content:
When I was sweating away this summer, I never thought the weather would turn, but it’s almost time to crank up our radiators and crack out the big duvet.

They’re the tasks no one likes doing, but luckily for you, I’ve worked as a cleaner for more than a decade. I’ve discovered some shortcuts to make the hated jobs that bit easier.

Here’s a video to show my hacks in action so you can follow along at home. Below, I explain in more detail how they work. Let me know in the comments section if you’ve tried them out.

Tip one: Keep your summer duvet fresh in storage

If, like me, you want to get your winter duvet out, your summer one needs to be cleaned and packed away to keep it fresh come spring.

News.title: Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs
News.content:
The Tottenham boss told Sky Sports: “I think we played very well against a great team. We had many chances to score in the first half. Three or four. The second half is normal to suffer against this quality. I am very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character.

“We suffered in the game but every situation of the game. I like the situation we were in with the red card. We need this situation. We have not accepted the defeat. We have to react in all ways we can. It is a bad way, it is not the right way. I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character.

“We win the game if we play as a team. We didn’t win this game playing as a team. Every game like today, we will win many games.”

When asked about Solanke, he replied: “He is a good player for Tottenham. There for not too many strikers better than Solanke. Today he was captain because he deserved it, especially in this moment because he suffer because Tottenham didn’t score or win any games. He is a great guy, great player and we are behind him.

“We have to believe in ourselves and this football way. If we believe, improve and play as a team, we will score many goals and win many games. If we don’t play as a team, it is impossible.”

News.title: Guimaraes looks a £75m bargain as ‘super sub’ makes difference
News.content:
Before the game we talked about two things, the challenge ahead against a team that had not lost in the Premier League. They full deserved to be where they are and it was going to be really tough. The second was to restore our identity and be ourselves again.

We weren’t pleased with our performance against Brighton and we wanted to put it right. But the context is that this was a difficult one [opponent]. But we reacted in a way that was unique and made it so special.

[Leeds] are very well organised, very physical and very committed in everything that they do. They are a threat. They are incredible the way they attack the ball and set-pieces, with belief. They came close to punishing us. They have individual quality and they are in a good moment.

When you play at 12.30 at home and you go one-nil down there’s a lot to do. You have to restore a lot of things. Energy is one of them. We had an incredible response. The crowd changed. You could see it.

We brought a lot of leadership on [with his three subs]. We brought goal threat, to win duels, people who can play forward and penetrate against their high press.

The timing, movement and execution of it [the winning goal], yes, it was a beauty.

News.title: Resurgent Verstappen on fire in the Singapore smog
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the sprint race for the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix from the Marina Bay Circuit. Given the way the championship standings are, it looks like Kimi Antonelli has one hand on the drivers’ title. That means that the most significant thing is the battle for individual race victories. That includes grands prix, but also sprint races, like we have today.

Formula One is very keen on sprint races, increasing their number significantly next year, but we have never had one in Singapore before. We will find out today whether there was good reason for it. I suppose the logic is that even a processional sprint race is better than a free practice session and that having two qualifying sessions on a street circuit such as this is exciting, too.

Still, although he might be strolling towards the championship, he and Mercedes are not the dominant force they were at the start of the season when he won five in a row having finished second in the opening race. In fact, in the last 10 grands prix, Antonelli has won three and Russell two. With Max Verstappen’s win in Malaysia last weekend it meant each of Red Bull, McLaren, Ferrari and Mercedes have won races this season.

It is Verstappen who is in strong form in an upgraded Red Bull, as he snuck pole position from George Russell by just over a tenth of a second. He was followed by Charles Leclerc in the Ferrari and then Oscar Piastri in the McLaren. Antonelli, in the upgraded Mercedes, found things more difficult, finishing down in seventh nearly 0.7sec off the pace.

Anyway, the sprint gets under way in about 30 minutes and we will be here for all the updates from that, as well as qualifying later today.

News.title: Majestic All Blacks copy Springbok playbook to dismantle Australia
News.content:
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of this Bledisloe Cup Test as New Zealand host Australia at Eden Park in Auckland.

The All Blacks are enduring one of the toughest periods in their history, having suffered three successive Test defeats against South Africa in August and September, which saw the Springboks claim the inaugural Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series tour. Dave Rennie’s men are under immense pressure to avoid a fourth consecutive Test defeat for the first time since 1998.

You could argue there’s never been a better opportunity for Australia to beat New Zealand at Eden Park. The Wallabies are enjoying a six-Test unbeaten run – their longest such streak since 2017, with five games in this rejuvenated period coming under new head coach Les Kiss. In their most recent outing, Australia secured an extraordinary 42-38 victory over a much-changed South Africa side in Perth, despite being reduced to 11 players at one point.

Australia will feel further encouraged due to several key absences for New Zealand, as Ardie Savea, Ruben Love, Richie Mo’unga, Caleb Clarke, Fehi Fineanganofo, Billy Proctor and Anton Lienert-Brown are all out injured. In a reshuffle for the All Blacks, Damian McKenzie will begin at fly-half for the first time in 2026. Other notable inclusions for the home side see all three Barrett brothers, Codie Taylor, Tupou Vaa’i, Cam Roigard and Will Jordan starting.

Meanwhile, the visitors are without the suspended Hunter Paisami, with Isaac Henry taking his place at centre. The likes of Ryan Lonergan, Len Ikitau, Harry Wilson, Ben Donaldson and Max Jorgensen, who were all key to the triumph against the Springboks, retain their starting spots.

All the statistics overwhelmingly favour New Zealand. The All Blacks have not lost any edition of the Bledisloe Cup since 2002, winning 51 series to Australia’s 12, and are unbeaten at Eden Park since 1994, when they lost to France. Australia are winless at Eden Park since 1986, tasting defeat there 30 times in 34 games, and have lost their last 11 Tests against New Zealand.

However, given the landscape heading into this historic rivalry between these two heavyweights, it genuinely feels like anything could happen.

Kick-off is at 7:10am.

News.title: Black British Business Awards 2026 winners revealed
News.content:
The chief executive of Dr. Martens has been named the Black British Business Person of the Year at the 2026 Black British Business Awards (BBBAwards).

Ije Nwokorie, who became chief of Dr. Martens in January last year and is the only black chief executive in the FTSE 250, was awarded in recognition of his role shaping Dr. Martens’ growth strategy.

He is recognised inside Dr. Martens for his strong communication with staff, according to the judges.

Before joining Dr. Martens, Mr Nwokorie spent more than 11 years at Wolff Olins, the marketing giant, before working as a senior director at Apple.

Born in the US but brought up from age six against the backdrop of post-civil-war Nigeria, Mr Nwokorie has described how he and his family went from the lifestyle trappings of 1960s America to a small Nigerian village and a home with no running water.

On winning the award, Mr Nwokorie said: “This recognition means a lot to me. While this award bears my name, it reflects the talent, dedication and generosity of the incredible teammates, mentors and leaders who have shaped me as a person and a professional.

“It is a powerful reminder that there is nothing more important in our leadership journeys than the time we invest to help others thrive.”

Alongside his executive career, he has served as a trustee at Charity: water for nearly a decade and held board roles at cultural and humanitarian organisations including the Institute of International Visual Arts and Malaria No More UK.

He also served as chairman of trustees for the Chineke! Orchestra, a British orchestra championing change and the first in Europe to feature a majority of black and ethnically diverse musicians.

The Black British Business Awards started in 2014 to celebrate the achievements of black people in British business. The Telegraph is the national media partner for the awards.

Mr Nwokorie was presented with the award at an exclusive ceremony sponsored by JPMorgan Chase at London’s Hilton Park Lane hotel.

Speaking at the ceremony, Sophie Chandauka, the executive founder of the awards, said: “You lend the BBBAwards credibility not simply to celebrate excellence, but to ensure the best and brightest from all communities get a fair shot. That commitment has made the BBBAwards the UK’s premium awards programme for black business achievement.”

A spokesman for JPMorgan Chase said: “We couldn’t be prouder to support and celebrate such an outstanding breadth of black British talent.

“Their accomplishments continue to inspire future generations and demonstrate the exceptional value they bring to businesses, communities and the wider UK economy.”
