Under Section 77(5), only party members whose names appear on the membership register submitted to INEC within the prescribed period are eligible to participate in party primaries, congresses and conventions.

Section 77(6) requires political parties to use the submitted register for their primaries. In contrast, Section 77(7) provides that a party that fails to submit its register within the stipulated period is ineligible to field candidates.

Pantami’s Omission

The exclusion of Mr Pantami, the former Minister of Communications and Digital Economy, comes after a separate legal challenge to his emergence as the PDP governorship candidate in Gombe State.

On 24 September, the Federal High Court in Gombe nullified his initial nomination and ordered the party to conduct a fresh primary within 30 days.

The suit followed complaints by PDP governorship aspirants, including Usman Aliyu and Khamisu Mailantarki, who challenged the process that produced Mr Pantami as the party’s candidate in May.

The court held that the process failed to comply with the party’s procedures and applicable electoral laws, excluding some aspirants who had been screened and cleared to participate.

Mr Pantami subsequently contested the fresh primary on 29 September and emerged as the party’s candidate again.

Adebutu’s Omission

Mr Adebutu’s omission follows allegations that his name was absent from the PDP membership register submitted to INEC.

Two groups, the Ogun Democratic Accountability Forum and Elections Integrity Watch, questioned his eligibility, alleging the register did not include his name.

The Ogun PDP rejected the allegations, insisting that Mr Adebutu was a duly registered member and that the party had complied with the statutory requirements for submitting its membership register to INEC.

His absence from the final list, along with his running mate’s, leaves the PDP without a listed governorship candidate in Ogun State.

Chinda’s candidacy raises separate questions

The Supreme Court judgment has also prompted questions about the eligibility of Kingsley Ogundu Chinda, the APC’s governorship candidate in Rivers State.

Mr Chinda registered with the APC on 27 April 2026 and formally announced his defection from the PDP to the APC on 2 June, after the APC had conducted its governorship primary on 21 May.

The sequence has raised questions about whether he was a registered APC member when the party held its primary and whether his name appeared on the membership register submitted to INEC within the required period.

The Rivers APC has dismissed calls to disqualify him, maintaining that his candidacy remains valid.

World.title: 2027: PDP reacts to Adebutu’s exclusion from governorship candidates’ list
World.content:
The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Ogun State has reacted to the omission of its candidate, Oladipupo Adebutu, from the final list of candidates contesting the 6 February 2027 governorship election in the state.

PREMIUM TIMES had reported that the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) excluded Mr Adebutu from the list.

The commission did not explain the exclusion from the list, which its Secretary, Rose Oriaran-Anthony, released on Saturday in Abuja.

It cleared candidates from 13 parties and their running mates, including the All Progressives Congress (APC), Olamilekan Adeola, and the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Lawal Adebisi.

In a statement on Saturday, the PDP blamed the APC, the ruling party in Ogun State, for excluding its candidate out of desperation.

“The public should be informed that the omission of our candidate’s name in INEC’s list is as a result of the undue pressure mounted by the ruling party on INEC out of fear of losing the election to our party,’ Mr Adebayo said.

He said Mr Adebutu never left the PDP and was duly registered within the designated period for digital registration, with his membership card printed, verified, and submitted to INEC on time.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The spokesperson urged the people of Ogun State “to be calm and rest assured that our governorship candidate, Hon. Oladipupo Adebutu’s name will be published … and he will emerge as the Governor of Ogun State.”

Read the full statement:

OMISSION OF PDP GOVERNORSHIP CANDIDATE FROM INEC LIST

(Desperation of the All Progressives Congress unmasked as PDP surges with unstoppable momentum)

The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) enjoins the good people of Ogun State to remain calm and rest assured that our Governorship Candidate, Hon. Oladipupo Adebutu, will be published by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and will emerge as the Governor of Ogun State in the 2027 General Elections.

The public should be informed that the omission of our Candidate’s name in INEC’s list is a result of the undue pressure mounted by the ruling party on INEC out of fear of losing the election to our party.

We state emphatically that our candidate, Hon. Oladipupo Adebutu, has never left the Peoples Democratic Party and was duly registered as a member during the designated digital registration period, with his party membership card printed, verified, and submitted to INEC on time.

While we urge the good people of Ogun not to be perturbed or distracted from our focus on voting out the APC, we remain resolute, unfazed and unwaveringly confident that our candidate is marching straight to a decisive victory in the Ogun 2027 Governorship election.

No amount of desperate manipulation, political witch-hunts, or calculated distractions can alter the mandate of the people of Ogun State who are overwhelmingly eager for true leadership and positive change.

Once again, we call on all our teeming supporters, party faithful, and the general public to remain steadfast, vigilant, and unintimidated as the unstoppable movement to rescue Ogun State and bring RELIEF to our people continues to gain momentum.

Signed:

Arc. Kayode Adebayo,

Publicity Secretary, PDP Ogun State.

World.title: EXPLAINER: Tinubu’s petrol relief plan, Atiku’s subsidy proposal — how they differ, who pays
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu’s administration has extended a discount at Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC Ltd) retail stations and proposed forward crude sales to domestic refineries and a negotiated ceiling on petrol supply costs.

For his part, Atiku Abubakar, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate, wants qualifying locally refined petroleum products to receive production support, potentially through crude supplied below market prices.

The government maintains that its measures do not restore the former petrol-subsidy regime. Atiku says they contradict the government’s objections to his proposal.

The distinction lies in where support enters the supply chain, how it is financed and whether consumers receive the intended savings.

What has the federal government announced?

On 8 October, the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, announced measures intended to cushion households and businesses against rising fuel prices.

According to a presidency statement, NNPC Retail agreed to forgo its petrol profit margin and sell at cost for an initial 30 days.

The announcement followed a ₦66-per-litre discount introduced by NNPC Retail on 1 October to mark Nigeria’s 66th Independence anniversary.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In an official statement on 9 October, NNPC Ltd confirmed that the promotion would continue until 31 October across its retail stations nationwide.

Mr Oyedele clarified the same day that the discount was financed through a reduction in NNPC Retail’s profit margin, rather than payments from the federal budget or Federation Account.

He explained that NNPC Retail purchases petrol from Dangote Refinery and other suppliers at market prices before adding its retail margin, which he said accounts for less than five per cent of the pump price.

He argued that higher sales could offset lower earnings per litre and help preserve the company’s profits and dividends to the Federation.

Mr Oyedele had also indicated that the proposed margin discount could be higher or lower than ₦66, depending on NNPC Retail’s calculations, as reported by PUNCH.

Therefore, it is not clear whether the 8 October arrangement will provide additional savings beyond the Independence anniversary promotion.

Who can access the discount?

A 10 October PUNCH report found that motorists had to use the NNPC Fuel App and pay digitally to obtain the ₦66 reduction.

At outlets visited in Abuja, customers paying directly at the pumps were charged ₦1,405 per litre, compared with ₦1,339 for those using the app.

The app requirement formed part of NNPC’s original promotion. However, it could limit access for motorists without smartphones or suitable digital-payment arrangements, including some commercial transport operators whom the government says it intends to prioritise.

The Abuja observations do not establish pump prices or purchasing arrangements at every NNPC station nationwide.

NNPC has not published the number of customers who have received the discount or the volume of petrol sold at reduced prices.

The presidency illustrated the margin waiver using a hypothetical landing cost of ₦1,300 per litre, saying NNPC Retail would sell at that price rather than add its usual margin.

The figure was an example, not an announced nationwide pump price.

What about the ₦1,350 ceiling and crude sales?

The government is also negotiating a ₦1,350-per-litre ceiling on petrol’s ex-gantry or landing cost.

Ex-gantry price is the price at which petrol leaves a refinery or supply facility. Landing cost generally refers to the cost of importing petrol. Neither is necessarily the final price paid by motorists, which may include transportation, distribution and retail margins.

Under the proposed arrangement, refiners and importers would initially absorb costs above the ceiling and recover the difference later, when crude prices or exchange rates become more favourable.

Mr Oyedele described this as price smoothing, with the ceiling subject to monthly review.

The government has not published the proposed agreements or recovery formula. Without those details, it is difficult to establish whether future prices would accommodate earlier shortfalls or what would happen if market conditions remained unfavourable.

The administration also plans to increase forward crude sales to domestic refineries as production rises and previously committed supplies become available.

Forward sales could improve supply certainty but would not necessarily reduce crude prices. Their financial implications depend on the agreed prices, volumes and payment terms, which have not been disclosed.

How would Atiku’s production subsidy work?

Atiku proposes support for qualifying petroleum products refined in Nigeria rather than imported finished products.

In written responses to PREMIUM TIMES, Phrank Shaibu, director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, said domestic refineries, including modular refineries, could qualify.

One proposed mechanism involves supplying crude at prices below the prevailing market rate, with the difference treated as production support.

“The final formula would be set out in the programme’s implementation framework and budget,” he said.

Mr Shaibu said the calculation would consider crude benchmarks, verified volumes, refining yields and expected consumer savings. He described the proposed programme as capped, budgeted and subject to independent audits.

Atiku has pledged to begin implementing what he calls a transparent production subsidy from his first day in office. His campaign, however, has not disclosed the discount rate, eligible crude volume, annual spending ceiling or formula for determining consumer savings.

Former Rivers State Governor Rotimi Amaechi illustrated the proposal during his 2 October appearance on Channels Television’s Politics Today.

Using hypothetical figures, he said crude valued at ₦15,000 could be supplied to participating refineries at ₦10,000, with the ₦5,000 difference constituting the subsidy.

“His ₦15,000/₦10,000 example was illustrative; it was not an approved price or final subsidy formula,” Mr Shaibu clarified.

Mr Amaechi said the programme would include modular refineries rather than benefit Dangote Refinery alone.

At an ADC town hall on 8 October, Mr Amaechi reiterated the proposed distinction between crude prices for domestic refineries and international buyers.

According to New Telegraph, he said the government would not make direct payments to finance the subsidy.

His explanation distinguishes a direct government payment from the financial implications of selling crude below its market value. The question of who would bear that difference remains unresolved.

PREMIUM TIMES previously reported that Mr Amaechi said an Atiku administration would seek amendments to the Petroleum Industry Act if existing law prevented implementation.

Which approach could reduce petrol prices faster?

The government’s discount operates at the retail stage. Eligible customers can receive an immediate reduction at participating NNPC stations, subject to the app and payment requirements. However, hundreds of private filling stations nationwide are not eligible for the government’s programme, meaning millions of Nigerian petrol consumers would still buy petrol at prevailing market rates.

Atiku’s proposal would operate earlier in the supply chain by reducing crude costs for qualifying domestic refineries.

Cheaper crude could reduce refining costs, but it would not automatically produce equivalent reductions at filling stations. Distribution expenses, marketers’ margins and competition would still influence pump prices.

Mr Shaibu said lower consumer prices would be a condition for receiving production support.

“The detailed pricing, monitoring and enforcement rules would be specified in the implementation framework,” he said. “Refiners would have to comply with those rules to receive or retain support.”

He promised safeguards against diversion, arbitrage and excessive refinery margins, supported by published costs and independent audits.

The campaign has not specified how much of any crude-price discount refiners must pass to consumers or the penalties for non-compliance.

The government faces a comparable challenge. A reduction in petrol prices at selected stations does not guarantee lower transport fares.

The extent of any wider benefit would depend on how many commercial operators obtain the discount and whether their savings influence fares.

Why Dangote’s market position matters

Petroleum engineer and economist Izielen Agbon has questioned whether subsidising production in a concentrated market would produce sustained price reductions.

Speaking on Channels Television’s Politics Today, he argued that support for a dominant private refinery would not guarantee lower pump prices without sufficient competition.

Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) data for August illustrate the market structure.

Nigeria recorded average daily petrol receipts of approximately 50.5 million litres, comprising 35.9 million litres from domestic sources and 14.6 million litres from imports.

Dangote Refinery accounted for approximately 35.87 million litres of daily domestic receipts, according to regulatory data reported by PREMIUM TIMES.

The Port Harcourt, Warri and Kaduna state-owned refineries were listed as not producing.

Dangote therefore accounted for almost all domestically sourced petrol during the period (about 71 per cent of the total petrol consumed), although imports remained a significant share of total supply.

On 6 October, PUNCH reported, citing unnamed refinery officials, that Dangote had stopped selling petrol to major marketers involved in imports while continuing sales to other buyers.

The sources said the decision was intended to prevent blending with imported petrol. Some marketers disputed that explanation and raised competition concerns.

PREMIUM TIMES contacted Dangote Refinery for clarification. No response had been received at the time of the earlier filing.

Neither the reported sales restriction nor Dangote’s market share alone establishes anti-competitive conduct.

Mr Agbon has advocated restoring state-owned refineries to provide a competitive benchmark.

NNPC Ltd announced a memorandum of understanding with two Chinese companies in May to explore restarting the Port Harcourt and Warri refineries. None of the refineries is, however, currently operational, and there is no fixed date for them to resume operations.

Who would bear the financial cost?

The government’s discount reduces the revenue NNPC Retail would otherwise receive from eligible petrol sales.

Mr Oyedele maintains that the company is financing the reduction from its retail margin without reimbursement from the federal budget or Federation Account.

He also disclosed that NNPC Retail sells approximately 70 million litres of petrol monthly, according to PUNCH’s 10 October report, which cited his Channels Television interview.

Applying the ₦66 discount to that entire volume would reduce gross sales revenue by approximately ₦4.62 billion in a month.

The estimate assumes every litre qualifies. Actual forgone revenue depends on eligible purchases and sales volumes.

It is not an established subsidy expenditure or loss of profit. The effect on earnings would depend on the company’s margins, costs and any increase in sales.

NNPC has not published the total volume sold at discounted prices since 1 October.

The proposed ₦1,350 supply-cost ceiling presents a different financial issue. Refiners and importers would initially absorb costs above the ceiling, expecting to recover them later. The eventual burden depends on the shortfall, volume covered and recovery terms.

The ADC’s crude-discount proposal would also have a cost, even without a direct Treasury payment.

Crude sold below its market value represents forgone revenue for the seller. If a producer supplies crude worth ₦15,000 for ₦10,000, it receives ₦5,000 less than the assumed market value unless compensated elsewhere.

The financial burden could fall on a public producer, a private producer or another party under a compensation arrangement.

The campaign has not explained which mechanism it intends to adopt or how it would account for the concession.

Mr Shaibu said the programme would be financed by cutting government waste and unnecessary expenditure, without imposing new taxes or reducing the minimum wage or student support.

The campaign has not identified the expenditure lines to be cut or estimated the savings.

In a 20 September statement, the APC Presidential Campaign Council estimated that Atiku’s proposal could cost ₦17 trillion to ₦21 trillion annually, depending on the crude discount, volumes covered and whether support applied to entire barrels or only petrol sold domestically.

These are the APC’s projections, not independently established costs. The statement does not provide sufficient calculations to reproduce the estimates.

The government’s wider relief package includes cash transfers, subsidised credit, compressed natural gas deployment and other measures. A consolidated estimate of their fiscal implications has not been published.

What does the domestic crude supply framework provide?

The Domestic Crude Supply Obligation (DCSO) provides an existing framework for supplying crude to Nigerian refineries.

In its 10 August report, the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) said domestic refineries received 53.7 million barrels of crude oil and condensate between April and June 2026, representing 97.4 per cent performance against allocated volumes.

The commission said Dangote Refinery required 63 million barrels during the quarter, while producers offered 68.1 million barrels. The refinery accepted 52.6 million barrels, approximately 78 per cent of what was offered.

The figures distinguish crude offered from crude accepted and delivered. They do not establish why Dangote accepted less than the volume offered.

NUPRC said the framework operates on a willing-buyer, willing-seller basis, with transactions subject to commercial agreements.

What does the Petroleum Industry Act permit?

Section 109 of the Petroleum Industry Act addresses domestic crude supply obligations.

It provides for commercially negotiated sales between producers and licensed refiners, taking prevailing international prices for comparable crude grades into account.

The provision supports crude availability for domestic refining but does not expressly establish a government-financed discount for refiners.

Section 205(1) provides that wholesale and retail petroleum-product prices should generally follow unrestricted free-market pricing conditions.

Section 205(2), however, permits regulatory intervention where a licensed activity constitutes a monopoly service or involves an excessively dominant supplier.

The law also contains provisions addressing competition, commercial transactions and cost recovery.

A voluntary retail-margin waiver or negotiated crude discount would raise different legal issues from a compulsory below-market sale or mandatory price ceiling.

In a September statement, NMDPRA said it did not fix pump prices, citing the market-pricing provisions of the PIA. The authority also referred to its powers to address anti-competitive practices and abuse of market dominance.

PREMIUM TIMES asked NMDPRA whether the ADC’s proposed consumer-price conditions would constitute regulated pricing and whether existing law provides sufficient enforcement powers.

The authority acknowledged the enquiry but did not provide a response as of the time of this report.

The government’s proposed ₦1,350 ceiling would likewise require clarity on whether participation is voluntary and how the arrangement would be enforced.

Mr Shaibu said an Atiku administration would not implement its programme outside the law.

“If the existing legal framework prevents its implementation, an Atiku administration would submit the necessary bill to the National Assembly to amend or repeal the relevant provisions,” he said.

The campaign has not identified which provisions might require amendment or explained how its first-day implementation pledge would work if legislation were necessary.

What can Nigeria learn from Germany?

Atiku has cited Germany’s temporary fuel-tax reduction as an example of government intervention.

The German government announced a reduction of 14 euro cents per litre in energy tax on petrol and diesel, equivalent to approximately 17 cents after the associated value-added tax effect.

Scheduled for October to December 2026, the measure was estimated to provide €2.5 billion in tax relief.

Germany’s approach reduces fuel taxes, unlike Nigeria’s proposed retail-margin waiver or discounted crude. Its published relief amount, duration and estimated fiscal cost nevertheless provide a useful reference for assessing temporary interventions.

What happens when the relief ends?

In an 8 October statement issued through Mr Shaibu, Atiku questioned what would happen after the government’s initial 30-day intervention.

“What happens on Day 31? Nigerians wake up to the same brutal prices, the same punishing transport fares and the same rising cost of food,” he said.

PREMIUM TIMES reported his criticism separately.

NNPC has since confirmed that its existing promotion will continue until 31 October. Whether the government’s additional margin-waiver arrangement will produce further savings remains unclear.

The proposed ₦1,350 supply-cost ceiling would be reviewed monthly, but its recovery terms have not been published.

The ADC has not announced an end date for its production subsidy.

Mr Shaibu said the programme would be reviewed against fiscal limits, verified domestic output, consumer savings and market conditions.

“Specific numerical thresholds and a sunset rule have not yet been announced and should be published as part of the completed framework,” he said.

The government can demonstrate the reach of its intervention by publishing discounted sales volumes, the value of the reductions and the number of customers who benefited.

The ADC, meanwhile, would need to disclose its crude-pricing formula, funding arrangements, legal basis and conditions for passing savings to consumers.

Without those details, neither proposal can yet be reliably costed or assessed for its likely effect on petrol prices.

World.title: Abia 2027: The naysayers can rant but can’t erase, By Ferdinand Ekeoma
World.content:
The photo you are seeing here was Isi Gate, Umuahia, before Governor Alex Otti assumed office.

The same sorry spectacle greeted Abians at every other junction and corner. Contrary to the Igbo adage “Ihe Oma na Anya Gbaba Ndu” (There is a covenant between the eyes and good things), in the past, what existed was “Ihe Ojo na Anya Gbaba Ndu” (There was a covenant between the eyes and bad things), and our people accepted their fate with equanimity during the period under review.

This spectacle diminished the standing of every Abian at home and in the diaspora. It buried our dignity in the mud. It made Abia and Abians objects of caricature.

The majority of opposition elements, especially the embittered ones vilifying the present government and the Governor on a daily basis today, are not doing so because they want good governance. No! They are doing it because the era of iniquity they profiteered from, and which they desperately want to return, has become a laughable illusion. They know this reality, but they are afraid to acknowledge it.

The noise is not about good governance. If it were, they would have pushed for it when they had the opportunity to do so.

Alternatively, they would have been humble enough to acknowledge the massive changes that have happened in Abia under Governor Alex Otti’s watch. It is about their stomachs. It is about our common patrimony which they controlled and squandered with impunity when they called the shots. It is about the audacity of shamelessness. It is about lack of repentance, and of course, it is about self-inflicted deceit.

As the election year draws closer, we will not fall prey to the strategy of distraction, which the noise makers are pushing through disinformation. We will not keep ourselves busy responding to stage-managed false narratives or explaining things to those who are deaf to the truth. Instead, we will occupy ourselves with the task of telling our story, which is both factual and verifiable.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

We will be presenting verifiable facts of our achievements, while humbly acknowledging areas of shortcomings and explaining measures being put in place to improve on them.

In 2023, Governor Alex Otti made promises to Ndi Abia. They believed him because of his character, capacity and accomplishments, and subsequently voted him in. Today, he and his team will be showing the things that have been achieved. Luckily, our people are smart, intelligent and discerning. They are telling the story even more than the government itself, because they were the biggest victims of the poor governance of the past. They can feel the difference and they are telling it.

The countdown begins!

*Ferdinand Ekeoma is the Special Adviser on Media and Publicity to the Governor Alex Otti of Abia State

World.title: Ogun PDP raises alarm over Adebutu’s omission
World.content:
By Jimoh Babatunde

The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Ogun State has expressed concern over the omission of its 2027 governorship candidate, Hon. Oladipupo Adebutu, from the list published by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), alleging political pressure from the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC).

In a statement signed by its Publicity Secretary, Arc. Kayode Adebayo, the party assured members and supporters that Adebutu’s name would be published by INEC, expressing confidence that he would participate in the 2027 governorship election.

The PDP maintained that Adebutu remained a member of the party and had completed his digital membership registration within the stipulated period.

According to the statement, his membership card was printed, verified and submitted to INEC within the prescribed timeframe.

The party alleged that the omission resulted from pressure allegedly mounted on the electoral commission by the APC, which it accused of seeking political advantage ahead of the election.

However, the PDP did not provide evidence in the statement to substantiate the allegation.

The party urged its supporters and residents of Ogun State to remain calm, insisting that the omission would not derail its preparations for the election.

It also called on party members to remain steadfast and focused on its campaign, expressing confidence in Adebutu and the party’s prospects.

The PDP further urged INEC to publish Adebutu’s name, reiterating its commitment to what it described as efforts to bring relief and positive change to the people of Ogun State.

INEC’s position on the omission and the allegations against the APC was not contained in the statement.

World.title: Pantami’s camp urges calm over omission from INEC list
World.content:
Pantami

By Ben Ngwakwe, Gombe

The camp of former Minister of Communications and Digital Economy, Prof. Isa Pantami, has appealed for calm among his supporters following the omission of his name and that of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) from the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) list of governorship candidates for the 2027 election in Gombe State.

The appeal was contained in a statement issued by the spokesperson for the Pantamiyya Movement, Prof. Suleiman Mohammed, and shared on Pantami’s official Facebook account.

Mohammed described the development as a temporary challenge rather than a final determination of Pantami’s political future, urging PDP members and supporters of the Pantamiyya Movement to remain calm, hopeful and focused as the electoral process unfolds.

“This is a temporary challenge and a normal part of the electoral process, not a final determination, in sha Allah,” the statement said.

According to the statement, Pantami’s camp was aware that his name was missing from INEC’s published list despite his emergence as the PDP governorship candidate following a fresh primary election conducted on September 29.

The fresh primary followed an order by the Federal High Court in Gombe, which led to another exercise to determine the party’s candidate for the 2027 governorship election.

However, while the names of candidates fielded by several other political parties appeared on INEC’s published list, neither Pantami nor the PDP was listed.

The omission has raised questions about the status of the party’s nomination and the next steps available to the PDP and its candidate.

The statement from Pantami’s camp did not specify whether the party or the candidate would seek clarification from INEC, pursue an administrative resolution or explore legal options over the omission.

Nevertheless, the camp urged supporters to remain composed, stressing that the omission should not be interpreted as a final decision on Pantami’s participation in the 2027 Gombe governorship election.

The development comes amid preparations by political parties and aspirants for the 2027 general elections, with the finalisation of candidate lists remaining a key part of the electoral process.

World.title: SDP welcomes INEC listing of 13 Nasarawa Guber candidates
World.content:
By Edwin Philip, Lafia

The Social Democratic Party (SDP) in Nasarawa State has welcomed the listing of its governorship candidate, former Inspector-General of Police, Mohammed Abubakar Adamu, by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), describing it as a development that has eased uncertainty surrounding the party’s participation in the 2027 general elections.

In a statement titled “Our March to Victory Is Unstoppable,” the Director of Digital Media and Communications of the Mohammed Abubakar Adamu Campaign Organisation, High Chief Otaru Douglas, said INEC’s listing of Adamu as the party’s candidate had addressed speculation following a recent Supreme Court judgment on the eligibility of political parties and their candidates to participate in the elections.

Douglas said the campaign organisation remained focused on engaging voters across the state, adding that it would continue to promote its plans for security, job creation, youth and women’s empowerment, and people-centred governance.

According to him, the campaign would sustain its engagement with residents across wards and communities to explain its policy proposals ahead of the election.

“We congratulate our Principal, the leadership of the SDP at the national and state levels, and our teeming supporters across the 13 Local Government Areas for their steadfastness and loyalty.

“This INEC affirmation is not just a listing; it is a pointer to the inevitable victory that awaits us at the polls and the defeat our opponents are smelling already,” he said.

INEC lists 13 candidates

Other governorship candidates listed by INEC in Nasarawa State include Nuhu Amgbazo of the African Democratic Congress (ADC); Christopher Mammam of the Action Democratic Party (ADP); and Aliyu Ahmed Wadada of the All Progressives Congress (APC).

Also listed are Ibrahim Kashim Aboh of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA); Onawo Muhammed Ogoshi of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM); and Dahiru Musa Doma of the Action Peoples Party (APP).

The list further includes Gaza Jonathan Gbefwi of the Labour Party (LP); Khalid Muhammad of the National Rescue Movement (NRM); Emmanuel David Ombugadu of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP); and Abdulahi Omame Abisabo of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP).

Others are Kigbu Tanko of the Young Progressives Party (YPP) and Giza Abubakar Abdu of the Zenith Labour Party (ZLP).

Meanwhile, the name of Musa Shugaba Abdullahi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) was not on the list.

The party could not be reached for comment as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: 2027: Enugu NRM candidate warns against political violence
World.content:
The governorship candidate of the National Rescue Movement (NRM) in Enugu State, Engr. Dr. Christopher Ndubuisi Okonkwo, has condemned reports of attacks on supporters of a fellow governorship aspirant, calling on security agencies to investigate the incidents and bring anyone found responsible to justice.

In a statement, Okonkwo expressed concern over reports that armed individuals attacked supporters who had gathered to welcome their governorship candidate.

He sympathised with those reportedly injured and their families, stressing that political differences should not deprive citizens of their right to participate freely and peacefully in the democratic process.

The NRM candidate condemned political violence, intimidation and acts that endanger lives, insisting that no political ambition or disagreement could justify attacks on citizens.

He urged the Enugu State Government and relevant security agencies to investigate the reported incidents, establish the circumstances surrounding them and ensure that anyone found culpable was prosecuted, regardless of political affiliation or status.

Okonkwo said the protection of lives and property would be a priority under his proposed administration, adding that effective policing, timely intelligence, community engagement and accountability would be central to tackling insecurity in the state.

He also appealed to political parties and their supporters to remain peaceful and law-abiding, noting that political competition should not undermine peaceful coexistence.

The governorship candidate called on Governor Peter Mbah to condemn and investigate what he described as repeated attacks aimed at suppressing political campaigns in the state.

He warned against allowing the situation to deteriorate, urging the authorities to take preventive measures to protect political parties and their supporters from violence.

Okonkwo stressed the need for the government and security agencies to act promptly to prevent further escalation.

He reiterated that every resident of Enugu State deserved protection, irrespective of political affiliation, and called for peaceful political engagement ahead of the 2027 governorship election.

World.title: Lagos-Calabar Highway: Group petitions Tinubu, NASS
World.content:
President Tinubu

….Seeks independent engineering assessment, cost audit of Ondo route realignment

By Dayo Johnson, Akure

A community organisation, Ilaje Omuro Community Connect (IOCC), has petitioned President Bola Tinubu, the National Assembly and anti-corruption agencies over the alleged realignment of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway away from the coastline of Ondo State.

The group described the reported route change as an economic and geographical injustice against Ilaje communities, demanding an independent engineering assessment, a comparative cost audit and the publication of relevant project documents.

In a statement signed by its counsel, Babatunde Omobone, IOCC said it represented more than 1,000 indigenes of Ilaje Local Government Area and urged the Federal Government to provide a transparent explanation for the reported change.

The 750-kilometre Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway is one of the major infrastructure projects of the Tinubu administration. Flagged off in March 2024, the highway is designed to run from Victoria Island, Lagos, through Ogun, Ondo, Edo, Delta, Bayelsa, Rivers and Akwa Ibom states to Calabar, Cross River State.

The Federal Government says the project is intended to expand coastal trade, tourism and logistics, with planned features including six lanes, concrete pavement, solar lighting and train tracks.

Controversy over the Ondo axis emerged following reports that the Federal Ministry of Works had realigned the highway away from the Ilaje coastline towards an inland corridor.

According to IOCC and other stakeholders from Ilaje and Itsekiri communities, the original survey and Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) indicated that the highway would enter Ondo State from Ogun State at Olosunmeta and pass through Araromi, Abetobo, Abe-Oroyo, Ogogoro, Ayetoro, Awoye, Molutehin, Ugbonla, Ilowo, Ilepete, Obe-Enikanoselu, Obe-Rewoye, Ikorigho, Jinrinwo and Igbo-Egunrin before reaching the Igbokoda waterfront and linking Ode-Ugborodo and Escravos in Delta State.

The group put the stretch at about 60 to 110 kilometres.

It alleged that the route had instead been diverted from Oke-Upare inland through Ovia North and Ovia West in Edo State to Gelegele, said to be 10 to 20 kilometres from the sea, before connecting to Warri in Delta State.

IOCC claimed the alternative alignment would span between 130 and 190 kilometres and traverse swampy terrain requiring extensive bridge construction.

Umahi defends realignment

The group questioned the engineering justification given by the Minister of Works, Senator David Umahi, for the reported change.

Umahi, at a briefing in Abuja last Wednesday, defended the decision, saying it was based on sound engineering considerations and that the government had no regrets over it.

“We have no regret for decisions taken at Ondo. For us, it is their right to write a petition; it is my right to take the right decision,” the minister said.

He explained that sections of the original route contained pits more than 100 metres deep, with no sharp sand within 300 metres, making construction technically difficult and more expensive because of the extensive filling and ground stabilisation required.

However, IOCC disputed the cost argument, estimating that construction along the original coastal route would cost between N4 billion and N7.5 billion per kilometre, compared with N7.5 billion to N12 billion per kilometre for the inland alignment, which it said would involve difficult terrain and extensive bridges.

The group cited previous road projects in similar terrain to challenge the suggestion that the Ilaje corridor was unsuitable for construction.

It referenced the Igbokoda-Ugbonla road, built by the Ondo State Oil Producing Areas Development Commission (OSOPADEC), and a Ugbonla-Awoye road contract reportedly awarded by the Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC) in 2010.

“If roads can be constructed within the Ilaje coastal environment, what specific engineering, geological, environmental or financial considerations make the proposed coastal highway route impracticable?” the group asked.

It called on the Ministry of Works to publish the feasibility studies, geotechnical and soil investigations, EIA reports and comparative cost-benefit analyses for both alignments.

IOCC also demanded an independent assessment by qualified engineers, arguing that advances in bridge construction, coastal protection and tunnelling should be considered before the coastal corridor was ruled impracticable.

Group warns of economic consequences

Beyond the technical questions, IOCC said the reported realignment had significant economic and social implications for coastal communities.

The group said Ilaje had Nigeria’s longest coastline, estimated at between 80 and 100 kilometres, and contributed more than 60,000 barrels of crude oil daily, yet continued to face sea incursion, coastal erosion, poor road access and limited economic opportunities.

It listed Abereke, Orioke, Magbehinwa, Idiogba, Mese, Ayetoro and Awoye-Odofado among the communities it said could be affected.

According to the organisation, excluding the coastal axis could limit opportunities in fisheries, agriculture, tourism, trade and logistics, discourage investment and further isolate communities whose ancestral homes, fishing grounds and livelihoods were already threatened.

The petition follows a joint resolution by Ilaje and Itsekiri leaders in Lagos on September 19, 2026, at which the two groups reportedly agreed to work together to ensure that the highway retained its original coastal route and threatened legal action over the alleged diversion.

Senior Advocate of Nigeria, Ebun-Olu Adegboruwa, and pan-Yoruba socio-political group Afenifere have also criticised the reported realignment, arguing that moving a coastal highway inland could undermine its intended purpose.

Seeks Tinubu’s intervention

IOCC urged Tinubu to intervene, the National Assembly to exercise its oversight powers and the Federal Ministry of Works to provide a comprehensive public explanation supported by verifiable data.

It also called on the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to scrutinise any credible evidence of financial misconduct, abuse of office or improper influence connected with the route change.

“This is a call for accountability, not a declaration of guilt. Any allegation of wrongdoing should be investigated fairly, and any findings should be based on verifiable evidence,” the group said.

The organisation further demanded meaningful consultations with affected communities, traditional institutions and civil society before a final decision was taken on the alignment.

It stressed that its campaign was not directed against any individual or state but was intended to ensure fairness in the implementation of a major national infrastructure project.

“The Ilaje people are Nigerians. Ondo State is an integral part of the Nigerian federation. The coastal communities of Ilaje deserve to be considered fairly in decisions concerning a major national coastal highway,” the group said.

World.title: What Pastor Adeboye told me when I met him — Sowore
World.content:
Omoyele Sowore, AAC presidential candidate and Pastor Enoch Adeboye, the General Overseer of the RCCG.

Presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC), Omoyele Sowore, has recounted his meeting with the General Overseer of the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG), Pastor Enoch Adeboye, saying the cleric told him he prayed for him regularly and believed he would triumph.

Sowore said Adeboye also told him that he knew his ways were pure during their meeting at the church’s national headquarters in Ebute-Metta, Lagos.

The activist disclosed this in an interview on the Naija Unfiltered Podcast, about a week after attending the RCCG’s National Thanksgiving Service.

In a post on X after the service, Sowore had said Adeboye offered to pray for him during a private meeting.

Recounting the encounter on the podcast, Sowore said Adeboye recognised him and recalled praying for him.

“He said to me, ‘You know, I know you very well, and I pray for you all the time, and I know your ways are pure, and that you will triumph,’” Sowore said.

He explained that he was initially directed to wait near Adeboye’s car after the service but was later informed that the cleric wanted to meet him in the church’s vestry.

According to Sowore, the conversation also touched on their first meeting in 1996, when he approached Adeboye for support in a campaign against cultism in Nigerian universities.

The presidential candidate said he had visited the cleric after completing the National Youth Service Corps programme to seek his support in tackling the growing problem of cultism on campuses.

He recalled that Adeboye endorsed the campaign and directed that N10,000 be given to him to support the effort.

“We used it to go and campaign against cultism,” he said.

Sowore said Adeboye later asked for permission to pray for him during their recent meeting. He agreed but told the cleric he would not close his eyes while the prayer was being offered.

“So he did pray for me, and we stood up, and we laughed,” he said.

Asked whether he gave his life to Christ, Sowore said the discussion did not take that direction, stressing that he was not involved in organised religion.

“We didn’t have that kind of conversation because giving life to Christ is for people who are into organised religion. I am not into organised religion,” he said.

He added that he did not discuss his presidential ambition with Adeboye, describing the encounter as a personal conversation prompted partly by the cleric’s surprise that they had met three decades earlier.

World.title: Maritime students urge NIMASA to ease certification rules
World.content:
…Movement seeks Lagos marine ministry, launches three-month statewide engagement

By Adeola Badru

The Maritime Students for Tinubu and Hamzat Movement (MSTM) has urged the Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency (NIMASA) to introduce transitional arrangements and financial relief for seafarers affected by new certification requirements.

The movement warned that regulatory changes should not impose excessive financial burdens on students and young maritime professionals seeking to obtain the qualifications required to practise.

It also called on the Lagos State Government to establish a dedicated Ministry of Marine and Blue Economy to coordinate the state’s maritime resources, create jobs and strengthen youth participation in the sector.

The Convener of MSTM, Omotayo Temitope, made the calls during the movement’s inaugural meeting, town hall engagement and press conference in Lagos.

He said professional standards must be upheld without making it unnecessarily difficult for aspiring maritime officers to acquire the qualifications required to practise.

Temitope said the circular on the implementation of the Merchant Shipping Regulations 2025 had introduced additional course and certification requirements, creating administrative and financial challenges for aspiring maritime officers.

While affirming the movement’s support for strict regulatory compliance, he said the cost of implementing new requirements should not be borne entirely by students and young professionals.

“While we firmly support high professional standards, the immediate human and financial burden of regulatory shifts must not fall entirely on students and young professionals,” he said.

The convener stressed that MSTM did not support shortcuts or any compromise of professional standards but wanted an implementation process that took into account the circumstances of those affected.

He urged NIMASA to engage transparently with maritime institutions, student representatives and seafarer associations to identify and document cases of hardship arising from the new requirements.

He also called on the agency to consider subsidised access to newly mandated courses and structured relief measures to address outstanding certification challenges.

According to him, such measures would help sustain professional standards while preventing regulatory changes from creating additional barriers for aspiring seafarers.

Movement backs Lagos Blue Economy initiatives

Temitope also expressed confidence in the Special Adviser on Blue Economy to the Lagos State Governor, Oluwadamilola Emmanuel, citing efforts to harness the state’s ocean and aquatic resources.

He referenced initiatives such as the Omi EKO Project, saying Lagos had significant opportunities to deploy its marine resources to promote tourism, fisheries, environmental sustainability and commercial enterprise.

However, he urged the state government to ensure that young people, particularly maritime students, cadets and residents of riverine communities, benefited directly from such initiatives.

He called for practical training, cadetship berths and clearly defined employment pathways to equip young people with the skills and experience needed to participate in the maritime industry.

MSTM seeks dedicated ministry

The National Coordinator of MSTM, Oyewale Elijah Omokoyejo, called on the Lagos State Government to give serious consideration to establishing a dedicated Ministry of Marine and Blue Economy.

Omokoyejo said the state’s extensive coastline, inland waterways, port infrastructure and riverine communities required coordinated administration beyond water transportation.

He said a dedicated ministry would provide a unified institutional framework for managing inland shipping, fisheries and aquaculture, marine tourism, environmental protection, offshore logistics and youth skills acquisition.

According to him, the proposed ministry would also strengthen the link between maritime education and employment by connecting academic training with practical industry experience and professional opportunities.

He said the initiative could ensure that the state’s maritime resources were managed under a coordinated policy framework that supported economic activities and expanded opportunities for young people.

Movement begins statewide consultations

On the movement’s political orientation, Omokoyejo said MSTM supported the political vision of President Bola Tinubu and Lagos State Deputy Governor, Dr Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, but stressed that its responsibilities to maritime students extended beyond electoral activities.

He said the movement intended to build a sustainable platform for addressing the practical challenges facing students and young professionals, irrespective of political cycles.

“Political support gives the movement a platform to engage, but service to maritime students is what gives that platform true meaning,” Omokoyejo said.

He identified limited access to sea-time opportunities, certification difficulties and post-graduation unemployment as structural challenges requiring systematic attention from government and industry stakeholders.

To better understand these challenges, the national coordinator announced the commencement of a three-month statewide engagement campaign covering maritime institutions, technical colleges and riverine communities across Lagos State.

He said the campaign would involve campus visits, town hall meetings and community consultations to document the experiences of cadets, marine engineering students and young people in underserved coastal communities.

According to him, the exercise would enable maritime students and other young people to present their concerns directly and ensure their needs were adequately reflected in policy discussions.

Omokoyejo said the findings would be compiled into a document to be known as the Maritime Students Agenda, outlining students’ concerns and priorities and providing a basis for engagement with government and industry stakeholders.

The document is expected to highlight the practical difficulties confronting young people seeking to enter the maritime sector and serve as a reference for discussions on policies and programmes affecting their education, professional certification and employment prospects.

In their joint declaration, Temitope and Omokoyejo reaffirmed MSTM’s commitment to bridging the gap between student advocacy, government policies and maritime industry development.

They said the future of Nigeria’s maritime and Blue Economy sector depended partly on the ability to train, support and integrate young people into the industry.

“When maritime students are properly trained, supported, and included in national economic planning, Nigeria’s entire maritime and Blue Economy sector will grow stronger and more resilient,” they said.

World.title: 1 in 6 Nigerian youths faces mental health challenge, experts warn
World.content:
… As YEDI, Grassroot Soccer take mental health awareness to Mushin community

By Chioma Obinna

Concerned by the growing burden of mental health challenges among young people and widespread misconceptions surrounding the condition, health experts have called for early help-seeking, community-based interventions and stronger collaboration between health professionals, families and religious institutions.

They spoke during a community outreach organised by Youth Empowerment and Development Initiative (YEDI), in partnership with Grassroot Soccer, to commemorate the 2026 World Mental Health Day in the Mushin area of Lagos State.

The outreach combined football, drama, personal testimonies and health education with free medical checks, counselling and medication to encourage residents to prioritise their mental and physical wellbeing.

A programme consultant with Grassroot Soccer Incorporated in Nigeria, Dr Babatunde Odusolu, said one in six young people aged 15 to 24 in Nigeria experiences some form of mental health challenge, underscoring the need for accessible information and early intervention.

He said the partnership was designed to make mental health education accessible to adolescents and young people through football-based learning, trained youth mentors and referral services.

“It’s ensuring that young people are aware of their mental health and they seek help as quickly as possible,” Odusolu said.

According to him, the initiative, known as MindSKILLZ, uses sport to deliver health messages in ways young people can understand, while providing pathways for those who need professional assistance.

“If during this outreach people are identified that have mental health issues, it could be mild, it could be moderate or severe, they are referred appropriately,” he said.

Odusolu said the intervention went beyond the one-day event, noting that YEDI and its partners also supported school-based and community programmes across Lagos.

He explained that participants identified as needing further care would be referred to appropriate facilities and followed up to ensure continuity of support.

The programme also provided a platform for people with lived experiences of mental health challenges to share their stories in a safe environment, helping to challenge the stigma that often prevents people from seeking care.

“In this part of the world, it is believed that once you say you have mental health issues, then you are mad. But you can see that the speakers are demystifying it by saying to people that it is not madness,” Odusolu said.

He added that personal testimonies could help others recognise their struggles, speak out and seek professional support without fear of discrimination.

Speaking on why YEDI took the message to the grassroots, Executive Director of YEDI, Tomisin Adeoye, said the organisation deliberately took its mental health campaign to the community after conducting a needs assessment to determine where awareness and services were most needed.

Adeoye explained that YEDI uses evidence-based programmes to address health concerns, including malaria, HIV and mental health, particularly among young people.

“We are going to use football for good to pass across our information. Because football is universal, and we can see that people are interested in football,” she said.

According to her, football, drama and interactive sessions were used to make the message engaging and easier for residents to understand.

“People don’t want to measure mental health. People just think that it has to do with people that are mad. But it’s beyond that,” Adeoye said.

She explained that mental health encompasses psychological and social wellbeing and requires greater public understanding beyond commonly held misconceptions.

Adeoye said the outreach was also intended to empower participants with accurate information they could share with family members and others in their communities.

“Before we talk about the community taking initiative, they need to understand what mental health is all about,” she said.

She added that the availability of counsellors and referral partnerships ensured that the programme offered more than awareness, providing access to further support for participants who needed it.

Beyond mental health education, the outreach revealed other health concerns among residents who received free medical screening.

A retired Deputy Director of Nursing Services at Lagos University Teaching Hospital, Mrs Sarah Onyebuka Ojei, said some participants presented with anxiety, worry and agitation, while screening also identified elevated blood pressure and blood sugar levels.

She said some residents were unaware of their conditions, while others had stopped taking prescribed medication because they could no longer afford it.

“In every three people we check, you see that the blood pressure is raised,” Ojei said.

She explained that some participants disclosed that financial hardship had prevented them from purchasing their medication, making the free medical services particularly important.

The screening also identified cases of obesity, underweight, elevated body temperature and other conditions requiring further assessment.

Ojei said participants with suspected malaria were directed to undergo appropriate tests, while those with other health concerns received counselling and referrals for further evaluation and treatment.

She stressed that early detection and appropriate follow-up could prevent health problems from becoming more serious.

The outreach operated a referral process through which participants moved from initial nursing assessments to laboratory investigations and medical consultations where necessary.

Those requiring more advanced care could be referred to primary healthcare centres, general hospitals, teaching hospitals or specialist psychiatric facilities, depending on their needs.

Ojei also emphasised the importance of confidentiality in mental health counselling, noting that people experiencing emotional or psychological difficulties might hesitate to speak if they feared their private concerns would become public knowledge.

“We establish rapport, good relationships, make them feel that we are human beings, we are not gods. We talk with them, try to ask them some open-ended questions,” she said.

She explained that the approach was intended to help participants feel comfortable enough to discuss their concerns and receive appropriate guidance.

Speaking, the General Secretary of the Catholic Youth Organization of Nigeria at Christ the King Catholic Church, Ilasa-Maja, Ogechi Idioha, said the church had a responsibility to support members’ mental wellbeing alongside their spiritual development.

She said the church provided its premises for the outreach to enable health professionals to educate and sensitise residents about mental health.

“People come to church and they try to get better spiritually. But then the mental aspect is also needed and also important, actually,” Idioha said.

She noted that stigma and shame often prevented young people from discussing personal challenges, even with friends and people they trusted.

According to her, creating safe spaces where people can speak openly about their experiences would help them access support before their difficulties escalated.

Idioha added that the church also provided opportunities for education and counselling through its family-focused programmes and health services.

Also speaking, Rev. Fr. Bonosa Kwadwo Fosu of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits), who represented Fr. Thomas Djabaku, said religious institutions needed to recognise when individuals required professional mental health services rather than relying exclusively on spiritual interventions.

Fosu said the church’s work with young people, including counselling and spiritual accompaniment, could complement the services provided by mental health professionals.

He, however, cautioned against treating every psychological challenge as a purely spiritual problem.

“If you have the knowledge of knowing that this is something you cannot solve on your own, you refer it to the professional,” he said.

The cleric added: “So, it shouldn’t be like, oh, it’s only prayer. Going to see the psychologist is also a prayer because God has granted the psychologist the skill, the tools to use.”

He urged religious leaders to acquire the knowledge needed to recognise situations beyond their competence and refer affected individuals to qualified professionals.

Fosu also expressed concern that increasing dependence on mobile phones and social media could weaken face-to-face relationships and the communal support systems that traditionally helped people cope with personal difficulties.

He urged families and communities to make time for direct interaction, particularly during family gatherings and other communal activities.

“Phones have come to stay with us. But when we gather as a family, can we put phones aside? When we gather as a group, as a church, can we put phones aside and then deal with each other physically and personally?” he asked.

He maintained that prayer, community support and professional intervention should work together to promote mental wellbeing.

A beneficiary of the outreach, Fatima, expressed appreciation for the free medical checks and medication, saying the exercise helped her understand aspects of her health she had previously been unaware of.

She said the screening gave her information about her temperature and malaria status, while the availability of free medication made the intervention particularly beneficial.

Fatima encouraged other residents to take advantage of medical screening and seek information about their health.

The organisers said the outreach was part of continuing efforts to improve mental health literacy, reduce stigma and connect young people and other community members to appropriate services.

They maintained that sustained awareness, early identification, confidential counselling and effective referral systems were essential to ensuring that people experiencing mental health challenges received the help they needed.

World.title: Pantami, Adebutu, Gwarzo Missing in INEC’s Final List of Gombe, Kano, Ogun Guber Candidates
World.content:
*Gwarzo remains our candidate, Kano NDC insist

Ahmad Sorondinki in Kano

The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has published its final list of candidates for the February 6, 2027 governorship elections, with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidates for Gombe and Ogun states, and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) governorship candidate in Kano State, missing.

However, INEC cleared the APC governorship candidate in Rivers State, Kingsley Chinda for the 2027 governorship election in the state.



Chinda was number five in the 19-man list of Rivers State governorship candidates released by the electoral commission.

The lists, signed by INEC Secretary, Rose Oriaran-Anthony and published on the INEC website yesterday, showed 16 governorship candidates of other political parties in Gombe State and 13 in Ogun State, and none of them was from the PDP.

The governorship candidates missing were Ali Pantami of PDP in Gombe State, Aminu Gwarzo of NDC in Kano State and Ladi Adebutu of PDP in Ogun State.



However, the Kano State Chairman of NDC, Alhaji Hussaini Mairiga, has insisted that Gwarzo remains the governorship candidate of the party in the state.

INEC did not publicly state the specific reason for dropping the candidates’ names but the decision was believed to be connected to a Supreme Court ruling in the case of INEC v. Zenith Labour Party, which confirmed the continued validity of Section 77 of the Electoral Act 2026.



The commission released the list in line with the promise of its Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, who spoke at a press conference in Abuja early last week.



Pantami, who was on the provisional list published on August 29, was missing from the new list.

Pantami had earlier emerged as a PDP candidate after dumping APC on May 19. But Ahmed Mailantarki, one of the aspirants who sought the PDP ticket, challenged his victory in court.



A Federal High Court in Gombe nullified the election and ordered a fresh primary, which he won again.

Pantami won the rerun primary conducted on September 29, defeating Khamisu Mailantarki and Usman Aliyu Garry.

But his biggest obstacle was the September 24 Supreme Court judgment, which restored Sections 77(5), (6), (7) and 84(2) of the Electoral Act 2026, barring parties from fielding candidates whose names were not in the membership register submitted to INEC within the stipulated time.



While uncertainty trailed his participation in the election, Mohammed Haruna, an INEC National Commissioner, had hinted that in line with the Supreme Court ruling, some parties would not field candidates in 2027.

Under Section 32(2) of the Electoral Act 2026, parties have 14 days to notify INEC in writing, with an affidavit, if a nominated candidate’s name is missing.



In Kano State, Gwarzo’s removal from the final list means he cannot contest the governorship election on the NDC platform.

In Ogun State, neither Adebutu nor his running mate, Kolapo-Sowunmi, appeared in the list, raising questions about the status of the PDP’s governorship ticket ahead of the poll.



Speculations have emerged that Adebutu’s name may not have been included in the party register submitted to INEC, as required under the provisions of the Electoral Act.



Hoever, the PDP has urged residents of the state to be calm and rest assured that its governorship candidate, Adebutu’s name would be published by INEC and he will emerge as the Governor of Ogun State in the 2027 general election.



A statement by the publicity Secretary of PDP in Ogun State, Kayode Adebayo urged the public to be informed that the omission of its candidate’s name in the INEC’s list was as a result of the undue pressure mounted by the ruling party on INEC out of fear of losing the election to our party.



“We state emphatically that our candidate, Hon. Oladipupo Adebutu, who has never left the Peoples Democratic Party at any time duly registered as a member of the party within the designated period of the digital registration with his party membership card printed, verified and submitted to INEC at the stipulated time.



“While we urge the good people of Ogun not to be perturbed nor distracted from our focus of voting out the APC, we remain resolute, unfazed and unwaveringly confident that our candidate is marching straight to a decisive victory in the Ogun 2027 Governorship election.



“No amount of desperate manipulation, political witch-hunts, or calculated distractions can alter the mandate of the people of Ogun State who are overwhelmingly eager for true leadership and positive change.”

Reacting to the omission of his name from the final list of candidates, Pantami, in a statement shared on his personal social media handles, assured his supporters that efforts were underway to resolve the issue, describing the omission as a temporary challenge in the electoral process.



In the statement signed by Professor Suleiman Mohammed Gombe, he said the development has reportedly raised questions among supporters of the PDP and the Pantamiyya Movement across Gombe and beyond.

He urged supporters to remain calm and hopeful, insisting that the omission did not represent a final determination of the matter.



According to the camp, its legal and liaison teams are engaging with relevant organs of the PDP and INEC to ensure compliance with the court order and correct the omission within the period allowed by law.

Gwarzo Remains Our Candidate, Says Kano NDC Chairman

Meanwhile, the Kano State Chairman of NDC, Alhaji Hussaini Mairiga, last night dismissed any notion of a change in the party’s ticket, insisting that the structure of the ticket remained entirely intact as originally planned.

Speaking during a telephone interview, Mairiga insisted that the joint ticket of NDC’s gubernatorial candidate and his running mate, Mustapha Rabiu Kwankwaso, was duly processed, finalised, and submitted to the electoral body in strict accordance with all established electoral guidelines and statutory deadlines.



“Gwarzo’s name was submitted to INEC, and he and his running mate, Mustapha Rabiu Kwankwaso, are the authentic flag bearers of the party,” Mairiga stated emphatically, reiterating the party’s unwavering backing for their chosen candidates.

Addressing the discrepancies observed in the newly published list, the chairman attributed the development to administrative friction rather than an official rejection by the commission.



He suggested that human error or a logistical miscommunication within the broader bureaucratic process likely triggered the anomaly.

“I believe there is a mix-up somewhere, and I do not think the list is from the commission, since we are sure that the name we submitted is what stands,” Mairiga added.

World.title: Akume: 1999 North-South Power Rotation Agreement Favours Tinubu’s Re-election Bid
World.content:
*North-central endorses president as sole candidate for 2027 election

*First Lady, govs, SGF, Yilwatda defend Tinubu’s second term ambition

*Tinubu inaugurates APC Presidential Campaign Council October 14

Igbawase Ukumba in Lafia

The Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), Senator George Akume, has disclosed that the 1999 agreement between northerners and southerners to rotate power for eight years between the North and the South is in favour of the re-election of President Bola Tinubu in 2027, insisting that the North will only produce the president in 2031 when the incumbent completes his eight years.



Akume stated this yesterday in Lafia, Nasarawa State, during the endorsement of President Tinubu at a grand rally organised for the president’s re-election by the North-central zone of the All Progressives Congress (APC), under the auspices of the North-Central Grassroots Mobilisation Network.



This comes as the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu; governors of Benue, Plateau, Niger, Kogi, Kwara, and Nasarawa states; and Akume have given reasons why Tinubu deserves a second term, saying his administration has transitioned from difficult reforms to visible prosperity.



Meanwhile, President Tinubu will inaugurate the APC Presidential Campaign Council on October 14, with former Zamfara State governor Senator Abdulaziz Yari, Imo State Governor Senator Hope Uzodimma, and other party chieftains expected to play key roles.



The North-central APC rally drew governors, senators and elders from Benue, Plateau, Niger, Kogi, Kwara, Nasarawa states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).



Addressing APC supporters who intermittently chanted “Tinubu! Tinubu!”, the First Lady said the president believed in the country’s unity, security, and prosperity.

She said her address was centred on the president’s Independence Day message on October 1 titled “From Reforms to Prosperity.”



According to her, “after two years of reforming critical sectors, it is now time for benefits to reach Nigerians”.

“Mr. President is saying that they have gone reforming a lot of sectors, but now is the time for prosperity. And we can see our economy is stabilising, foreign exchange is going down, and investors are coming back to Nigeria,” she noted.



Drawing on her 12 years in the Senate, she said the current dispensation witnessed unusual infrastructure activity.

“I have been in the Senate for 12 years. This is the first time I have seen governors fixing roads and building a lot of infrastructure. And we’ve seen now in the health sector,” she stated.



She highlighted a food bank initiative providing free nutritious food for children, pregnant women, and breastfeeding mothers, as well as treatment for malnourished children. She urged students to take advantage of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND).



Describing Tinubu as bold and courageous, she charged supporters to become ambassadors.

“Tell everyone that Mr. President, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, is a leader who is very bold and not afraid to take difficult decisions. He’s a leader who can be trusted to lead us into prosperity,” she said.

“Vote for continuity, vote for capacity, vote for prosperity, vote for the reelection of Mr. President, and all the candidates of APC all the way from top to bottom,” she added.



Speaking at the rally, Akume insisted that the parties agreed to rotate power between the North and the South in 1999.

“I want us to consider one thing – that we agreed in Kaduna in 1999 to ensure that power rotates between the North and the South – eight years in the South, and eight years in the North.



“Yesterday, our father (Buhari) made his sojourn in peace. He was on the throne for eight years. Today, Asiwaju (Tinubu) is expected to serve eight years. In 2031, northerners can field over 1,000 candidates. So, anybody from the North who is running for President today is not sincere. Let’s reject him 100 per cent, and I urge you not to accept him,” Akume told APC leaders and supporters.



“You talk of education; more universities have been established, and above all, you have the NELFUND student loan scheme so that because of the circumstances of your birth, you can never be denied tertiary education,” Akume declared.



Moving the motion for Tinubu’s adoption as sole presidential candidate in 2027, the SGF said: “There are so many things that this great man, this visionary, has done. He deserves something more than that, and therefore, by the authority of this great congregation, I, Senator George Akume, former Governor of Benue State for eight years, former Senator for 12 years, former Minister for four years, and now Secretary to the Government of the Federation, do now propose that the people of the North-Central zone meeting in this great congregation have resolved that come 2027, our sole candidate for that election is His Excellency, Bola Ahmed Tinubu; there is no other candidate.”

Akume also described all the presidential candidates who had previously promised subsidy removal but made a U-turn, promising to reverse it if elected, as insincere to Nigerians.



According to him, “that is what we call policy flip-flop, policy flip-flop. The idea is to deceive you; don’t be deceived”.

Akume’s motion was seconded by the Governor of Nasarawa State, Abdullah Sule, on behalf of the governors of Kogi, Benue, Niger, Kwara, Plateau states and the people of the FCT.



Governor Sule argued that “for a man who has actually improved our oil production from less than one million to now 1. 8 million barrels per day, a man who has improved our foreign reserves from less than $20 billion to now $40 to $50 billion, for a man who has improved the capital market capitalisation of less than N80 trillion to now over N160 trillion; a man who has introduced students’ loan for education; a man who has introduced all the infrastructure that you are seeing, I second the motion that Bola Ahmed Tinubu becomes our one and only candidate for the 2027 election”.



On his part, the National Chairman of APC, Prof. Nantawe Yilwatda, also highlighted Tinubu’s major achievements in many sectors, especially the construction of roads across the North-central and several political appointments given to the region and urged the voters in the region to reciprocate that kind gesture on January 16, 2027, by voting massively for the president’s re-election.

Tinubu Inaugurates APC Presidential Campaign Council October 14

In a related development, President Tinubu will inaugurate the APC Presidential Campaign Council on October 14.

Former Zamfara State governor, Senator Yari; Imo State Governor Uzodimma; former minister Dr Edu; and other party chieftains will play key roles.



The inauguration is scheduled to take place at the Presidential Villa’s Banquet Hall in Abuja.

In a statement issued yesterday, the Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Yari, disclosed this on Friday after meeting with the President at the Presidential Villa, where he briefed State House correspondents on preparations for the forthcoming campaign.



Yari said: “The President had approved the proposed campaign timetable; activities would commence with a rally in Kaduna on October 24.”

According to the campaign schedule, the rally will be followed by engagements in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, and Maiduguri, the capital of Borno State.



Ahead of the formal inauguration, Nigeria’s First Lady, in collaboration with the Director of Women Mobilisation of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Dr Edu, and other members of the directorate, has commenced grassroots mobilisation of women across the country.



Edu and her team have set a target of mobilising 40 million women voters for the Tinubu-Shettima ticket through a strategy covering 176,846 communities and polling-unit structures across the 36 states and the FCT.

The planned inauguration will precede the October 24 rally in Kaduna, which is expected to mark the beginning of the party’s nationwide campaign activities.

World.title: Citing Policy Reforms, Stronger External Buffers, Fitch Revises Nigeria’s Outlook to Positive, Affirms ‘B’ Rating
World.content:
*Oyedele: Outlook further validates FG’s difficult but necessary reforms

Ndubuisi Francis in Abuja

Citing the federal government’s ongoing policy reforms and its increased confidence that the current momentum will not be disrupted by the general election due in early 2027, Fitch Ratings has revised the outlook for Nigeria’s Long-Term Issuer Default Ratings (IDRs) from Stable to Positive, affirming the rating at ‘B’.



The global ratings agency released its latest stance on the country at the weekend, underscoring key drivers behind its revision of Nigeria’s Outlook, including expected policy continuity; stronger external buffers; a restrictive monetary stance; reduced inflation; and higher oil production and refining capacity.



Reacting to Fitch’s positive outlook, the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele, reaffirmed the federal government’s resolve to sustain reform momentum and a disciplined, market-reflective, and transparent foreign exchange regime.
