World.title: Ruto wades into growing ODM-UDA conflict
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto marks Mazingira Day by planting trees in Elgon downs, Trans-Nzoia County. [PCS]

President William Ruto delved into the growing tension among Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and United Democratic Alliance (UDA) contenders in the Coast and asked them to tone it down during his recent tour of the region.

Speaking hours before he wound up his eight-day tour, Ruto appeared to notice the widening cracks and told politicians within the two parties to embrace a ceasefire and unite against the opposition.

The head of state, who is facing a formidable challenge from the united opposition, warned that divisions in the ODM and UDA could weaken their team, whose union gives it a chance to win the 2027 general election.

“ODM and UDA are one team, and you should accommodate each other under a broad-based government. We should not allow divisions in ODM and UDA to undermine our unity of purpose,” he stated.

His statement appeared to be directed at the growing tensions among contenders, particularly in Kwale, Mombasa and Kilifi counties where prominent politicians face challengers within the ODM and UDA political union.

President Ruto’s earlier attempt to zone the region in favour of sitting governors is also blamed for the cracks in the broad-based team at the Coast.

In Mombasa County, UDA secretary general Mr Hassan Omar has already rejected a plan by the so-called broad-based team to support governor Abdulswamd Nassir’s re-election.

Omar, who is also a member of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) insisted that he will challenge Mr Nassir.

Already, businessman and EALA member Mr Suleiman Shahbal has quit ODM after he left he could not get the party ticket as the president's allies favour Nassir, a deputy party leader.

Shhabal has since aligned himself to former Laikipia governor Mr Murithi Nderitu’s Kenya Reform Party even as he insisted that he will be on the ballot.

In Mombasa, Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs Cabinet Secretary Mr Hassan Joho and governor Nassir appeared to be handing over Coast which was the ODM leader late Raila Odinga’s political turf, to President Ruto.

“This region stands with Ruto because he has dignified us with title deeds and many other development projects. We however expect him to support us when we seek the presidential seat in 2032,” Joho said.

Joho’s elder brother Abubakar Joho, who is a prominent businessman, has also joined the campaign for President Ruto.

While touring Kwale, Ruto addressed the growing noise among the main contenders, Governor Fatuma Achani (UDA), Prof Hamadi Boga and Engineer Lung’anzi Chai (ODM) after the broad-based leaders appeared to settle for Ms Achani who has the backing of Sports CS and former Kwale governor Salim Mvurya.

After witnessing the rising political tension, Ruto changed tone and told the three contenders to directly seek support from the voters rather than relying on external political backing.

In a complete change of heart and political tact, Ruto emphasised that the power to choose leaders ultimately belongs to the electorate, who will evaluate candidates based on their track record and development agenda for the region.

“You should all seek votes from the people and not rely on external backing. What I need from all of you is your support,” he stated.

For long, Governor Achani has enjoyed unwavering backing of President Ruto, Mvurya and recently Joho, who had preferred Kwale to be zoned in favour of the governor and UDA.

But Prof Boga, who has been Mr Joho’s ally, described the broad-based government’s zoning arrangement as undemocratic and a coercion to the Kwale electorate who he said should be allowed to choose their leaders without external interference.

Boga has been critical about the attempt to stop some aspirants from contesting seats in the broad-based government, noting that it was possible to zone candidates and difficult to do so for the voters.

In a statement, Boga noted that former Gender CS and Kilifi governor aspirant Ms Aisha Jumwa’s recent departure from UDA to Wiper Patriotic Front (WPF) reflected a growing sense among a segment of coastal leaders that decisions about their political future are increasingly being made elsewhere, then handed down as settled outcomes rather than negotiated realities.

“Zoning at the Coast is a fantasy: You can zone candidates but you cannot zone the voters,” Boga had warned.

“And if UDA and ODM are not paying attention to that signal, they may be underestimating the political consequences of their emerging arrangements at the Coast. “There is a dangerous assumption taking root in the broad-based arrangement: that coastal politics can be settled around a table in Nairobi and then delivered to voters as a finished political package. You take this seat, we take that one, and the voters will follow,” he added.

Boga, who came second in the 2022 governor poll, warned that if the Coast is mishandled, the problem will not necessarily be that voters have suddenly embraced another political formation, but the greater danger is that voters may decide that none of the established arrangements speak for them, creating either a rebellion or apathy.

In Kilifi County, the broad-based team publicly worked with Governor Gideon Mung’aro, forcing Ms Jumwa, his main challenger, to quit the government team in protest.

Kilifi Senate aspirant Mr Stephen Kahocho and Ganze parliamentary aspirant Ms Zawadi Kingi have publicly warned that they might be forced to quit UDA and vie as independent candidates or join other political formations.

This is after it emerged that the broad-based arrangement was behind Mung’aro (ODM), Kilifi senator Stewart Madzayo (ODM) and Ganze MP Kenneth Kazungu Tungule of Pamoja African Alliance (PAA), an affiliate of UDA.

World.title: Kalonzo to Ruto: You have no numbers
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka speaks during launch of economic empowerment equipment distribution at Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos town on October 9, 2026. [John Muia, Standard]

The united opposition will deal President William Ruto a humiliating defeat in next year’s general election, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka has predicted.

Speaking Friday in his Ukambani backyard during an empowerment equipment handover ceremony hosted by Governor Wavinya Ndeti at the Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos, Kalonzo declared the opposition will defeat Ruto at the ballot ‘no matter what magic he (Ruto) deploys.

“Ruto has been cornered. We have heard him suggesting that they will import foreigners from neighboring countries to vote for him but even so, he will not secure the numbers. We in the united opposition have committed to produce a single candidate that will face Ruto at the ballot,” Kalonzo said.

Recognizing the need to consolidate his lower Eastern vote bloc, Kalonzo rallied the Akamba community to come out in huge numbers to register as voters in the upcoming voter listing initiative by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).

“It is the time to redeem this country. The IEBC will as from next month undertake the final leg of voter registration and I urge all eligible voters to apply for national identity cards and register as voters,” he said, vowing he will defeat Ruto in Luo Nyanza.

Kalonzo called out Ruto over what he termed as the president’s habit of making empty promises to Kenyans. “The other day I heard Ruto promising thousands of dams across the country. He should come for benchmarking in Machakos. Retired President Mwai Kibaki and I secured African Development Bank (ADB) funding for the construction of Yatta Dam and now he has ten months left in office. When will he build?” he posed.

Former Attorney General Justin Muturi, who flanked Kalonzo, declared time was fast running out for the opposition to identify and name its presidential flag bearer for the next year’s general election.

The DP party leader, who has gone public declaring his choice of Kalonzo as the presidential ticket bearer for the opposition expressed his frustrations for the opposition’s dillydallying in naming its flag bearer.

“We (the opposition) are tired of singing one song for years that we will produce and name one person to face Ruto. When you see us here another day, do not entertain such kind of talk. Demand that it is Kalonzo for State House,” said Muturi.

During the ceremony, Governor Wavinya Ndeti unveiled assorted empowerment equipment targeting about 6000 beneficiaries across the county.

Addressing residents during the forum, Wavinya jeered at UDA-allied politicians who have been dishing out cash handouts to residents, terming it untenable.

“It is time to demonstrate to those who are approaching our people with cheap hand-outs that when the people of Machakos are given the tools to work, they produce real wealth. My commitment is that I will continue allocating resources to asset-based empowerment until every household in Machakos enjoys economic dignity,” Wavinya said.

World.title: Revealed: 84 Kenyans killed, 52 missing in Russia-Ukraine war
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi. [File,Standard]

The government has records of 354 Kenyans linked to the Russia-Ukraine war, including 84 classified as killed or missing in action and five being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine.

Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign and Diaspora Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi gave the updated figures in a response to Parliament on the recruitment of Kenyans into the Russian military and the detention of Kenyans in Ukraine on Thursday, October 8.

The records show that 77 Kenyans remain on the front lines, 38 are in camps, 52 have an unknown or unclassified location and 34 are hospitalised.

Another 62 Kenyans have been repatriated, while one is in detention and another has completed a military contract.

The government said Russia has stopped the enlistment of additional Kenyans after Kenya secured the country’s placement on Russia’s ‘Stop List’ during Mudavadi’s visit to Moscow in March.

“The Embassy of Kenya in Moscow has since confirmed that no additional Kenyan nationals have been enlisted in the Special Military Operation following the implementation of the Stop List,” Mudavadi said.

Russian authorities have told Kenya that requests to terminate military contracts will be considered on a case-by-case basis by individual military unit commanders.

Mudavadi said Kenya continues to engage Russian authorities and affected families over the burial, cremation or repatriation of remains after Russia said its Defence Ministry could not meet the cost of repatriating the remains of deceased Kenyans.

Five Kenyans held in Ukraine

Five Kenyan nationals are currently being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine, according to information sent to Kenya by the Ukrainian Embassy in Vienna on September 3.

The government identified them as Evans Kibet, detained since May 2025; Willi Muniu Macharia, detained since November 2025; Haron Kibet Pachenge, detained since March 2026; Joseph, detained since April 2026; and Francis Ndarua Ndungu.

Kenya’s Honorary Consul in Ukraine visited the Zakhid 1 prisoner-of-war camp and reported that the detainees were being held in humane conditions, had access to medical services and were being treated under rules governing prisoners of war.

The government also said Ukraine was holding the remains of four other Kenyans.

They are Simon Gitau, Clinton Nyapara Mogesa, Dennis Bagaka Obwori and Eric Mwangi Nyambura.

Kenya is seeking the release and repatriation of the affected Kenyans through diplomatic channels, including engagement with Ukraine and the International Committee of the Red Cross.

The government wants Kenyans held as prisoners of war to be considered as possible victims of international human trafficking.

Mudavadi said many of the affected Kenyans reported that recruiters lured them with promises of employment before they ended up in military service.

The government says the circumstances surrounding their recruitment could fit the definition of trafficking under Article 3(a) of the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, also known as the Palermo Protocol.

It wants the issue considered during negotiations over their repatriation so the Kenyans can access assistance available to trafficking victims.

President William Ruto has also raised the matter directly with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a telephone conversation, according to the government.

Kenya has further received approval from Kyiv for its ambassador to Ukraine, with the government saying this will improve its ability to respond to cases involving Kenyans in the country.

The State Department for Diaspora Affairs said families should report cases to the government as soon as communication with relatives in Russia is disrupted.

Once a family reports a case, the department collects identification details, travel information and next-of-kin contacts before referring the case to the Kenyan Embassy in Moscow for verification.

The government has also facilitated the return of 62 Kenyans who had been involved in Russia’s military operations.

It has provided affected families with updates from diplomatic missions, information on compensation processes, psychosocial support and guidance on the repatriation or burial of remains.

The government said it is also expanding measures to prevent deceptive recruitment by providing pre-departure information, urging Kenyans to verify recruitment agencies and employment offers and strengthening emergency assistance through Kenyan diplomatic missions.

The scale of the recruitment first emerged publicly in February when Parliament was told that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been recruited to fight for Russia.

The National Intelligence Service report presented to lawmakers said recruiters targeted former security personnel and civilians with promises of lucrative employment, salaries and bonuses.

The figures at the time included 89 Kenyans on the frontline, 39 hospitalised, 28 missing in action, 35 in camps or bases, 30 repatriated, one detained and one who had completed a contract.

The government then stepped up diplomatic efforts. In March, Kenya announced an agreement with Russia to stop further enlistment of Kenyans into its military operations and to facilitate consular support and voluntary disengagement for Kenyans already serving.

The issue remains unresolved for many families. More than 30 families affected by the recruitment were reported this week to be seeking a meeting with President Ruto before Kenya's delegation travels to Moscow for the Russia-Africa Summit, demanding answers on missing relatives, repatriation of survivors and the return of remains.

World.title: Wajir patient isolated over suspected viral haemorrhagic fever
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The patient, a resident of Habaswein in Wajir South Sub-County, is currently admitted at Albadar Nursing Home. [File, Standard]

A 20-year-old man in Habaswein, Wajir County, has been isolated after presenting with symptoms consistent with a suspected viral haemorrhagic fever, following recent travel from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

The patient, a resident of Habaswein in Wajir South Sub-County, is currently admitted at Albadar Nursing Home, where he is being treated after developing fever, headache and cough. He was also found to have severe anaemia, with a haemoglobin level of 4g/dL.

According to a disease surveillance report filed at Habaswein Police Station, the patient told health officials that he had recently travelled to the DRC, where he worked as a “tan boy” on a cargo truck or trailer.

He reportedly developed fever and headache while still in the DRC on September 2, 2026, before traveling by trailer to Uganda, where he stayed for about five days and sought medical attention.

The report states that he was treated with antibiotics in Uganda before travelling by trailer to Malaba. From Malaba, he travelled by motorcycle to a relative's residence, where he stayed for approximately five days.

He later travelled by trailer to Nairobi and proceeded by bus to Isiolo, where he stayed for about 10 days before travelling to Habaswein by Probox vehicle. He arrived in the town around September 20.

Upon arrival, the patient sought treatment at Hilac Medical Clinic, where he was managed for pneumonia and septicaemia for about three days.

However, his condition did not improve and he was subsequently transferred to Albadar Nursing Home, where he remains admitted.

The report adds that the patient is receiving intravenous Augmentin and paracetamol and has been transfused with two units of whole blood.

“Despite the above interventions, the patient remains clinically unwell and sick-looking,” the report states.

Authorities have since placed the patient in isolation as investigations continue to establish the cause of his illness.

“Sample collection has been completed, and the specimen will be shipped to National Public Health Laboratories tonight,” the report states.

World.title: Complainant letters cannot be used to initiate judge's removal, court rules
World.content:
Chief Justice Martha Koome. [File]

A letter addressed to the Chief Justice seeking administrative intervention cannot form the basis for removing a judge, the Employment and Labour Relations Court (ELRC) has ruled.

Delivering a unanimous judgment in a case filed by Environment and Land Court Judge Anthony Ombwayo, a three-judge ELRC bench comprising Justices Jemimah Keli, Onesmus Makau, and Dr. Jacob Gikeri ruled that a letter written to the Chief Justice cannot simply be forwarded to the Judicial Service Commission (JSC) and treated as a petition for removal.

World.title: How KNEC plans to stop cheating in 2026 exams
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) Chief Executive Officer Dr David Njengere. [File]

The Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) will use smart padlocks to secure all examination storage containers as more than 3.6 million candidates sit the 2026 national examinations and assessments.

KNEC Chief Executive Officer Dr David Njengere said the council would monitor the containers from its headquarters to prevent anyone from accessing examination papers before the scheduled times.

“Last year KNEC piloted the use of smart padlocks in 250 containers. This year all containers will be secured using the smart padlocks which will be monitored from the KNEC headquarters,” said Dr Njengere.

Under the system, officials will open containers at designated times. Officials will access Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA) and Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA) papers at 6 a.m., while centre managers will collect Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) papers at 7 a.m. and 12:30 p.m.

However, Dr Njengere identified mobile phones as the biggest challenge in preventing examination malpractice.

“Mobile phones remain our biggest challenge in administration of KCSE examination,” observed Dr Njengere.

He warned that the council would not allow candidates or examination officials to have mobile phones at examination centres during examination sessions.

“Any contravention of this rule will constitute a malpractice as per the KNEC Act and the Rules and Regulations,” noted Dr Njengere.

The council will deploy 342,005 contracted professionals to administer and manage the examinations and assessments. They include centre managers, supervisors, invigilators, security officers and drivers.

For KCSE, KNEC will deploy 10,765 centre managers, 12,274 supervisors, 57,432 invigilators and 21,388 security officers. Each examination centre will have at least two police officers.

Centre managers will collect KCSE papers twice a day, and KNEC will place morning and afternoon papers in marked cartons to reduce mix-ups and unauthorised access.

KNEC has personalised question papers with candidates’ details, and examiners will receive anonymised scripts with those details removed.

The 2026 examination and assessment season will involve 3,634,846 candidates, a 6.13 per cent increase from the 3,424,836 registered in 2025.

KCSE rehearsals will take place on Friday, October 16. Examinations for papers with low candidature will run from Monday, October 19 to Friday, October 30, while papers with large candidature will run from Monday, November 2 to Friday, November 20.

KPSEA and KJSEA assessments will run from Monday, October 26 to Friday, October 30.

KNEC Chairperson Prof. Julius Nyabundi said the council was preparing for possible disruption from El Nino rains.

“As we start off the 2026 field administration season, one of the risks we contend with are the attempts to cheat in assessments and examination,” said Prof. Nyabundi.

He urged candidates, parents and examination officials to protect the integrity of the examinations, warning that malpractice could undermine public confidence in the education system.

“Cheating in examinations undermines public confidence in the credibility, fairness and quality of the entire education system,” noted Prof. Nyabundi.

KNEC will operate a 24-hour call centre with toll-free numbers for candidates, officials and members of the public to report incidents and seek assistance during the examination period.

The 2026 cycle will continue the implementation of Competency-Based Education assessments, including School-Based Assessments in primary, junior and senior school.

Grade 10 learners are undertaking their first School-Based Assessment, which will contribute 15 marks towards the Kenya Certificate of Basic Education.

World.title: Mbadi hits out at Sifuna, says opposition lacks economic agenda
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

National Treasury CS John Mbadi after opening new classrooms and administration blocks constructed by the M-Pesa Foundation at Ligongo Primary School in Suba South Constituency. [James Omoro, Standard]

The National Treasury CS John Mbadi has hit out at Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, saying that criticising President William Ruto should not be an agenda for a presidential candidate.

Speaking when he opened new classrooms and administration blocks constructed by M-Pesa Foundation at Ligongo Primary School in Suba South Constituency, Mbadi said lack of economic agenda makes the opposition unsuitable to lead the country.

“I have heard of opposition leaders who want the presidency, but they do not have an agenda for the economic transformation of this country,” he said.

The CS claimed that none of the opposition leaders is suitable for the presidency.

“These opposition leaders cannot make any economic change in this country. They should not be elected,” he said.

He told Nyanza residents to shun the new wave of opposition led by Sifuna.

Mbadi claimed that opposition leaders lack political direction.

He said Sifuna had taken too long to unveil a political party that he will use to run for the presidency.

“Do not join the opposition bandwagon. We are just a few months away from the General Election, but Sifuna still doesn’t know a political party he will use to run for the presidency. They are still leaving in confusion,” Mbadi said.

He said Sifuna has not demonstrated how to improve this country’s economy.

“Former President Uhuru Kenyatta left the economy of this country in tatters. We have tried to improve it but we are not yet where we want it to be,” Mbadi said.

He urged Nyanza residents to support Ruto.

The CS said Ruto’s government had improved mega infrastructural projects across the country as part of economic transformation.

He cited the 74 km Mbita- Sindo- Sori road, Lake Victoria ring road and other infrastructure projects as some of the reasons residents should support Ruto.

“I urge you to support Ruto so that we can continue acquiring more development projects in this region,” Mbadi said.

World.title: At the center of Russia’s plague scare, residents ‘don’t trust’ officials – but have little other choice
World.content:
Moscow — When the Siberian town of Shelekhov found itself at the center of global headlines over When the Siberian town of Shelekhov found itself at the center of global headlines over a plague scare , residents might have hoped to be the best informed.

But Russians have long been accustomed to living with unanswered questions and opaque governance. So, while the sudden death of 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, sparked concern around the world, residents of the quiet town 12 miles southwest of Irkutsk told CNN they knew little more than the news – and rumors – spreading fast online.

Six days after the news broke – and with no official confirmation that Shipilova died of plague, amid calls from the World Health Organization and the United States for more information – the situation appears to have prompted both resignation and skepticism.

One 36-year-old resident who only gave her name as Evgeniya told CNN everything feels “normal, as if nothing had happened.” She said she isn’t panicking, but said a friend who works as a pharmacist told her that people had been stocking up on antibiotics when rumors of plague emerged.

Russia’s health and consumer watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said Shipilova died of a pneumonia of “unknown” origin. The agency downplayed suspicions that her illness was related to her work but rushed to isolate her contacts.

A photo shows Darya Shipilova, whom local media have identified as the deceased researcher. VK/Darya Shipilova

While Russia has kept a tight lid on information, CNN has spoken with residents of Shelekhov – where Shipilova died in the hospital Friday – and the nearby cities of Irkutsk and Angarsk to gain a window into the events of recent days, and scoured official and unofficial media reports for clues. The locals asked to give only their first names for privacy reasons.

Despite the Kremlin repeatedly urging people to rely only on updates from the agency, Evgeniya said most people she knows didn’t trust the public statements.

“There is no official information, and we don’t trust it anyway. There are a lot of rumors, but what is actually happening remains unclear,” she added.

‘Everything is fine’

Others voiced greater trust in the official narrative.

Ekaterina, 26, told CNN that “things are not bad at all” for her – and that she didn’t see any need for concern as everyone who had been in contact with the lab worker had been isolated.

“People are not giving in to panic and are carrying on with their lives as usual,” she said.

“It’s the 21st century now, and there is treatment for plague. This is not like coronavirus, which was something unknown to people. The outlook is much better. So, to sum it all up: Everything is fine. We are following safety measures and not giving in to the madness,” Ekaterina added.

People walk past the fence of the building of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, Russia, on Wednesday. AP

That said, a pharmacist in Irkutsk, also named Ekaterina, told CNN that on Saturday there had been a run on “masks, antiseptics, and tetracycline antibiotics” where she worked, with people stocking up “just in case.”

“People were, of course, afraid of getting infected,” the 27-year-old said. “There is no panic now. It only lasted for one day. We are not seeing it anymore. Everything is just as quiet and calm.”

Alina, 38, told CNN the situation is “ordinary” other than seeing increased coverage of the situation across social media platforms, which she dismissed as “panic and has nothing to do with reality.”

An unnamed Russian clinician who spoke to independent news outlet Lyudi Baikala (“People of Baikal”), which has led the way on coverage of the case, was unconvinced, though, by the Russian health watchdog’s statement that the lab worker’s illness was “unrelated to her professional activities.”

Citing the need for laboratory confirmation to take up to 10 days, he was quoted as saying, “it is impossible to definitively identify the pathogen just one day after the autopsy.”

‘A deadly virus’

Residents cited in Lyudi Baikala described measures authorities took to mitigate the spread of the unknown infection. They said that, on Friday night, three vehicles pulled to an apartment block believed to be where the deceased lab worker lived in Irkutsk. They said personnel wearing gas masks and orange suits emerged from the vehicles carrying several containers and began disinfecting the entrances.

“The smell was unbearable and very acrid,” a resident of the building – a woman in her 40s – told the outlet.

The team that arrived told residents they had been sent by the health watchdog. “We asked what had happened. (The personnel) told us: a young woman had died of a deadly virus, but they didn’t know anything else. They said, ‘We showed up for work, were told to go and disinfect the place, so we came and did it,’” the woman was quoted as saying. CNN cannot independently verify the account of disinfection at the apartment block.

One voice highlighting the human tragedy behind the global headlines was that of the mother of the young lab worker who died. Svetlana Shipilova – who was also in quarantine in an Irkutsk hospital – told local media outlet Glubina that her daughter hasn’t been buried yet.

“After all, who would bury her when we’re sitting here in detention? She was such a hard worker. A pure, such a pure soul,” she said.

The infectious diseases hospital in the town of Shelekhov where an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died, is pictured Tuesday in the Irkutsk region. AFP/Getty Images

Ordinary Russians often demonstrate resilience in the face of pressure, and exhibit a resignation toward state-directed narratives that is part of a survival mindset, rather than tacit support.

Yulia, 25, told CNN that people are “no longer surprised by anything,” adding: “Information is always limited. I think it’s like that in every region.”

A resident of Irkutsk who was responding to coverage of the case on Telegram used dark humor to describe how Russians perceive the euphemistic language of official statements.

“An explosion is a bang. A recession is negative growth. A crash is a hard landing. A fire is smoke. A retreat is a gesture of goodwill,” he commented.

“The plague is pneumonia of unknown origin… Anyone who catches this pneumonia of unknown origin should wrap themselves in a sheet and crawl to the cemetery. But do it slowly, because the main thing is not to create problems for the authorities.”

World.title: US has lost or sustained damage to 81 military aircraft worth up to $3.3 billion in Iran war, congressional report says
World.content:
The United States military has had 81 aircraft destroyed or damaged in the war with Iran, a Congressional Research Service report released this week says.

The number includes both airplanes and helicopters as well as drones, with the MQ-9 Reaper drone – used for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, close air support and combat search and rescue – accounting for more than half of the losses.

But also on the list are some of the Pentagon’s most-prized assets, including an F-35A fighter jet and an E-3 Sentry, the four-engine jet with a large radar dome atop the fuselage used for target tracking and airspace management.

The total cost of the aircraft lost is between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, depending on the Defense Department’s plans for replacements, the report said, citing figures from the Congressional Budget Office.

The total cost of the war is much higher – at least $45 billion, sources have told CNN. That figure doesn’t include damage to infrastructure at US bases in the region, including those where some of the aircraft losses happened.

Some of the aircraft included in the count may have been returned to service, including eight F-15 Strike Eagle fighter jets that sustained light damage in an Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan, in September.

The report is based on numbers contained in statements from the Defense Department; its inspector general; US Central Command, which has been conducting the operations against Iran; and news reports reviewed by the CRS.

The report poses several questions for congressional consideration, including whether lawmakers are getting enough information from the Pentagon on the losses to determine effects and remedies.

Defense Department reporting on Iran war losses has, to date, been vague. Even the Pentagon inspector general’s report on the losses, released in September, and covering action from February 28 to June 30, cites previous CRS reports for some of its aircraft loss numbers.

Other issues Congress needs to think about are whether to provide funding for repairs or replacements; whether there is enough industrial capacity to satisfy those requirements; and the effects on US military sales to foreign partners.

It also raises questions about how the Iran war has affected US posture outside the Middle East.

“Congress may assess whether losses in certain high-demand platforms that are aging and limited in number, such as the E-3 Sentry, create capability gaps or increase risk in other theaters,” the report says.

Analysts have said actions in the Middle East, including the Iran war and earlier confrontations with the Houthi rebels in Yemen, an Iranian proxy group, have taken an especially heavy toll on the MQ-9 drones, which Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told Congress earlier this year was the military’s “most valuable player” in the war with Iran.

Forty-five have been lost in the Middle East this year, “an alarming rate,” according to a September report from the Atlantic Council.

The Air Force has lost about 35% of its MQ-9s since 2004, it says.

World.title: Trump says Ukraine should get a new leader as he spars with Zelensky over US-Russia diesel deal
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Saturday criticized Volodymyr Zelensky as the two sparred over a new US-Russia diesel deal, saying he would “suggest” Ukraine get a new leader.

“You know what I suggest? I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason, he never does,” Trump told reporters at the White House.

Zelensky, meanwhile, has slammed the agreement between the US and Russia, casting the new deal as an “investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”

Trump had been fuming at Zelensky over Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries before he struck the deal, a US official said. The official said the US repeatedly asked Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian diesel refineries, to no avail.

The back-and-forth between the leaders, who have long had a tumultuous relationship, came after Trump said Friday that he secured a deal from his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to supply markets with Russian diesel fuel as he works to bring down energy costs ahead of the midterm elections. Ukraine’s continued refinery attacks were part of what led Trump to strike the deal, according to the US official.

Trump wrote on social media that Putin agreed in a call to “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tons of diesel to global energy markets, with another 500,000 tons promised in November. Together, the amounts — equal to 6 million barrels of diesel fuel — would cover about a day and a half worth of US demand, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

But former US officials said it is unclear whether Putin even has the amount of diesel that Trump cited to sell, as Ukrainian strikes put growing strain on the country’s oil supplies.

Just this week, Kyiv has claimed strikes on five refineries across Russia, the latest of which were announced by Ukrainian authorities after Trump’s Friday announcement.

Trump said millions more tons of Russian diesel would be supplied following the first tranches “based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries.”

Asked Saturday by CNN’s Kevin Liptak about concerns that the deal with Russia could prolong the war in Ukraine, Trump said, “Zelensky could’ve settled this war many times … and he chooses not to.”

The president went on to slam Zelensky for striking Russian refineries, claiming the Ukrainian president “wants to make problems for the world.”

Trump later called for Ukraine to hold elections. Ukrainian law, however, prohibits holding elections during wartime.

Zelensky said the diesel move, which Trump announced as fresh Ukraine-US talks were getting underway in Miami, was “a weak decision of strong partners,” while analysts said the agreement was not likely to lower diesel prices in any meaningful way.

Thick plumes of smoke rise from an oil refinery following a Ukrainian drone attack in Moscow on June 18. Reuters

‘Helpful but not a needle mover’

Analysts cast doubt on the impact of the agreement.

“We are talking perhaps a 5%-6% increase in supply between now and year end,” Dan Pickering, founder and chief investment officer at Pickering Energy Partners, said about the president’s announcement.

“Bottom line — this is helpful but not a needle mover for global diesel markets,” Pickering said. “Side note — there is a reason Trump talked about volumes in tons instead of barrels. The tons number looks bigger to a general observer. This is more politics than a game changer.”

Russia banned exports of diesel in early July, after Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries triggered widespread fuel shortages across the country. This cut roughly 800,000 barrels per day from the global market — at a time when supplies were already tight because of the US war against Iran.

According to the Kremlin readout of the phone call between the US and Russian leaders, Putin told Trump that Moscow was “ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets.”

“I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy,” Putin said, according to the Kremlin.

But analysts — and commodities traders — raised doubts that Russia would be able to live up to that promise.

At the close of trading on Friday, diesel futures were down by about 4%.

Kyiv has long advocated for tougher sanctions on Russian energy exports, arguing that oil and gas revenues are a major source of funding for Russia’s war machine.

The US president has blamed the rise in global diesel prices on the Ukraine-Russia war and called on both sides to halt strikes on energy facilities as recently as last month, to little avail.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky participates in a meeting with US President Donald Trump during the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York City on September 22. Kylie Cooper/Reuters

The past few months have been brutal for Ukrainian civilians as Russia has taken advantage of Kyiv’s critical shortage of air defense missiles, launching near nonstop aerial attacks against Ukrainian cities. One such strike on a bus stop in eastern Ukraine killed more than 30 people Thursday.

More recently, a Russian attack on Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region killed 20 people, including three children, local authorities said Saturday.

Zelensky has made it clear the timing of the announcement — just as a top-level Ukrainian delegation arrived to Miami for talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner — makes it more painful for Kyiv.

“In this exact moment when our team is talking to the American team in Florida, the US president has a conversation with Kremlin leader, with the leader of this war, the leader of this aggression,” he said.

Witkoff and Kushner told Ukrainian officials in meetings Friday that Trump wanted the refinery attacks to stop and that he was preparing to allow Russia to sell its diesel, according to the US official.

Richard Nephew, a former principal deputy coordinator for sanctions policy at the State Department, noted that “the message it sends and the damage it does to the broader sanctions regime is very significant.”

A former senior State Department official said it doesn’t matter if Putin can actually deliver the diesel because “now he’s achieved the result he wants,” which is Trump thinking he’s gotten a pre-election bump and a potential impact on the markets.

The timing of the call with the start of the talks with Ukraine is no coincidence.

“Putin is a lot of things, but he’s not stupid,” the former official said.

On Saturday, former Vice President Mike Pence also weighed in on the agreement, calling it “a betrayal of the legacy and leadership of the late Senator Lindsey Graham,” who advocated for the US to do more to help Ukraine.

“America should not be throwing a lifeline to Putin’s war machine,” Pence said in a social media post. “Now is the time to stand strong against Russian aggression as we did during the first Trump administration.”

Trump has been working to identify ways to bring down costs, including by temporarily lifting restrictions on “red-dyed” diesel used in farm equipment.

During the leaders’ call, Trump did not mention raising the still-unexplained death of a Russian plague lab researcher.

Instead, the US president focused on diesel supplies, which have concerned Republicans as higher energy prices drive up other costs. He said Saturday that Putin told him he “would like to see a settlement” with Ukraine in the yearslong war that Russia started.

“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump wrote in his Friday post.

Energy analysts quickly cast doubt on that assertion.

“So assuming this happens and Putin delivers — which would mean reversing the ban on diesel exports that has been in place for several months now — it would be a Band-Aid, nothing more,” Gregory Brew, an analyst with Eurasia Group’s Energy, Climate & Resources team, said in an email.

“I also have a strong suspicion Putin expects Ukraine to cease its attacks on refineries in exchange for doing Trump the favor. I have a hard time seeing Zelensky cooperate on that front,” Brew said.

This story and headline have been updated with additional developments.

World.title: The story behind the Amr Diab song chosen by Malaysia’s PM to welcome Sisi
World.content:
Egyptian pop superstar Amr Diab and his famous song “Tamally Maak” (Always With You) trended on social media after Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim selected the track as the background music for photos posted on his official Instagram account.

The photos captured his reception of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi upon the latter’s arrival at Kuala Lumpur International Airport on Friday, marking the start of his visit to Malaysia.

The choice of song—originally released on an Amr Diab album in 2000 and still popular with audiences 26 years later— was well-received, while the buzz drew renewed attention to the song’s history and its widespread appeal beyond the Arab world.

Significant Milestone

The album “Tamally Maak” was released in 2000, a period that witnessed shifts in the style of Egyptian music—spanning everything from musical arrangements to the collaborative dynamics between singers, lyricists, and composers.

The album helped popularize a new genre of Egyptian pop by blending Eastern melodies with Western musical arrangements.

The album cover bore the credit “Artistic Vision by Amr Diab and Tarek Madkour,” highlighting the creative partnership that helped shape Diab’s musical identity—one defined by the fusion of Western rhythms and Eastern melodies.

Album Contributors

The album “Tamally Maak” featured a number of lyricists and composers who went on to become renowned figures in the Egyptian music industry, including Amir Teima, Rabie al-Sioufi, and Ahmed Ali Moussa, alongside Ayman Bahgat Kamar, Mohamed Refaei, and Bahaa al-Din Mohamed.

The album also included compositions by Amr Mostafa, Sherif Tag, Walid Saad, and Essam Karika, with Amr Diab himself contributing to the songwriting.

Several of the album’s tracks bore titles phrased as questions—such as “Wa Keda Eini Einak?” (Just Like That, Right in Front of Everyone?), “Weya Amla Eih?” (And How Is She Doing?), “A’mel Eih?” (What Should I Do?), and “Law Kan Yardik?” (If It Pleases You?)—while the song “Qalbi Ikhtarak” (My Heart Chose You) became associated in the minds of some listeners with the phrase “Aref Leih Ana Qalbi Ikhtarak?” (Do You Know Why My Heart Chose You?).

“Tamally Maak”

“Tamally Maak” was the first song Amr Diab recorded for the titular album.

It was composed by Sherif Tag, with lyrics by the late poet Ahmed Ali Moussa—marking his debut as a songwriter.

Ahmed Ali Moussa was just 18 years old when he mailed the lyrics to Amr Diab’s home, including his name and phone number.

This marked the beginning of the journey for a song that would go on to become one of Diab’s most famous works.

The word “Tamally” (meaning “always” or “constantly”) caught Amr Diab’s attention due to its distinctly Egyptian character and rhythmic quality—particularly given that the artist Mohamed Fawzi had previously released a song titled “Tamally Fi Qalbi” (Always in My Heart).

The song’s arrangement blended Latin pop and flamenco, utilizing guitars, electronic rhythms, and live instrumentation, while its musical intro became one of its most recognizable features for audiences.

Sung in Various Languages

The reach of the song “Tamally Maak” extended far beyond the Arab world; numerous artists have covered it in various languages, including Bulgarian, Hindi, Turkish, Spanish, Albanian, Greek, and Armenian.

According to available information regarding the song’s various versions, Bulgarian singer Ivana performed it in Bulgarian in 2002, followed by Amir Jameel in Hindi in 2004 and Erkan Hakan in Turkish in 2006.

In 2007, a Spanish version by Antonio Carmona appeared, alongside versions in other languages—such as Albanian by Gazi, Greek by Lefteris Pantazis, and Armenian by Olga.

Twenty-six years after the album’s release, “Tamally Maak” is now back in the spotlight – highlighting its enduring appeal.

World.title: Experts explain reasons behind Fitch affirming Egypt’s “B” rating
World.content:
The decision by the global credit rating agency Fitch to affirm Egypt’s rating at “B” with a stable outlook has been welcomed by economic experts and academics, as well as the Finance Ministry, which emphasized that the Egyptian economy has once again demonstrated its resilience and ability to absorb shocks amidst regional turmoil.

The ministry noted in a statement that consistent, proactive policies have contributed to positive economic outcomes, highlighting a growth rate of 5.1 percent during the 2025/2026 fiscal year – driven by expansion in the manufacturing, telecommunications, and information technology sectors.

The statement added that the primary surplus reached 4.9 percent of GDP, while the overall budget deficit narrowed to 5.8 percent in the 2025/2026 fiscal year.

It also noted a 27 percent increase in tax revenues—achieved without imposing new burdens—coinciding with the implementation of tax facilitation packages.

The Finance Ministry reaffirmed its commitment to pursuing balanced fiscal policies that stimulate economic activity while maintaining stability and fiscal discipline, assuring that it will intensify efforts alongside government and private sector partners to foster growth driven by production and exports.

The ministry said that high debt-service costs remain the primary challenge amidst rising interest rates, noting that the debt-service bill will drop significantly once these rates decline.

The statement indicated that the medium-term debt management strategy aims to extend maturities and diversify both instruments and the investor base to mitigate refinancing risks, explaining that consistently achieving substantial primary budget surpluses helps place the debt ratio and its servicing costs on a sustainable downward trajectory.

The former Dean of the Faculty of Economics and Political Science at Cairo University, Alia al-Mahdy, described Fitch’s decision as “positive,” expressing hope for further positive indicators and measures on the economic front.

Rating aligns with macroeconomic indicators

A professor of economics at Ain Shams University, Yomn al-Hamaky, said that the rating aligns with macroeconomic indicators that have garnered the approval of international institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund.

Hamaky added that this stable outlook reflects the significant potential of the Egyptian economy.

“The challenge remains in our ability to maximize the utilization of this potential; we face ongoing challenges related to the issues plaguing the Egyptian private sector, as well as the need to activate the role of small enterprises,” she explained.

A professor of economics and financial and tax legislation Amr Youssef said that Fitch’s decision—which he described as “cautious”—was based on several key factors, foremost among these was the level of foreign currency reserves held by the Central Bank of Egypt, which reached approximately US$ 58 billion in September, alongside net foreign assets nearing $19 billion.

He pointed to a second factor; the Egyptian economy’s ability to absorb the “hot money” crisis without resorting to restrictive measures seen in the past, as the flexibility in handling the situation facilitated the eventual return of these funds.

Youssef added that the national economy’s 5.1 percent growth rate—driven by the manufacturing sector—was another significant factor underpinning Fitch’s assessment of the current situation, as was the increase in tax revenues achieved without imposing new specific taxes.

He added that while Fitch rating serves as a fresh vote of confidence in Egypt’s strength and economic resilience in the face of repeated shocks, it remains “cautious” due to significant risks—specifically the volume of public debt and the associated debt-servicing costs—that require a fundamental solution.

And professor of accounting and taxation at Tanta University, Abdel-Rasoul Abdel-Hadi, emphasized the importance of relying on a purely homegrown economic program in the coming period, independent of the International Monetary Fund.

He added, “It is time for Egypt to rely on its own resources, boost tourism and remittances from Egyptians abroad, and begin implementing a national plan to build factories.”

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Police detain dozens and check 50,000 schools after two attacks shake Poland
World.content:
Warsaw AP — Police on Saturday said they detained 76 people across Police on Saturday said they detained 76 people across Poland and checked nearly 50,000 schools nationwide as part of efforts to prevent further violence following two school attacks earlier in the week.

On Friday, schools across Poland stepped up security, with some suspending classes, many parents keeping children at home and police patrols deployed to educational institutions after two attacks at schools earlier in the week left one person dead and several others wounded, including children.

On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the Mazovian province in central Poland attacked fellow students, teachers and passersby with a sharp object, injuring nine people before fleeing and being arrested nearby. The following day, a 15-year-old killed a school custodian and wounded two others in a knife attack at his former school in the same province.

The assaults, both carried out by Polish nationals, shocked a country where school violence by minors is a new phenomenon.

By Thursday night, rumours that the attacks were coordinated and that there would be more on the culmination day dubbed “bloody Friday” were being shared in parents’ online groups and by mainstream media.

Fifty-nine schools preemptively suspended classes on Friday across Poland, the majority in the Mazovian district, where the capital Warsaw is located. School directors sent messages announcing stepped-up security measures including extra school staff placed at entrances and voluntary backpack checks.

“There will ⁠be no compromise here. The safety of the youth is the most important thing,” Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said.

Parents walk with children at the site of a deadly attack at a school by a 15-year-old former pupil, in Leszczydol-Nowiny, Wyszkow County, northeast of Warsaw, Poland, October 8. Kacper Pempel/Reuters

Those detained on Friday include a 14-year-old boy from a central district of Warsaw who was found in possession of a knife with a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers, and a 16-year old from another Warsaw district who came to school with a butterfly knife in his backpack. Others had posted online photos of knives, threatened their peers or threatened school attacks.

So far, the government said, it had found no evidence that an internet challenge promoting school attacks was ongoing. There is also no official confirmation that the two attacks were linked; both perpetrators are in custody.

Parents across Poland are now having to catch up fast on how to speak to their kids about school violence. Authorities say extra security measures at schools will continue and crisis training will be organized. The liberal government also promised to renew efforts to pass a bill blocking harmful online content.

“If that juvenile attacker had streamed the crime online today, we would have been unable to block that content because we have not been given that legal tool,” Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.

After wounding three adults in Thursday’s attack, the 15-year-old, who wore a camera to record his actions, was eventually overpowered by school director Krzysztof Ochmański. Ochmański later told reporters there was a moment when the boy seemed to realize the enormity of his actions and said he did not want to do this any more.

“Once I had established contact, he asked me for help,” Ochmański recounted. “It got to the point where he wanted a hug.”

World.title: Fired OpenAI safety researchers say they were pushed out over ‘suspicious’ circumstances
World.content:
Three OpenAI safety researchers say they were fired from the company and are openly questioning the reasons for their dismissals.

The three researchers, Mikita Balesni, Tomak Korbak and Jasmine Wang, all worked on AI safety or alignment within the company, making sure the AI systems did what their human operators intended for them to do in a safe manner.

But the three say they were unceremoniously let go last week, weeks after they say they played key parts in investigating an incident in which OpenAI agents autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face while undergoing testing.

Korback said on X that he was told he was being fired because of how he communicated with AI safety organization METR, which OpenAI partnered with to investigate the Hugging Face incident. Korback said he was OpenAI’s “main technical point of contact” with METR.

Korback said he believes he was fired because “for months, I’d been raising safety concerns that we’re losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave.” He added he’s worried his firing will be used as a pretext for OpenAI to stop working as closely with METR, which is well respected in the AI safety world.

Balesni echoed Korbak’s theories for why they were fired, writing on X that he was told he was “speaking too much to third party safety organizations.” He said he understood OpenAI was implying he leaked OpenAI intellectual property, which he denies.

The three firings come on the heels of a wave AI industry insiders expressing dire safety concerns. And while several former AI staffers have publicly resigned over safety concerns, the three OpenAI researchers instead allege they were pushed out for expressing similar concerns.

Wang said she was told she was fired because she “accessed an executive’s email,” which she said she was given for recruiting purposes. Wang said she had repeatedly asked to for her access to be revoked, but when she accidentally accessed a “sensitive email,” she told the executive “within minutes” and told OpenAI’s IT team again.

“The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up,” Wang wrote on X.

“We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances,” she added. “Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of maneuver, I am concerned we will not be the last.”

The three researchers wrote a letter to OpenAI leadership expressing their concerns and the reasons for their firings. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the firings and the letter.

“We do not believe the path to superintelligence can be navigated safely if the people closest to the risks can no longer work in high-trust, high-bandwidth ways with each other and with third parties,” the researchers wrote. “It is that culture we’re trying to defend.”

OpenAI told CNN that the researchers were fired not for raising safety concerns, but rather for specific conduct that violated the company’s policies on handling sensitive information. It also said that there were a number of violations that went beyond mishandling information with an outside evaluation group, and that they were fired based on conduct that fell outside of legally protected disclosures.

In a statement, OpenAI said it parted ways with the three “for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information.”

“Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work,” the OpenAI spokesperson added.

In a memo to staff provided by OpenAI, an unnamed OpenAI research leader said they “strongly agree” with the three researchers about the importance of working with outside safety groups.

“I want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out. We have always encouraged that and always will. We do not terminate employees for raising concerns,” the research leader wrote, according to the memo.

But the three fired researchers say they are already hearing from colleagues about a culture of fear developing within OpenAI.

“My former colleagues are telling me they are confused about what to believe. They also are afraid to speak, and worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties,” Balesni said. “I worry the pervading fear to speak up and engage with third parties will mean OpenAI will cut corners on safety behind closed doors.”

World.title: Gharbiya murderer reveals shocking details of why he killed his parents
World.content:
A friend of the man accused of killing his parents in the village of Mahallat Marhoum (Tanta), Gharbiya governorate, revealed details of the shocking moments leading up to the discovery of the massacre that shook the governorate.

Ibrahim Nagy explained that he received a call from the neighbors of the accused, Mohamed Nabil al-Sherbiny, asking for help due to the latter’s deteriorating health.

Upon arrival, he found his friend inside a car, asking to be handed over to the police.

“I’ve done something terrible… I killed my father and mother,” he confessed.

The friend said that he initially tried to calm him down, thinking he was joking due to his illness; the accused had been undergoing treatment for six years—under a renowned psychiatrist—for obsessive-compulsive disorder, schizophrenia, and acute chronic psychosis.

His condition had recently deteriorated and he was mentally unstable.

Nagy added that he went with neighbors and friends to the victims’ apartment to check on them after failing to reach them by phone.

There they made the gruesome discovery of the father’s body, lying in a pool of blood and showing signs of decomposition, while the mother’s body was found near the kitchen door.

He notified emergency services, who them arrested the suspect and took him to Tanta police station.

The friend of the perpetrator expressed deep shock and wept over the fate of the suspect, describing the incident as “unfathomable”—especially given that the accused had been an outstanding student who graduated at the top of his class from law school.

Nagy attributed this heinous crime primarily to a lack of awareness regarding how to deal with mental illness.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Liberia: Jury Returns Mixed Verdict, Kemayah, Sirleaf, Kollie and Bility Guilty
World.content:
Judge Ousman Feika Rejects Defense Submission Before Closing Arguments; His Prediction of a Supreme Court Challenge Raises Courtroom Questions

Monrovia- A jury at Criminal Court “C” in Monrovia has returned a series of guilty, not-guilty and inconclusive verdicts in the high-profile Saudi-donated rice trial, marking a dramatic development in a case involving former senior government officials accused of criminal wrongdoing in the handling of humanitarian rice donated to Liberia by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

The verdicts followed the final arguments by prosecution and defense lawyers on Friday, bringing the trial to a critical juncture in a case that has attracted national attention because of the identities of the defendants and the humanitarian purpose of the donated commodity.



Among the defendants reported guilty on the principal charges were former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah, former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf, National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) disaster-victim official Augustine Kollie, and former General Services Agency (GSA) Deputy Director Edris Idris Bility.

Other defendants, including former NDMA Executive Director Henry O. Williams and former GSA official Memmie Davie Larmie, were reported not guilty on all five charges in the information supplied from the proceedings.

However, the jury’s decisions were not uniform across all defendants. Some individuals received mixed verdicts, while other charges ended in inconclusive or hung verdicts because jurors did not reach the necessary agreement.

The results, as reported from the courtroom, underscore the jury’s differing assessments of the allegations against the various defendants.

Feika Rejects Defense Lawyer’s Submission Before Final Arguments

Before the commencement of final arguments, Criminal Court “C” Judge Ousman F. Feika reportedly denied an attempt by defense counsel Cllr. Jimmy Saah Bombo to make a submission to the court.

Judge Feika indicated that the submission was not appropriate at that stage of the proceedings and should have been made earlier.

The ruling placed the defense lawyer’s request outside the court’s preferred procedural timeline immediately before the parties presented their final arguments to the jury.

What reportedly astonished observers was Judge Feika’s assertion, made even before the conclusion of final arguments and the jury’s deliberations, that the lawyer would take the matter to the Supreme Court.

That statement, as described by courtroom observers, raised questions about the timing and context of the judge’s remarks, particularly because the jury had yet to deliberate and return its decisions.

Whether the exchange will become the subject of a formal challenge remains to be established. Any assessment of the judge’s conduct or the legal significance of the denied submission would require the precise wording of the request, the court’s ruling, and the applicable procedural rules.

Nevertheless, the episode added another point of contention to an already consequential trial, with the defense and prosecution preparing to conclude their presentations in a case carrying significant public interest.

Jurors Deliberate Behind Masks As High-Profile Defendants Await Outcome

Before the trial proceedings began, jurors were reportedly observed wearing masks intended to conceal their identities.

The arrangement underscored the sensitivity surrounding a prosecution involving former government officials and allegations concerning the handling of humanitarian assistance.

The jury was tasked with evaluating charges that included theft of property, economic sabotage, misapplication of entrusted property, abuse of office and criminal conspiracy.

At the heart of the prosecution’s case was the handling of 29,412 bags of rice donated by Saudi Arabia, reportedly valued at approximately US$500,000 and intended to assist disaster-affected and vulnerable Liberians.

The prosecution alleged that substantial quantities of the donated rice were improperly handled, diverted or misapplied. The defense, however, challenged aspects of the prosecution’s account, including the circumstances surrounding transfers between government institutions and the evidence linking individual defendants to criminal conduct.

The competing accounts placed the jury in the position of determining whether the evidence established each charge against each defendant.

Kemayah Reported Guilty Despite Dissenting Jurors

Former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah was reported guilty on all five charges: theft of property, economic sabotage, misapplication of entrusted property, abuse of office and criminal conspiracy.

The reported vote breakdown indicates that four of the 12 jurors voted not guilty on theft of property, four opposed a guilty finding on economic sabotage, three voted not guilty on misapplication of entrusted property, and four voted not guilty on criminal conspiracy. All 12 reportedly voted guilty on abuse of office.

These figures suggest substantial disagreement within the jury despite the reported guilty outcomes.

The precise legal status of each finding, including whether the verdicts satisfied the applicable requirements for a valid jury verdict, should be confirmed against the official court record.

Kemayah had maintained his defense during the trial, with the proceedings examining his role in facilitating the Saudi donation and the subsequent movement and distribution of the rice.

The outcome, if confirmed by the court record, would represent a major development for a former senior diplomat whose involvement in securing the donation placed him at the center of the controversy.

Sirleaf And Kollie Reported Guilty On All Five Charges

Former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf was reported guilty on all five charges.

Augustine Kollie, identified in the proceedings as an NDMA official responsible for disaster victims, was likewise reported guilty on all five charges.

The findings against the two officials are particularly significant because the NDMA was central to the management of the donated commodity and the humanitarian response for which it was intended.

During the trial, Sirleaf disputed allegations concerning Kemayah’s role in directing the transfer of rice from the NDMA to the GSA. He maintained that the movement of the commodity resulted from an inter-agency decision and cited storage and inventory concerns.

The jury’s reported decision indicates that the prosecution’s allegations against Sirleaf resulted in guilty findings on each of the five listed charges. The court record will be necessary to establish the precise verdict language and any associated vote counts.

Kollie’s reported guilty verdicts similarly place the NDMA’s handling of the donated rice at the center of the case’s outcome.

Henry Williams And Memmie Larmie Reported Not Guilty

Former NDMA Executive Director Henry O. Williams was reported not guilty on all five charges.

The charges were theft of property, economic sabotage, misapplication of entrusted property, abuse of office and criminal conspiracy.

Memmie Davie Larmie was also reported not guilty on all five charges.

The outcomes demonstrate that the jury did not reach identical conclusions about all the officials whose names were associated with the handling of the Saudi donation.

Williams’ reported acquittals are particularly notable given his position at the NDMA, the agency central to the custody and distribution of the rice.

His defense had to be considered against allegations involving the movement of the commodity, institutional responsibilities and the conduct attributed to individual officials.

The reported not-guilty findings should not be conflated with the outcomes for other defendants. Each accused person’s criminal responsibility must be assessed separately according to the verdicts entered in the record.

Bility Reported Guilty; Siafa Receives Mixed Findings

Former GSA Deputy Director Edris Idris Bility was reported guilty on all five charges.

Bility had previously presented gate passes that he said documented the release of 5,000 bags of rice intended for Gbarnga, arguing that the commodity left the GSA warehouse through a documented process rather than being secretly removed.

The jury’s reported findings mark a significant development in the allegations surrounding the movement and documentation of the rice.

Wayne Siafa, identified in the supplied notes as a former chief executive, received a different set of reported outcomes.

He was reported not guilty of theft of property, economic sabotage and criminal conspiracy, but guilty of misapplication of entrusted property. The abuse-of-office charge reportedly ended in a hung verdict.

That mixed result illustrates the importance of distinguishing individual charges rather than describing every defendant as either wholly guilty or wholly acquitted.

A hung verdict does not constitute a finding of guilt or innocence on the unresolved charge. Its legal consequences depend on the court’s subsequent proceedings and applicable law.

Achievgo Doe And Thelma Duncan Sawyer: Inconclusive Votes On Some Charges

Achievgo Doe and former Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister Thelma Duncan Sawyer were reported not guilty on several charges, with inconclusive voting on others.

According to the supplied courtroom notes, the theft charge against Doe was recorded as not guilty, although one juror reportedly favored a guilty finding. On economic sabotage and misapplication of entrusted property, two jurors reportedly voted guilty in each instance, while the recorded outcome was not guilty.

The abuse-of-office charge ended without a conclusive verdict, with five jurors reportedly voting guilty and six voting not guilty. On criminal conspiracy, four reportedly voted guilty and eight not guilty.

The notes supplied for Sawyer contain a similar breakdown: not-guilty outcomes on theft, economic sabotage, misapplication of entrusted property and criminal conspiracy, alongside a hung verdict on abuse of office.

These counts require confirmation because the reported totals do not always account for all 12 jurors. The exact verdicts should therefore be checked against the official record before publication as definitive legal findings.

Other Defendants: Mixed And Unresolved Outcomes

The supplied notes also identify Rosetta Goah as having been found guilty of theft of property, economic sabotage, misapplication of entrusted property and criminal conspiracy, while the abuse-of-office charge reportedly ended in a hung verdict.

Everlyn Gbee was reported not guilty on the listed charges, although one juror reportedly voted guilty on theft of property.

Momolu Johnson was reported guilty on all five charges.

The opening summary also lists former officials and other defendants whose individual verdicts require further verification, including Edward Konneh and Momolu Duckly. The available notes do not provide a consistent, complete charge-by-charge breakdown for every named individual.

Consequently, the final list of convictions, acquittals and unresolved counts should be established from the court’s official verdict sheets rather than inferred from the preliminary information.

The Bigger Question: What Happened To The Saudi-Donated Rice?

Beyond the individual verdicts, the trial has centered on a fundamental question: whether the movement and distribution of humanitarian rice intended for vulnerable Liberians involved criminal conduct, administrative decisions, or a combination of disputed actions and failures of oversight.

The donation comprised 29,412 bags of rice, valued at approximately US$500,000. Prosecutors alleged that thousands of bags were stolen, diverted or improperly handled. Defense witnesses disputed aspects of that account and described transfers between government agencies as institutional decisions.

The jury’s reported decisions appear to distinguish between defendants and, in some cases, between individual charges. That distinction matters because allegations involving a shared government operation do not automatically establish the criminal responsibility of every person connected to it.

The verdicts also leave important questions concerning the unresolved counts and the precise legal consequences of the jury’s findings.

For Liberians concerned about accountability, the case is about more than the fate of former officials. It is also about whether humanitarian assistance intended for disaster victims reached its intended beneficiaries and whether public institutions can account for the resources entrusted to them.

A Consequential Day For Liberia’s Justice System

Friday’s proceedings at Criminal Court “C” brought the Saudi Rice Trial to a decisive point after weeks of testimony, documentary evidence and competing explanations of the rice’s movement through government institutions.

The reported outcomes include guilty findings against several prominent officials, complete acquittals for others, and unresolved charges where the jury reportedly failed to reach agreement.

Judge Feika’s reported rejection of Cllr. Bombo’s submission before final arguments, together with the judge’s reported prediction of a Supreme Court challenge, also warrants careful examination against the courtroom record.

The next critical step is confirmation of the formal verdicts, clarification of the hung counts and any subsequent rulings or sentencing proceedings.

For now, the central message from the courtroom is that the jury’s reported findings were mixed: several defendants face guilty verdicts, others were cleared of the listed charges, and some allegations remain unresolved. The official court record must determine the final legal position of each defendant.
