World.title: Say cheese: A guide to 5 iconic Mexican quesos and the regions that produce them
World.content:
In Mexico, an endless debate spills across social media and enlists everyone from linguists and historians to cooks and passionate eaters: What belongs in a quesadilla? While cheese is an optional topping for many Mexican dishes — from tacos and tortas to chilaquiles and sopes — there is one contentious item that, depending on who you ask, is non-negotiable.

Now, we are not here to solve the great quesadilla debate, but unveiling the passion behind it shows just how central cheese is to Mexican gastronomy. From north to south, every region has crafted its own variety of queso tailored to its local heritage. Here are five of Mexico’s most iconic cheeses:

Queso Oaxaca (or quesillo)

The cheese at the very heart of the debate — and a cornerstone of Mexican street food — is queso Oaxaca, locally known as quesillo. It is celebrated for its soft, buttery texture and its exceptional meltability over high heat, whether tucked into a sope, folded inside a quesadilla or pressed into a torta.

What differentiates quesillo from other cheeses is its distinct curdling method: It is hand-stretched into long, milky strands and wound into a ribboned ball. Achieving this pliable texture relies on warm preparation techniques that keep the cheese flexible enough to stretch and interlace without breaking.

Quesillo is indispensable in Mexican households as it can turn a simple tortilla (corn or flour) into a quick homemade quesadilla for dinner, transform refried beans and bread into crispy, freshly baked molletes, or serve as a quick, savory snack eaten straight from the fridge.

Originally from: Oaxaca

Queso de cincho

Loosely translated as “cinch cheese,” queso de cincho originates in the central state of Morelos and the southwestern state of Guerrero. Its name refers to the rigid mold used during pressing, which is bound tightly with woven ixtle palm fibers (the same durable rope material used in traditional horse tack and saddlery).

Also known as queso prensado estilo Guerrero, this firm, aged cheese carries a strong aroma and is typically rubbed with a paste of dried guajillo chiles. While frequently crumbled over enchiladas or chilaquiles, one of its most traditional preparations is simmered directly in salsa as a guisado. Thanks to its dense consistency and high protein content, it serves as a substantial centerpiece. Better yet, its low moisture content allows it to age naturally at room temperature for up to a year without spoiling.

Originally from: Guerrero and Morelos

Queso asadero

Just like quesillo, queso asadero is popular due to its creamy, melty texture and the gastronomic possibilities it offers. This type of cheese has similar uses to queso Oaxaca; it can be used in quesadillas, and it is common at northern cookouts, paired with a great steak. If you’ve been to one of those, the name “asadero” might sound familiar — it comes from the word asado (grilled), a clue on how to enjoy this cheese.

Originally from: Chihuahua

Queso fresco

View this post on Instagram A post shared by 𝑪𝒂𝒔𝒂𝒏𝒅𝒓𝒂 𝑺𝒂𝒍𝒊𝒏𝒂𝒔 🤠🌵 (@yo_soy_casandra)

Queso fresco is a crumbly, soft cheese that is high in moisture and protein. Due to its short aging process (which is where the name fresco — or fresh — comes from), it is difficult to keep for long periods. It must always be kept refrigerated and consumed within approximately two weeks.

Regarding its preparation and curdling, queso fresco is quite versatile, as it can be made with cow’s milk, goat’s milk or a blend of both. In contrast to meltable cheeses, queso fresco does not work as a quesadilla filling, but it is the perfect topping for side dishes, whether sprinkled over a salad, street corn or refried beans.

Originally from: Chihuahua

Queso Menonita

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ¡ah Chihuahua! (@ahchihuahua)

Last but not least is Mennonite cheese, a famous variety that also comes from the northern region of the country. As its name reveals, it originates from a specific community: the Mennonites. Groups of Mennonite immigrants arrived in Mexico during the 1920s, and their cattle-ranching techniques thrived in the north.

Mennonite communities settled mainly in the drylands of Chihuahua and relied on dairy products, especially cheese, for sustenance. Nowadays — although the name remains — this smooth, buttery cheese is no longer exclusively made by Mennonite communities. You can find it melting inside chiles rellenos, on Mennonite-style pizzas or in choriqueso (a dish of melted cheese combined with seasoned chorizo).

Originally from: Chihuahua

Cheese has been a companion to Mexican cuisine for centuries. One key to understanding its strong northern presence is the geographic distribution of agriculture and livestock in Mexico. As you travel from south to north, the climate becomes drier, making the land better suited for cattle ranching than crop cultivation.

It is no surprise, then, that cheese became a fundamental pillar of northern Mexico’s economy and gastronomy.

After all, what would a northern carne asada be without quesadillas (con queso)?

Lydia Leija is a linguist, journalist and visual storyteller. She has directed three feature films, and her audiovisual work has been featured in national and international media. She’s been part of National Geographic, Muy Interesante and Cosmopolitan.

World.title: Does having dual citizenship have any downsides?
World.content:
In 2016, my wife and I embarked on a road trip together across central Mexico — starting on Jalisco’s Pacific Coast and, over a month later, ending up on the Gulf Coast of Veracruz with innumerable side quests along the way in Michoacán, Guanajuato, Querétaro, Hidalgo, Mexico City, Estado de México and Puebla.

It wasn’t our first time in Mexico. We had, after all, spent our lifetimes visiting our extended families in Mexico as the children of immigrants.

But now we were able to see it on our own terms, as independent adults with our own incomes to spend and itineraries to plan. We rediscovered the country through our own eyes.

That summer, we had a revelation: We wanted to live in Mexico.

Three years later, in 2019, we prepared a similar trek around the southern part of the country, beginning in Oaxaca’s capital, then winding our way through mountain towns en route to the coast on a colectivo. Months prior, we had left our jobs as high school teachers with the intent to live in Mexico long term. Then, COVID-19 happened while we were staying in Mexico City’s central Narvarte Poniente neighborhood.

It was an uncertain and frightening time to be traveling. We ultimately decided, as U.S. citizens with a travel visa, to return to California after nearly half a year away. As tourists, we would have violated our 180-day limit and didn’t want to risk overstaying; had we been dual citizens, we would have had less pressure to return so suddenly.

Navigating the consulate and paperwork

But we hadn’t given up on our ambitions to live in Mexico as Mexican Americans. Shortly after returning to the San Francisco region, I began my application process to become a dual Mexican citizen.

In my case, I had a major advantage: My mom never rescinded her Mexican citizenship, despite having lived in the United States for more than 30 years after immigrating as a young woman. When she eventually moved back to Mexico, it inspired me to follow her southward. Through her, my direct path to citizenship had already been laid out.

The process took me a couple of years, though it could have been completed much more swiftly. I took my time and wasn’t in a rush during the pandemic. I visited different consulates in California, and after waiting in many lines and talking to many people, I gathered all of the documents — most importantly, proof of my mother’s citizenship and birth certificate — and approvals.

Then, it happened: I had become a Mexican citizen, and I had my Mexican passport. (I would eventually get my INE, but I opted to do it in Mexico, rather than at any Mexican consulate in the U.S.).

My wife had a trickier path. Her Mexican-born father’s documents had a typo. Therefore, some of his documents didn’t exactly match. If you aren’t yet familiar with the distress an aberrant punctuation mark can trigger in the imperfect machinery of Mexican bureaucracy, I pray you never have to.

Ultimately, my wife was forced to hire a specialist who helps Mexican descendants obtain their Mexican citizenship — it was frictionless and worth the price. To date, we highly recommend it for anyone who has the funding or has experienced any complications with the process.

A historic surge in binational applicants

During that time, we weren’t alone in our journeys toward Mexican citizenship. Many of our Mexican American friends had expressed a desire to do the same, and in some cases, a few had already started their processes as well. In fact, dual citizenship applications — particularly for the U.S.-born descendants of Mexican immigrants — are reaching a historic apex. De Los, a Latino-focused branch of the Los Angeles Times, recently reported that “Between 2024 and 2025, registrations for Mexican citizenship skyrocketed by 161% at the Los Angeles consulate.”

The trend is universal throughout the U.S. In Boise, Idaho, reports indicate a rise in applicants due to Mexico’s law change in 2023, which simplified the route to dual citizenship for anyone with at least one Mexican-born parent. Combined with the ongoing pressures of xenophobic turmoil, immigration raids and other sociopolitical factors, more people are looking to gain a sense of security and connection on both sides of the border through binational citizenship.

The benefits of dual citizenship are certainly ample: Traveling as a dual citizen offers financial breaks and accessibility perks (there are fewer foreign fees to be paid at Mexican airports and museums, for example); purchasing property in Mexico involves fewer legal hurdles; and at large, it grants unrestricted freedoms on both sides of the border, which is an ultimate privilege.

The unexpected costs of double bureaucracy

But that’s where things can get a little complicated, depending on your plans and lifestyle. In my case, I don’t use my Mexican passport solely for a beach getaway once a year; I live and work in Mexico as a dual citizen, with employers and responsibilities in both countries, and the implications are different.

Vehicle registration in California expired and needs to be updated in person? Guess who’s flying back for a visit to the California Department of Motor Vehicles? Navigating Mexico’s monthly tax payments? Might require a tax accountant. Of course, each scenario comes with a cost, and many life lessons.

When I applied for dual citizenship, I wasn’t necessarily thinking about those realities, or how I would have to pay and renew double the amount of things as someone fully integrated into two federal systems. Of course, in retrospect it makes complete sense. But it’s not the sort of thing that a bright-eyed applicant has at the forefront of their mind while pursuing dual citizenship — nor is it the kind of thing that parents or friends who are encouraging dual citizenship are thinking about, either.

Political debates and balancing two worlds

The issue of dual citizenship has even caused some political strife. Just weeks ago, President Claudia Sheinbaum proposed a ban on dual citizens being able to reach the highest levels of office within Mexico’s borders. “Why have dual nationality if you’re going to represent the people of Mexico?” she rhetorically posed. The bill has been criticized by the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) as a discriminatory human rights violation.

However, for the average person who doesn’t intend to run for the Mexican presidency, dual citizens generally don’t have much to shy away from. If you plan to work in both countries as a dual citizen, be prepared to pay the taxes (literally and metaphorically). If you don’t plan to work in Mexico for Mexican-based companies, you can simply declare your non-working status in Mexico when registering for your INE, and your biggest potential taxation headaches will disappear — at least in one of the two countries.

The benefits

For all of its potential downsides, there are double the benefits. On days when I enter the U.S. through California airports and switch over to using English with my U.S. passport, it feels like I’m home. I’m just as happy and relieved as soon as I arrive back in Mexico, activate my Spanish mode, and show my Mexican passport.

As someone who grew up around many undocumented Mexican immigrants in California, I don’t take that lightly. And I use it to constantly toggle my way between both worlds, as my fullest self.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: ‘A Pilgrimage Across Cultures’: Tamanna Bembenek on finding her third space in Mexico
World.content:
A couple of decades ago, I became fascinated by the concept of the “third place,” which Howard Schultz, then CEO of Starbucks, helped make popular. The idea came from sociologist Ray Oldenburg: a gathering place outside home and work. Maybe it was all marketing, but Starbucks wanted to define its cafés as neutral ground — a place to meet a friend, study or socialize without the usual expectations of home or work. Starbucks was never quite that place for me, but I remained fascinated by the concept. At the time, I interpreted it as a judgment-free space. As I grew older, the term stuck with me but I began to discover another meaning for myself — less about a place to go and more about the freedom to simply be. That is a feeling I have come to call “my third space.” Let me explain what I mean.

In the last few years, I’ve been thinking a lot about the concept in the context of belonging. I’ve always felt fortunate to have lived and worked in multiple countries, because it let me cherry-pick the best aspects and values from different cultures — and do so in a uniquely American way. Individuality is a value I’ve fiercely cherished, yet that same fierceness has made me feel more alone in recent years.

As the political divide has grown in the U.S., I felt I had to pick a political side to satisfy a psychological need to belong with a group of friends or family. As time passed, my identity became tethered to a party rather than to the values it claimed to represent. Social media compounded this, sorting everyone into ever-narrower boxes: age bracket, income bracket, zip code, follower count, which side of a hashtag someone landed on, or generational labels — Gen Alpha, Gen Z, millennials, Gen X, baby boomers, and I’m sure I’ve missed a few. It felt increasingly claustrophobic. Instead of feeling free to choose the values and characteristics that would nurture my own identity as a good human first — regardless of any other labels — I felt I had to fit into someone else’s box, under a category they had defined. Add geopolitical craziness and the current noise around artificial intelligence (AI), including claims that there is a 10% chance that AI will “kill all humans,” and I started feeling not only alone but increasingly anxious and hopeless!

So, I started reading books and listening to podcasts to figure out the root cause of this feeling and how to remedy it. I was already dedicating quality time to pursuing art but increasingly, I also found myself drawn to ancient history — Roman, Egyptian, Indian, Mesoamerican, just to start with. I noticed that exploring stories about ancient civilizations made me feel less alone. It felt soothing. Whether I was reading history or the myths woven through it, I was searching for common themes, a connection, a sense of belonging. There’s a timeless quality to such stories that reminds us of our own mortality and, paradoxically, makes us feel less alone in facing it.

Slowly, I found myself weaving these stories into my art through the use of icons, symbols and allegory. I started visualizing and composing art in my mind — integrating these concepts with my love and knowledge of art history and modern art, my reverence for the ancient craft of handwoven textiles, and my deep interest in astronomy and life sciences.

I have to admit that my current environment is what made all of this possible. Living in Mexico gave me the space I needed: regardless of nationality, identity, or age, I could simply live and let live. Maybe it helps to be geographically so close to the country I truly love and yet not feel so boxed in. Slowly, I began to understand that I wasn’t looking for a place where I could fit in. I was looking for the freedom to belong to something purposeful as I continue to grow as a person — my Indian heritage, my American values, and my old soul that keeps drawing me towards unfamiliar, ancient worlds — and perhaps to the wisdom and spirituality within them. Living in Mexico gave me the freedom to explore those connections, and painting became a medium to express that.

Allow me to show you what I mean, figuratively.

To create is human

Through trial and error, I have discovered that the antidote to my anxiety is not a massage or a spa day or a beach vacation (though they help from time to time) — it is creativity. Creating art in this way — finding connections between ancient cultures — has made me feel whole again, like I am part of something bigger. The more I paint, the more I realize how central creativity is to being human. That’s what my art is really about. There’s a narrative, a thought, a meaning behind every piece — observations, symbolic connections, and questions drawn from books and podcasts on history, archaeology, anthropology and astronomy. There are no political messages. Just a personal journey, trying to make sense of the world I live in today. Creativity is a process, not an outcome: It is a place where I lose my sense of time, immerse myself fully, get stumped, get frustrated, and still come out energized, rooted, grounded. In that space, I stop performing for others and follow my own curiosity.

Maybe that is why creativity makes me feel whole. I don’t have to settle into a single version of my identity. Pueblo life in Mexico, my American individuality, and the ancient civilizations that shape us all can coexist instead of competing. I can keep growing, changing, transforming — staying a “work in progress.” Creativity grants me that permission when society won’t. And while each painting begins with my own vision, it is also an invitation for the viewer to make it their own. You don’t have to see what I see or arrive at the same answers. That is the freedom I have found in my third space: I can be rooted in who I am and still have room to become someone new. Today, I am enough but I am not yet done growing.

A third space you can visit

That sense of wholeness — maybe even greatness — is exactly what I hope visitors feel walking through my upcoming show. If this speaks to you, please come see it in person: I have a collaborative exhibition with Mexican artist Miguel Cuauhtémoc called “A Pilgrimage Across Cultures,” running Nov. 1-15 at Galería Torres del Reloj in Polanco, Mexico City. Miguel grew up immersed in the symbols and rituals of ancient Mexico, and I grew up surrounded by the colors and deities of India. Separately, we both kept arriving at the same recurring image, the third eye, which we each use to explore higher consciousness. Neither of us knew the other was painting it until we saw each other’s work. That discovery felt like another kind of belonging — a connection we had painted before we had even spoken about it.

If you’re in town, please stop by and say hello. And if you’d like to browse the fuller portfolio first, here’s the link: www.tamannabembenek.com.

I’ve written about my personal journey at length elsewhere, if you want to 

Tamanna Bembenek was born in India, studied and worked in the U.S. and now lives in Mexico with her husband, Travis. They are the co-owners of Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Sheinbaum meets with US business leaders and ambassador amid controversy over US-backed police academy
World.content:
Listen to this article

During a week in which she has questioned intrusive U.S. security policies, President Claudia Sheinbaum met with U.S. business leaders at the National Palace, but avoided discussing security initiatives with U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson who was in attendance.

Sheinbaum said Thursday’s meeting with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico (AmCham) addressed issues related to the investment climate in Mexico, adding that she will address her concerns with Johnson at a later date.

“We focused on responding to the companies’ concerns, explaining the controversial new revenue law, discussing requests regarding trade and promoting the favorable environment for business investment in Mexico,” she said.

Also in attendance were the president of Mexico’s Business Coordinating Council, José Medina Mora, and the coordinator of the Advisory Council for Regional Economic Development and Relocation, Altagracia Gómez Sierra.

For its part, AmCham expressed interest in broader security issues, investment and greater private sector participation.

AmCham president Óscar del Cueto said his organization is eager for greater collaboration between the Mexican government and private enterprise, while also citing issues such as security, investment and greater private sector participation.

Several investment agreements were finalized (to be announced at a later date) and the U.S. contingent was given a detailed update on Plan México, Sheinbaum’s strategy for economic development, industrialization and regional growth.

The meeting took place amid an ongoing review of the Mexico-U.S. trade relationship as outlined in the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). AmCham has publicly stated that the USMCA should be used to deepen regional integration and preserve the competitiveness of the economies of Mexico, the United States and Canada.

Del Cueto insists the trade scenario presents a key opportunity for Mexico if the United States goes through a new stage of growth and industrialization and China loses dynamism.

“I firmly believe that next year we could be returning to the topic of nearshoring as the hot topic,” he said.

While Sheinbaum preferred discussing plans to allow for increased investment and greater North American productive integration, the kerfuffle involving Ambassador Johnson was a hot topic with the media.

After participating in a groundbreaking ceremony for an International Police Training Academy in the state of Querétaro on Oct. 2, Johnson — and Governor Mauricio Kuri — have faced criticism over the apparent failure to obtain federal authorization as required by law.

Sheinbaum publicly questioned the project several times, asserting that state governments cannot forge international security agreements or launch such academies without federal and Foreign Ministry authorization.

While clarifying that Mexico is not fundamentally against international cooperation, Sheinbaum explicitly demanded “cooperation with dignity and transparency” rather than “subordination,” adding that it is imperative that federal frameworks not be bypassed.

During a meeting with legislators on Thursday, Security Minister Omar García Harfuch addressed Mexico’s concerns about foreign interference in security matters, insisting that bilateral cooperation is subject to the provisions of Mexican law.

Sheinbaum said Johnson has agreed to meet soon with Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco to discuss the police academy and other issues related to security and the border.

With reports from Informador, Milenio, El Heraldo de México and Heraldo USA

World.title: Honduras Hunts Suspect After Journalist Slain Saturday
World.content:
The colonial cathedral in central Comayagua, the city where journalist José Ángel González García was found dead on 10 October, pictured in December 2018 (file photo). (Photo: Luis Alfredo Romero, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

CRIME · HONDURAS

Key Facts — The country Honduras, a close US security partner where Washington advises Americans to reconsider travel because of crime and terrorism.

— Why it matters Killings of media workers in Honduras almost never reach a conviction, which shapes press freedom and the country’s standing with US partners.

— Why now The Security Minister said on Saturday night that video shows a person leaving the house and that this person is being sought.

— What happened Journalist and university lecturer José Ángel González García was found dead with knife wounds at a home in Comayagua on Saturday 10 October.

— The numbers About 100 media workers have died violently in Honduras since 2001, and more than 96% of cases remain unpunished, according to the state human rights ombudsman.

— What it means for you No change to US travel guidance has been announced, and nothing points to a risk for visitors from this case.

— Still open No arrest has been confirmed, and investigators have not said whether the killing was linked to his journalism.

A Honduras journalist and university lecturer, José Ángel González García, was found stabbed to death at a home in the central city of Comayagua on Saturday 10 October. Security Minister Gerzon Velásquez said that night that video shows a person leaving the house and that this person is now wanted. For US readers, the case is another test of whether Honduras can solve attacks on the press, a long-standing concern in Washington.

González García taught at the Regional University Centre of the Centre (CURC) in Comayagua, a campus of the National Autonomous University of Honduras (UNAH), the country’s largest public university. Local reports describe him as a known figure in the city’s media as well as in the classroom.

His death has caused shock among students and colleagues, according to Proceso Digital, a Tegucigalpa news site. Academic and press groups have called for a full investigation, Infobae reported.

What Happened in Comayagua

Relatives found González García lifeless early on Saturday inside his home in the Lomas del Río neighbourhood of Comayagua, according to Infobae, Proceso Digital and El Heraldo. They alerted the authorities.

He had multiple wounds from a bladed weapon, Infobae reported. El Heraldo, a national daily, and La Prensa, its sister paper, also reported a knife attack inside the home. The official cause of death will come from the autopsy.

National Police officers sealed off the property. Agents of the Police Investigations Directorate (DPI), the force’s detective branch, then worked the scene. They were joined by forensic staff from the Public Prosecutor’s Office, which leads criminal cases in Honduras. The body was to be taken to the morgue in the capital for an autopsy, Proceso Digital reported.

The first lead came from the Security Minister. Velásquez, who oversees the National Police in the government of President Nasry Asfura, spoke to Proceso Digital on Saturday night.

“According to the first inquiries, there are videos showing a person leaving that residence, who is already wanted and shows some signs, such as hands with knife cuts,” he said. He did not name the person or say whether an arrest was imminent.

A Pattern of Unsolved Killings

The case lands on a grim record. The National Commissioner for Human Rights (CONADEH), Honduras’s independent state ombudsman, counts about 100 media workers who have died violently since 2001. More than 96% of those cases remain unpunished, according to CONADEH figures cited by Proceso Digital.

The killings are spread across 16 of the country’s 18 departments. Francisco Morazán, home to the capital Tegucigalpa, accounts for 23 cases. Cortés, around the industrial hub of San Pedro Sula, accounts for 19.

Not every death of a journalist is linked to the work. Infobae noted that no connection between this killing and his reporting or teaching has been established. It added that it has not been established whether he had received threats.

That distinction matters for the investigation and for how the case is counted. For a broader look at the national crime picture, see our guide Honduras for Expats: Homicide Falls to 26.2 per 100,000, but Location Decides Safety. Earlier cases are covered in Another Journalist Killed in Honduras.

One factor may speed this case: police say they already have video of a possible suspect less than a day after the body was found.

What It Means for You

For travellers, the US State Department keeps Honduras at Level 3, “Reconsider Travel”, because of crime and terrorism, in an advisory last updated on Tuesday 25 August. It warns that violent crime, including homicide and armed robbery, is common. It tells Americans not to travel to the remote eastern department of Gracias a Dios.

The advisory bars US government staff from driving between cities after dark, with one exception: the route between Palmerola International Airport/Soto Cano Air Base and Tegucigalpa.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Nothing so far suggests a risk to visitors from this case, which police are treating as a killing inside a private home. Standard precautions still apply: travel by day, use registered transport and follow local news.

For investors, media groups and NGOs working in Honduras, the case is a reminder that impunity remains a business and reputational risk. How fast the Honduras journalist case is solved will be watched by press-freedom groups and foreign partners.

What Is Not Known

No arrest had been confirmed by early Sunday 11 October. The identity of the person seen on video has not been released.

The motive is unknown. Investigators have not said whether the attack was a robbery, a personal dispute or linked to his work in the media. Reports also differ on the spelling of the Honduras journalist’s surname, given as González or Gonzáles.

The autopsy result, the exact time of death and any statement from the Public Prosecutor’s Office were not available at the time of writing. The UNAH campus in Comayagua has declared three days of institutional mourning, La Prensa reported. Everyone remains presumed innocent until a court rules.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was the Honduras journalist killed in Comayagua?

José Ángel González García, a journalist and lecturer at the CURC campus of the National Autonomous University of Honduras. He was found stabbed to death at a home in Comayagua on Saturday 10 October.

Has anyone been arrested?

No arrest had been confirmed by early Sunday. Security Minister Gerzon Velásquez said video shows a person leaving the house, that this person is wanted and had knife cuts on the hands.

Is Honduras safe for US travellers?

The US State Department rates Honduras Level 3, Reconsider Travel, because of crime and terrorism, and says do not travel to Gracias a Dios. Nothing suggests this case raises the risk for visitors.

Sources: Security Minister Gerzon Velásquez and CONADEH figures as reported by Proceso Digital; Infobae; El Heraldo; La Prensa; US State Department, Honduras Travel Advisory.

World.title: El Salvador Adds 38 Bitcoin as Donor Questions Grow
World.content:
Salvadorans try a bitcoin ATM in June 2021, months before the Bitcoin Law took effect. (Photo: Karlalhdz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

FINANCE · EL SALVADOR

Key Facts — The country El Salvador, a dollarised Central American nation of about 6 million people, made bitcoin legal tender in 2021 under President Nayib Bukele.

— Why it matters The state’s bitcoin buying is a condition in a roughly US$1.4 billion IMF loan, so it affects US bondholders and the country’s credit standing.

— Why now Cristosal, a human rights group, is demanding the names of the private donors the government says supplied the new coins, Diario Co Latino reported on Saturday.

— What happened The National Bitcoin Office tracker shows 38 bitcoin added since 3 September, the latest on Saturday 10 October, for 7,801 in total.

— The numbers At US$82,958 per coin early on Sunday, the reserve is worth about US$647 million. The 38 new coins are worth about US$3.2 million.

— What it means for you Nothing changes for visitors or remittance senders. Investors should watch whether the IMF treats the steady inflows as documented donations.

— Still open Who the donors are, how much each gave, and whether the coins added since 1 October are covered by the IMF’s documentation.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives El Salvador a 14% chance of holding US$1 billion or more in bitcoin by 31 December (11 October, 2:31 a.m. ET).

El Salvador’s government added another bitcoin to its reserve on Saturday 10 October, its 38th since the IMF staff-level agreement of 3 September. The country now holds 7,801 coins, according to the official National Bitcoin Office tracker. For US investors, the El Salvador bitcoin question is whether a reserve the IMF says should stop growing keeps quietly expanding.

The government says the new coins come from private donors, not public money, and the IMF has accepted documentation to that effect. Cristosal, a human rights organisation, now wants those donors named. Its analysis, dated 30 September, was reported by the Salvadoran daily Diario Co Latino on Friday and Saturday.

El Salvador has used the US dollar as its currency since 2001, so all amounts here are in US$.

One Coin at a Time

The National Bitcoin Office is the government unit that runs the state’s bitcoin policy and publishes its wallet addresses online. Its tracker, built on public blockchain data, listed 20 addresses holding 7,801.37 bitcoin early on Sunday 11 October.

Inflows arrive almost daily in single-coin amounts. The tracker shows 38 deposits of exactly one bitcoin each since 3 September. Ten of them arrived on or after Thursday 1 October, the day the IMF executive board completed the programme’s second and third reviews.

The same data show no net outflows beyond small network fees, so El Salvador bitcoin holdings have only grown. At the tracker’s own price of US$82,958 early on Sunday, the reserve was worth about US$647 million.

El Salvador's state bitcoin holdings, 3 September to 11 October 2026. What the IMF Agreed

El Salvador signed a roughly US$1.4 billion Extended Fund Facility with the International Monetary Fund, approved in early 2025. A core condition was that the public sector would keep its bitcoin holdings unchanged.

That did not happen. In its 3 September press release, the IMF said documentation had been provided “verifying that Bitcoin accumulation since the first review reflects private donations” and that “no public resources were used.”

The Fund added: “Going forward, no further Bitcoin accumulation beyond the documented donations is expected.” When the board approved the reviews on 1 October and released about US$138 million, it said again that “no further Bitcoin accumulation is envisaged beyond the documented donations.”

The board also said waivers were granted “for certain unmet performance criteria on Bitcoin accumulation”, based on corrective measures and renewed commitments. It asked the government to improve disclosure of public crypto holdings.

What Cristosal Wants

Cristosal is a human rights group founded in El Salvador that works across Central America. It has long been critical of the Bukele government.

Its 11-page analysis says state bitcoin reserves have grown by about 1,090 coins, roughly US$100 million, since the IMF’s first review in June 2025. It asks the government to publish the donation contracts, the donors’ identities, the amounts and the dates.

It also calls for forensic tracing of the coins on the blockchain. The aim, it says, is to rule out funds linked to hacks, mixing services or illicit markets.

The group warns that undisclosed donations could carry the risk of an “upfront bribe” if donors later won contracts or concessions. It offers no evidence that this has happened, and the claim remains a warning, not an allegation against any person.

Cristosal adds that current law sets no specific procedure for the state to receive bitcoin as a donation. It also points to gaps on crypto funding of political campaigns, ahead of the 2027 elections.

What It Means for You

For travellers and Salvadorans sending money home from the United States, nothing changes. The dollar remains the everyday currency, and businesses may refuse bitcoin since the 2025 reforms.

For holders of Salvadoran bonds, the El Salvador bitcoin issue is about programme credibility. The IMF has already granted waivers once. Steady inflows that cannot be matched to named donors could complicate future reviews and disbursements.

There is a stabiliser. The IMF has accepted the government’s documentation and the board released the money. The new coins are also small against an economy the IMF puts at about US$39 billion this year.

For background, see El Salvador IMF Board Releases US$138 Million and El Salvador Holds 7,762 Bitcoin as IMF Ends Mandatory Use.

What Is Not Known

The donors behind the El Salvador bitcoin inflows, the size of each gift and the dates are not public. It is not clear whether the IMF’s documentation covers the ten coins added since 1 October or only earlier inflows.

The government and the National Bitcoin Office had not publicly answered Cristosal’s analysis by early Sunday. The tracker does not show who sent each coin, only that it arrived.

What Prediction Markets Say

Bets on Polymarket give El Salvador a 14% chance of holding US$1 billion or more in bitcoin by 31 December, as of 2:31 a.m. ET on Sunday 11 October. That price has fallen about 28 points over the past month.

About US$10,800 has been traded on that contract. Reaching the mark at today’s holdings would need bitcoin near US$128,000, so the bet is mostly on the coin’s price, not on new donations.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much bitcoin does El Salvador hold?

The National Bitcoin Office tracker showed 7,801 bitcoin on Sunday 11 October, worth about US$647 million at early-morning prices.

Is El Salvador still buying bitcoin?

Its holdings keep rising by about one coin a day. The government and the IMF say the coins added since mid-2025 are private donations, not purchases with public money.

What is Cristosal asking for?

The rights group wants the government to publish the donors’ names, the amounts, the dates and the donation contracts, and to trace the coins on the blockchain.

World.title: Central African Republic Opens First Criminal Database
World.content:
CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Landlocked state in central Africa, host to UN peacekeepers since 2014.

— What happened It opened its first integrated criminal database in Bangui.

— When President Touadéra inaugurated the centre on Thursday, 8 October.

— Who paid MINUSCA funded building and servers; UNODC gave training and connectivity.

— US link Washington is assessed about 26% of MINUSCA’s costs.

— Still open No cost figure has been published by the UN or government.

A UN-funded centre gives Central African police and gendarmes one shared record of crimes and wanted people for the first time.

The Central African Republic has opened its first integrated criminal database, housed in a new centre at the Interior Ministry in Bangui. President Faustin-Archange Touadéra inaugurated it on Thursday, 8 October.

The UN peacekeeping mission MINUSCA paid for the building and its servers, and the UN drugs and crime agency supplied training. For a US reader, the project shows where part of Washington’s peacekeeping money ends up in one of Africa’s most fragile states.

What the Criminal Database Does

MINUSCA, in a press release dated 8 October, said the system is meant to improve information sharing and identify crime trends. It should also support coordinated responses, including to cross-border criminal threats.

Valentine Rugwabiza, the UN Secretary-General’s special representative and head of MINUSCA, explained the practical change at the ceremony.

Police and gendarmerie will now share “a common tool” on crimes and wanted individuals, she said. Oubangui Médias, a Bangui news site, reported her remarks.

She linked the project to MINUSCA’s mandate to protect civilians and to the fight against impunity. Until now, the two forces had no single shared record of offences and suspects.

The centre also houses the ministry’s Joint Project Management Unit, which follows reforms of the security sector. Alwihda Info, a regional news site based in neighbouring Chad, reported the same arrangement.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Paid and Who Spoke

According to the MINUSCA release, the mission financed the building, the equipment and the servers. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) provided technical expertise, training and help with connectivity.

The government supplied the land and carried out additional works. Neither the UN nor the ministry has published what the project cost.

General Bienvenu Zokoué, the Minister of the Interior and Public Security, called the handover more than an infrastructure project. It showed a shared will to modernise security management and strengthen the internal security forces, he said (translated from French).

Alwihda Info quoted him as saying the project had been a government priority for several years. Budget and logistical constraints had delayed it, according to the same report.

Kameldy Neldjingaye, who represents UNODC in the country, sounded a note of caution. “Technology alone is not enough,” he said, adding that the tool’s value depends on how national institutions use it under the law.

The Conditions the UN Attached

Rugwabiza asked the government for qualified and stable staff, and for dedicated national funding for operations and maintenance. She also called for reliable, lasting internet connectivity.

She said the services feeding the database must protect personal data and respect individual rights. Neldjingaye likewise stressed confidentiality and the safeguards set out in national law.

The next steps, according to MINUSCA, are to extend the system to the judicial police and the gendarmerie’s investigation service. Reliable data backup and a gradual rollout to the regions are also planned.

Those requests matter because MINUSCA’s support is meant to be temporary. Rugwabiza said capacity building aims at the “progressive and effective autonomy” of the institutions receiving it.

What It Means for US Readers

The United States is the largest funder of UN peacekeeping, and MINUSCA is no exception. UN assessment notices put the US share of the mission’s budget at about 26.1%.

For the period from 16 November 2025 to 30 June 2026, the UN assessed Washington roughly US$212 million for MINUSCA. That works out at close to US$1 million a day for one mission.

The Security Council last renewed the mission’s mandate on Thursday, 13 November 2025, in resolution 2800. A working criminal database is the kind of result donors cite when they ask whether peacekeeping is building lasting institutions.

For travellers, nothing changes yet. The US State Department rates the country Level 4, “Do Not Travel”, citing unrest, crime, kidnapping and terrorism.

The US embassy in Bangui offers no consular services, so Americans must rely on the embassy in Yaoundé, Cameroon.

What Is Not Known

The cost of the building, servers and training has not been disclosed.

It is not known how many records the database holds at launch. Nor is it known how many officers have been trained to use it.

The government has not said whether the 2027 budget will include money for running and maintaining the system. No timetable has been given for the rollout to the judicial police, the gendarmerie investigators or the regions.

It is unclear which law governs access to the data and who oversees it. The UN statements refer to national legal safeguards without naming them.

What Comes Next

The immediate test is whether police and gendarmes begin entering cases in Bangui and whether the connection holds. MINUSCA has encouraged other partners to contribute to the next phase.

The opening does not mean the country now has a nationwide crime records system. For now it is a single centre in the capital, with expansion still to be funded and scheduled.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the new criminal database?

It is a shared system at the Interior Ministry in Bangui that centralises information on crimes and wanted people. Police and gendarmerie are meant to use it to share intelligence and track crime trends.

Who paid for it?

The UN mission MINUSCA financed the building, equipment and servers, while UNODC provided expertise, training and connectivity. The government supplied the land and some works, and no cost has been published.

What is MINUSCA?

MINUSCA is the UN peacekeeping mission in the Central African Republic, led by Valentine Rugwabiza. Its mandate includes protecting civilians and supporting state institutions.

Does the United States help pay for MINUSCA?

Yes. UN assessment notices put the US share at about 26.1%, or roughly US$212 million for mid-November 2025 to June 2026.

Is the Central African Republic safe for Americans?

The US State Department advises Americans not to travel there, its highest Level 4 warning. The US embassy in Bangui does not provide consular services.

Sources: MINUSCA press release, 8 October 2026; Oubangui Médias, Bangui; Alwihda Info; UN Committee on Contributions, MINUSCA assessment; US State Department travel advisory (all accessed 11 October 2026).

World.title: Bolivia Holds Alleged PCC Member on 3 Brazil Warrants
World.content:
The Bolivian migration post at Puerto Quijarro, on the border with Corumbá, Brazil (Photo: CivArmy, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ORGANISED CRIME · BOLIVIA

Key Facts — The country Bolivia, a landlocked cocaine-producing country that shares a long, thinly policed eastern border with Brazil.

— Why it matters Brazil’s PCC and Comando Vermelho gangs are fighting over drug routes through eastern Bolivia, and La Paz now works with the US DEA and Brazil’s Federal Police against them.

— Why now The arrest comes as Bolivia readies two US-backed elite police units for the Brazilian border.

— What happened Police in Santa Cruz detained Marco de Oliveira Ferreira, named as a senior PCC member, after a domestic incident on Friday 9 October. Migration ordered his expulsion for Saturday 10 October.

— The numbers Three pending sentence warrants in Brazil, according to Bolivian police, for offences including drug trafficking, contract killing and criminal organisation.

— What it means for you No sign of risk to visitors. For investors, it shows Bolivia using fast expulsions and foreign police help to keep Brazilian gangs out of Santa Cruz.

— Still open Whether the handover at the border has taken place, where, and what role he held in the gang.

Bolivian police have detained a man they describe as a senior PCC member wanted in Brazil, after officers in Santa Cruz de la Sierra answered a domestic incident call on Friday 9 October. The Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) is a faction born in São Paulo’s prisons that the Spanish agency EFE, in a report carried by eju.tv, calls one of Brazil’s most dangerous criminal groups. For US readers, the case shows how Brazil’s gang war over cocaine routes now reaches into Bolivia, where Washington has stepped up police support this month.

Colonel Adrián Javier Álvarez, commander-general of the Bolivian Police, named the man as Marco de Oliveira Ferreira. He said the Brazilian had been living in Bolivia irregularly and had tried to hide his identity with forged documents.

The departmental migration office then issued an administrative expulsion order. Police said it would be carried out on Saturday 10 October, with Ferreira handed to Brazilian authorities at the border.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 with 28.4 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (13). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.2%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

How a Domestic Call Led to the Arrest

According to the police account, the incident happened at around 9:30 on Friday in Pampa de la Isla, a working-class district of Santa Cruz de la Sierra. Santa Cruz is Bolivia’s largest city and its business centre.

“This person, who was being sought by the intelligence bodies of the Bolivian Police, was involved in a domestic incident on 9 October,” Álvarez said, as quoted by the Santa Cruz daily El Día. Officers of the Special Force Against Crime (Felcc), the police unit for serious crime, then moved to establish who he was, Correo del Sur reported.

Police said identity checks and an exchange of information with Brazil’s Federal Police confirmed that he was wanted by the Brazilian courts. The nature of the domestic incident, and whether anyone was hurt, has not been made public.

“This individual will be placed before the Brazilian authorities at the border, so that he can serve the sentence against him in his country,” Álvarez said on Saturday, according to the Cochabamba daily Opinión.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Police Say He Is

Bolivian police say Ferreira has a record in Brazil for drug trafficking, contract killing and criminal organisation. They say three sentence warrants against him are still waiting to be served there.

These are police descriptions. Bolivian authorities have not released Brazilian court documents, his age or the length of the sentences. The Brazilian border newspaper Diário Corumbaense, citing Bolivian television channel Unitel, reported the same account. Santa Cruz lies about 650 kilometres from Corumbá, the Brazilian border town opposite Puerto Quijarro.

Expulsion is an administrative step, not an extradition. It allows Bolivia to send a foreigner with irregular status home quickly, without a court hearing on a foreign request.

Why Brazilian Gangs Matter in Bolivia

The government of President Rodrigo Paz, a centre-right leader in office since November 2025, links several recent killings in eastern Bolivia to a fight between the PCC and the Comando Vermelho (CV). The CV is a rival faction born in Rio de Janeiro’s prisons.

The two groups compete for drug routes along the Brazilian border, according to eju.tv and Infobae. The violence has hit the Chiquitania region and Bolivia’s Amazon lowlands.

Infobae reported that four civilians and an intelligence officer were shot dead in San Matías, a border town, in August. The government responded with a Safe Borders plan for the frontier.

Government Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo, Bolivia’s interior minister, announced last week two elite police units near the Brazilian border, created with US support. The government has also said Brazil’s Federal Police will soon open a permanent office in Bolivia.

Oviedo has said both gangs “are recruiting” Bolivians, Infobae reported. He named the US Drug Enforcement Administration, Brazil’s Federal Police and European Union police bodies as partners.

Infobae also reported that more than 120 newly graduated police lieutenants and sergeants begin a course against “narcoterrorism” on Monday 12 October. They will then be sent to four zones on the Brazilian border. The United States handed riot-control equipment to the Bolivian Police on 9 October, as covered in Bolivia Police Get US Riot Gear on 9 October.

What It Means for You

For travellers, nothing in the police account suggests a risk to visitors. The arrest followed a private domestic incident, not an attack. Normal precautions apply in Santa Cruz, as in any large Latin American city.

For investors and anyone watching US policy, the case fits a wider pattern. Bolivia under Paz is rebuilding police ties with Washington after years of distance under earlier governments, and the arrest of an alleged PCC member shows that cooperation with Brazil works in practice.

The risk is the other side of the same story. Brazilian factions appear to see Bolivia as a hiding place and a supply corridor, and border violence has not stopped. For more on the US view of Bolivian security, see Bolivia Stays on US Trafficking Watch List Again.

What Is Not Known

By early Sunday, neither Bolivian nor Brazilian authorities had publicly confirmed that the handover took place on Saturday, or at which crossing. Brazil’s Federal Police had not commented publicly.

It is not known what rank Ferreira held as an alleged PCC member, how long he had lived in Bolivia, or whether he ran any operation there. The Brazilian cases behind the three warrants have not been identified, and he has not had a chance to respond publicly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was arrested in Santa Cruz, Bolivia?

Bolivian police named him as Marco de Oliveira Ferreira, a Brazilian they describe as a senior member of the PCC gang. He was detained after a domestic incident on Friday 9 October.

Why is he being expelled rather than extradited?

Police say he lived in Bolivia irregularly and used forged documents. That allowed the migration office to order an administrative expulsion and hand him to Brazil at the border.

What is the PCC?

The Primeiro Comando da Capital is a criminal faction that began in São Paulo’s prisons. Bolivia’s government links it and its rival Comando Vermelho to violence over drug routes on the border.

Sources: Bolivian Police statements of 10 October 2026, as reported by Opinión, Correo del Sur, El Día, eju.tv, Diário Corumbaense and Infobae.

World.title: Uganda’s Army Rejects New York Times Report on Muhoozi
World.content:
UGANDA · MILITARY AND MEDIA

Key Facts — What happened Uganda’s army rejected a US newspaper feature on its chief.

— When Statement issued on Saturday, 10 October, by Col Chris Magezi.

— The target A Megan K. Stack feature published on Thursday, 8 October.

— The person Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, army chief and President Museveni’s son.

— Army’s line Claims are unfounded; foreign interference “will not be tolerated.”

— Still open No public reply yet from the newspaper or Washington.

Uganda’s military has turned a US newspaper feature into a fight over who shapes the country’s post-Museveni future.

The Uganda army on Saturday, 10 October, rejected a New York Times feature on its commander, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba. The feature links him to alleged human rights abuses.

The Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) called the report unfounded and part of a sustained character assassination campaign, the Daily Monitor reported.

The dispute matters beyond Kampala because Muhoozi is President Yoweri Museveni’s son and widely seen as a possible successor. Uganda is also a long-standing US security partner, with troops deployed against al-Shabaab in Somalia.

What the Uganda Army Said

The statement came from Col Chris Magezi, Acting Director of Defence Public Information, the army’s chief spokesman. He said the article “regurgitates long held, twisted opposition and activist narratives” against the government, according to the Daily Monitor.

Magezi defended Muhoozi as a decorated officer with decades of military service. He said the UPDF works within Uganda’s constitution and that serious accusations require serious evidence, not anecdotal or politically motivated sources.

Muhoozi, 52, has been Chief of Defence Forces since March 2024. He is also Senior Presidential Advisor for Special Operations, according to the army.

Museveni has ruled Uganda since 1986. The question of who follows him dominates the country’s politics, and Muhoozi’s rise has made the army central to that debate.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Uganda Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the US Newspaper Reported

The feature, written by Megan K. Stack and published on Thursday, 8 October, is titled “The Authoritarian Future Is Already Here.” The Daily Monitor said it describes a growing state surveillance system in Uganda, including facial recognition and digital tracking tools.

According to the same summary, the piece links Muhoozi to the detention and suppression of opposition figures. It names singer-turned-politician Robert Kyagulanyi, known as Bobi Wine, and Kizza Besigye, a veteran opposition leader on trial for alleged treason.

Kyagulanyi leads the National Unity Platform, Uganda’s main opposition party. Besigye, a former Museveni physician, ran for president four times before founding his own movement.

The feature also draws on the account of Kakwenza Rukirabashaija, an exiled Ugandan novelist. He alleges that Muhoozi visited him in detention, ordered him to undress and later offered him a bribe.

The Army’s Answer to Kakwenza

Magezi said Muhoozi and Kakwenza have “never met.” He called the writer “a known fiction teller” and his account “a fine figment of his imagination,” the Daily Monitor reported.

The spokesman also pointed to what he called contradictions in the story.

He said the account had Kakwenza bending over to look shorter, yet too injured at the ankles to stand. He called this “quite laughable.”

Kakwenza was arrested in December 2021 after social media posts about Muhoozi and Museveni. He left Uganda in 2022 and has since lived in exile, from where he continues to write about his detention.

A Wider Charge Against Foreign Media

The statement went beyond one article. Magezi accused The Telegraph, The Wall Street Journal and The Economist of bias against Muhoozi as well.

He said Muhoozi “is not their preferred successor of choice to a post-Museveni Uganda.” Uganda’s political future, he added, belongs only to its voters, and external interference “will not be tolerated.”

On the same Saturday, the army’s own website reported Muhoozi meeting the Commonwealth Secretary-General and a Malian military delegation. It also welcomed a new battle group to its Somalia mission area.

What It Means for US Readers

The row puts a major American newspaper at the centre of Uganda’s succession politics. Kampala’s sharp tone suggests the government sees Western coverage of Muhoozi as a political threat, not only a press matter.

For Washington, Uganda is a difficult partner. Its soldiers have formed a core part of African Union forces fighting al-Shabaab in Somalia, a long-running US counter-terrorism priority.

Yet Washington removed Uganda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act trade programme from January 2024, citing human rights. On Saturday, the Daily Monitor also reported that Uganda remains on Tier 2 in the 2026 US Trafficking in Persons report.

Investors watching Uganda’s oil projects on Lake Albert, led by France’s TotalEnergies and China’s CNOOC, track succession risk closely. A more confrontational tone from the army towards Western media adds to that picture, though it changes no policy by itself.

What Is Not Known

The full army statement could not be independently reviewed. Its content here rests on reports by the Daily Monitor and Nile Post.

It is not clear whether it was released as a press statement or on social media.

No public response from the newspaper to the army’s criticism had been reported by Sunday morning. Nor had any comment from Muhoozi himself or the US Embassy in Kampala.

Kakwenza’s allegations have not been tested in any court. The army’s account of his claims has not been tested either.

What Comes Next

Watch for any reply from the newspaper, the writer or the opposition.

Remarks by Muhoozi, who often posts on social media, are also likely. Any comment from the US State Department would raise the stakes.

The statement does not mean any legal action against the newspaper or its reporter. No such step has been announced.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who Is Muhoozi Kainerugaba?

He is Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces and the son of President Yoweri Museveni. Many Ugandans see him as a possible successor to his father.

What Did the US Newspaper Report?

According to the Daily Monitor, the 8 October feature describes growing state surveillance and links Muhoozi to the suppression of opposition figures. It also carries a writer’s allegations of abuse in detention.

How Did the Uganda Army Respond?

Spokesman Col Chris Magezi called the claims unfounded and part of a character assassination campaign. He said foreign interference in Uganda’s politics “will not be tolerated.”

Who Is Kakwenza Rukirabashaija?

He is a Ugandan novelist who was detained in December 2021 and now lives in exile. The army says he has never met Muhoozi.

Why Does This Matter to the United States?

Uganda is a key US security partner in Somalia but faces US pressure over human rights. The dispute touches both issues at once.

Sources: Uganda People’s Defence Forces; Daily Monitor, army statement on Muhoozi; Nile Post, army statement on Kakwenza; Daily Monitor, US trafficking report (all accessed 11 October 2026).

World.title: Senegal Arrests 6 Over US$1.9 Million in Fake Banknotes
World.content:
SENEGAL · CRIME

Key Facts — What happened Senegal’s gendarmerie arrested six people over fake dollar and euro notes.

— The numbers Seized notes valued at 1.1 billion CFA francs, about US$1.9 million.

— Where Operations in Dakar, Thiès, Mbour and Louga followed a 5 October tip.

— US link The haul included 6,600 fake US$100 bills, US$660,000 at face value.

— Also seized A 9 mm pistol, a dagger, a bulletproof vest and suspected mercury.

— Still open Charges, suspects’ identities and the notes’ origin have not been disclosed.

Raids in four Senegalese towns turned up 17,800 fake US and European banknotes valued at about US$1.9 million.

Senegal’s national gendarmerie has arrested six people in Dakar, Thiès, Mbour and Louga and seized fake banknotes in US dollars and euros. It put their equivalent value at 1,104,914,840 CFA francs (about US$1.9 million).

The haul, mostly fake US$100 and €100 bills, matters to foreigners because those are the notes visitors, traders and investors carry. Investigators also found a pistol, a dagger, a bulletproof vest and bottles believed to contain mercury.

What the Gendarmerie Seized

The Brigade de recherches de Dakar, the gendarmerie’s criminal investigation unit for the capital, announced the case on Saturday, 10 October. The Agence de Presse Sénégalaise (APS), the state news agency, carried the statement that evening, as did the Dakar news site Seneweb.

According to the statement, investigators acted on intelligence received on Monday, 5 October. The tip pointed to a suspected network holding foreign-currency notes for chemical washing and use as fraudulent payment.

The largest batch was 10,000 notes made to look like €100 bills, €1 million (about US$1.12 million) at face value. The gendarmerie valued them at 650 million CFA francs (about US$1.1 million).

Investigators also found 6,600 notes made to look like US$100 bills in a briefcase, or US$660,000 at face value. The gendarmerie valued them at 376.2 million CFA francs (about US$643,000).

A third batch held 1,200 so-called black notes in €100 denominations, €120,000 at face value (about US$134,000). Their stated value of 78,714,840 CFA francs (about US$134,000) matches the fixed rate of 655.957 CFA francs per euro.

Conversions use a market rate of 585.40 CFA francs per US$1 on 11 October 2026.

Beyond the notes, investigators seized a Taurus 9 mm automatic pistol, 20 blank 9 mm cartridges and 15 further cartridges. The list also includes two forgers’ stamps, a bulletproof vest, a dagger and bottles believed to contain mercury.

Seneweb headlined the case as “one billion in fake notes, pistol, dagger” and called it a big gendarmerie seizure. APS described it as trafficking in fake foreign currency worth more than one billion CFA francs (about US$1.7 million).

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Senegal Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the Washing Scheme Is Said to Work

The gendarmerie did not describe the scheme beyond the chemical washing process. Blackened notes and chemical cleaning are, however, hallmarks of what is widely known as the “black money” or “wash-wash” scam.

In the typical version, victims are shown stained paper and told it is real currency disguised for transport. They are then asked to pay for an expensive chemical that will supposedly restore the notes.

A few genuine notes are often “cleaned” in front of the victim to win trust. The rest proves worthless once the money for the chemicals has changed hands.

The gendarmerie said only that the bottles were believed to contain mercury, a toxic metal. It did not say how the substance was used, and the statement does not explain the two forgers’ stamps either.

A Four-Town Operation

Dakar, the capital, is home to Senegal’s main port, airport and banks. Thiès lies about 70 kilometres east, Mbour about 80 kilometres south-east on the coast, and Louga about 200 kilometres north-east.

Mbour sits next to the Saly beach resorts, which draw many European visitors. The gendarmerie did not say which arrests took place in which town.

Senegal’s gendarmerie is a military force that carries out police and criminal investigation work alongside the national police. Its Dakar research brigade investigates serious crime in the capital region.

Senegal is a West African country of about 18 million people. One US$ buys about 585 CFA francs, the currency it shares with seven other West African states.

What It Means for US Readers

The seized haul included 6,600 notes made to look like US$100 bills. The US Secret Service protects the dollar against counterfeiting worldwide, but the gendarmerie did not mention any US role in this case.

For American travellers, the practical lesson is to change money only at banks, ATMs and licensed exchange offices. Offers to swap, “clean” or multiply foreign cash are a clear warning sign.

Business visitors and investors should be wary of cash deals presented as discreet or urgent. Fraud schemes of this kind can reach foreigners through personal contacts, social media or email.

The case also shows police action against financial crime in a country courting foreign investors, including in oil and gas. There is no sign it affects Senegal’s currency or its banks.

What Is Not Known

The gendarmerie did not name the six suspects, give their nationalities or say what charges they may face. It is also not known whether they remain in custody or have been brought before a prosecutor.

Where the fake banknotes were printed, and whether any victims paid money, is unclear. The statement also does not say whether any genuine notes were among the seized bundles.

The gendarmerie did not say whether the pistol was registered or whether foreign authorities have been informed. All six are suspects, and none has been convicted of any offence.

What Comes Next

The gendarmerie said its investigation is continuing, which could lead to further arrests. In Senegal, suspects held by the gendarmerie are normally handed to a prosecutor, who decides on charges.

It asked the public to share information on its free lines, 800 00 20 20 and 123. The seizure does not mean fake banknotes are common in Senegal’s shops or banks.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Senegal’s gendarmerie seize?

It seized 6,600 fake US$100 notes and 11,200 fake 100-euro notes, some of them blackened. It also found a pistol, a dagger, a bulletproof vest and suspected mercury.

How much were the fake banknotes worth?

The gendarmerie put their equivalent value at about 1.1 billion CFA francs, or about US$1.9 million. As fakes, the notes have no real value.

What is a black money scam?

Fraudsters show victims blackened paper, claim it is real currency and sell them a costly chemical to clean it. The gendarmerie said the seized notes could be put through a chemical washing process.

Have the suspects been charged?

The gendarmerie has not announced charges or named the six people arrested. They are suspects, and the investigation is continuing.

Is it safe to use cash in Senegal?

Yes, with normal care: use banks, ATMs and licensed exchange offices. Refuse anyone who offers to exchange, clean or multiply currency.

World.title: Guinea-Bissau Party Loses 33 Members Over Poll Boycott
World.content:
GUINEA-BISSAU · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country West African state of two million, run by a junta since 2025.

— What happened 33 APU-PDGB officials and members resigned in one collective letter.

— When The letter is dated and stamped received on Friday, 9 October.

— Most senior signatory Party vice-president Samuel Dinis Manuel.

— The grievance Leader Nuno Nabiam kept the party out of the November 2025 elections.

— Still open Nabiam and the party leadership have not formally responded.

A former prime minister’s party is splitting as Guinea-Bissau’s military rulers search for a new election date.

Thirty-three officials and APU-PDGB members have quit the party of former prime minister Nuno Nabiam in Guinea-Bissau. Their collective letter, dated Friday, 9 October, says he took key decisions alone, above all sitting out the November 2025 elections.

The split matters beyond one party because Guinea-Bissau, a small West African state under military rule, has no date for civilian rule. APU-PDGB has just lost its vice-president and several regional leaders before any new vote.

What the Resignation Letter Says

APU-PDGB stands for Assembleia do Povo Unido – Partido Democrático da Guiné-Bissau, or United People’s Assembly – Democratic Party of Guinea-Bissau. Nabiam founded it and still leads it.

The two-page letter is addressed to him and signed by a “Group of Leaders and Members Resigning from APU-PDGB”. A stamp from the office of the party’s secretary-general shows it was received on 9 October.

The signatories say they are giving up both their posts and their membership. They blame “the deep leadership crisis” for what they call the weakening and gradual breakdown of the party (translated from Portuguese).

The letter lists three grounds. First, it says decisions of major political weight have been taken unilaterally, without consulting members.

Second, it rejects Nabiam’s decision not to run for president and to stop the party from contesting the legislative election. Both votes were held in November 2025, and the signatories say such a choice needed a full debate in the party’s bodies.

Third, it cites “constant violations” of the party statutes, including political agreements the leader signed alone. It names APU-PDGB’s entry into the Plataforma Republicana Nô Kumpu Guiné as one example.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Africa Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Is Leaving APU-PDGB

An attached list names 33 people with their membership card numbers, posts and signatures. The Bissau weekly O Democrata, which saw the letter, reported the resignations on Friday evening.

The most senior is Samuel Dinis Manuel, a vice-president and member of the party’s Standing Committee. He also coordinated youth, economic affairs, vocational training and employment.

Beto Infande, president of the party’s Forum of Cadres, signed, as did its secretary-general, Buo Manuel. Garcia Biifa Bedeta, a deputy national secretary, and Rosalia da Costa, listed as president of the party body ONAMA, also signed.

The list also includes local political committee leaders from Biombo region, the Bária section and the Prabis sector. Two signatories are listed simply as rank-and-file members.

The group says the “political and ethical conditions” no longer exist for it to stay under the current leadership. It does not say whether its members will join another party.

The 2025 Vote and the Embaló Alliance

Guinea-Bissau held presidential and legislative elections on Sunday, 23 November 2025. Three days later, on 26 November 2025, the army seized power before provisional results were released.

General Horta Inta-A, an army officer, now leads the transition as president. The deposed president, Umaro Sissoco Embaló, had been seeking a second term.

Nô Kumpu Guiné, Creole for roughly “Let’s Build Guinea”, was a 16-party alliance formed in September 2025 to back Embaló’s re-election. Le360, a Moroccan news site, reported its launch on 3 September 2025.

The dissidents’ complaint is therefore about a party that sat out the ballot itself while signing up to the incumbent’s camp. With the vote voided by the coup, that bet left APU-PDGB with no seats to defend and no clear role.

The letter arrives during a busy week for the transition. Officials said on Thursday that the planned 6 December election cannot go ahead, and no replacement date has been set.

What It Means for US Readers

Guinea-Bissau has long been a transit point for South American cocaine bound for Europe. A fragmented party system and an open-ended military transition make stable, accountable government harder to rebuild.

Washington has had no resident embassy in Bissau since 1998 and handles the country from its embassy in Dakar, Senegal. Embaló was among five West African leaders hosted at the White House in July 2025.

For travellers and businesses, the split itself changes little on the ground. It is a signal, though, that the civilian parties a future election depends on are weakening while the army sets the timetable.

What Is Not Known

Nabiam and APU-PDGB’s leadership had not issued a formal response by Sunday morning, 11 October.

On Saturday, the Bissau news blog Conosaba posted a short message under his name: “the struggle does not end here”. It did not name the defectors.

It is not known how many members APU-PDGB has in total, so the share of the party leaving cannot be measured. It is also unclear whether the signatories plan a new party or will join an existing one.

What Comes Next

The transitional president must now set a new election calendar after being told the December date is not possible. Parties that want to compete will have to renew their internal bodies first.

The resignations do not dissolve APU-PDGB, and Nabiam remains its leader. Whether more members follow will show how much of the party survives into the next vote.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is APU-PDGB?

APU-PDGB is a Guinea-Bissau political party founded and led by former prime minister Nuno Nabiam. Its full name means United People Assembly, Democratic Party of Guinea-Bissau.

How many people resigned?

The collective letter carries a list of 33 named officials and members. The most senior is vice-president Samuel Dinis Manuel.

Why did they leave?

They say Nabiam took major decisions alone, including keeping the party out of the November 2025 elections. They also object to his joining an alliance backing the former president without consulting party bodies.

Who runs Guinea-Bissau now?

A military-led transition under General Horta Inta-A has ruled since the coup of 26 November 2025. No date for a new election has been set.

Is Guinea-Bissau safe for American travellers?

The party split has no direct effect on security. Travellers should check the current US State Department advisory before going.

World.title: South Africa’s Largest Party to Appeal Lungisa Ruling
World.content:
SOUTH AFRICA · ELECTIONS

Key Facts — The country South Africa elects municipal councils on Wednesday, 4 November.

— What happened The ANC said on Saturday it will appeal the Lungisa judgment.

— The ruling A judge found Mbalula unlawfully removed Lungisa from the list.

— The ballot The order came too late to put Lungisa on ballot papers.

— Still open No appeal filing reported yet; grounds not detailed.

The ANC will challenge a ruling that its secretary-general broke party rules by dropping a mayoral hopeful at the last minute.

South Africa’s African National Congress (ANC) said on Saturday, 10 October, that it will appeal a High Court order. The ruling went in favour of Andile Lungisa, a member of the party’s national executive committee.

Lungisa wanted to run for mayor of Nelson Mandela Bay, the metro around the port city of Gqeberha. The ANC is the largest party in the national unity government.

Judge Nelisa Mali of the Johannesburg High Court ruled on Friday, 9 October. She found that secretary-general Fikile Mbalula acted unlawfully when he removed Lungisa from the candidate list.

The dispute lands less than four weeks before the 4 November local government elections. The ANC is fighting to win back control of major cities.

What the ANC Said

In a statement reported by IOL on Saturday, the party said it had noted the judgment and “resolved to appeal” it. It said the case raised “fundamental questions concerning the organisational autonomy of political parties.”

“These matters warrant further judicial consideration,” the statement said, according to IOL. The party added that choosing candidates is an internal matter under its own constitution.

It also urged members to remain united. The statement did not name a spokesperson.

It had not been posted on the ANC’s website by Sunday morning. The party did not say which court it would approach or when it would file.
