World.title: Teen revolt or revolution? The student protests threatening France's presidential race
World.content:
Three weeks into France’s student protests, questions are mounting over whether the demonstrations will fizzle out or evolve into a broader social movement.

 

The protests and school blockades began in Paris’s suburbs in mid-September, before rapidly spreading nationwide. Dramatic images of students climbing the iconic column at Paris' Place de la Bastille on Thursday managed to capture audiences worldwide.

The scenes carried historical weight given that the square stands on the site of the former Bastille fortress and state prison, stormed by Parisians on 14 July 1789 in a defining moment of the French Revolution.

Students protest against under-resourced schools at the Place de la Bastille in Paris, 8 October 2026. Aurelien Morissard/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

After its demolition, the Bastille became a lasting symbol of the triumph of regular citizens against political oppression. Taking to X on Thursday, hard-left France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon declared that the Bastille had been "retaken."

A range of student grievances lie at the heart of the movement, including long school days, overcrowded classrooms, run down schools and teacher absences. Their anger has resonated with young people across Europe, with students in Belgium and Italy also staging protests in recent days.

Could the student movement grow into something broader?

Another day of protests, backed by student and trade unions, is scheduled for Tuesday, 13 October. Meanwhile, a separate demonstration against the cost of living crisis and rising fuel prices — planned before the student movement erupted — is scheduled for 17 October.

There is speculation that the 17 October demonstration could mark the return of the yellow vest grassroots movement, which emerged in 2018 in reaction to a planned government fuel and diesel tax hike. For months, yellow vest protestors gathered every weekend to block roundabouts, motorways, and fuel depots across the country, with tense police clashes also occurring.

Students stand in front of a blockaded high school as they protest against under-resourced schools, in Paris, 9 October 2026. AP Photo

If student protests converge with wider social unrest, France could potentially face scenes reminiscent of May 1968. In recent weeks, many students have brandished banners referencing these historic demonstrations, which saw student protests escalate into a nationwide general strike.

At the time, several million workers joined the demonstrations, bringing the country to a standstill, but also sparking major wage negotiations. The movement also triggered a political crisis, prompting General de Gaulle, then France's president, to dissolve the National Assembly and call snap legislative elections in June 1968, in which his supporters secured a parliamentary majority.

Regardless, May 1968 left an indelible mark on France by dismantling rigid post-war social hierarchies. The demonstrations helped advance civil, student and labour rights, permanently embedding a tradition of mass protest into the nation's political identity.

France's tense political backdrop

At present, France's minority government is struggling to secure parliamentary support for its 2027 budget, as opposition parties resist proposed austerity measures. The country's public finances are squeezed, with the government projecting the public deficit to reach 5.4% of GDP for 2026, among the highest level in the eurozone.

The deepening cost-of-living crisis, driven largely by high fuel and energy prices, has intensified public frustration. The economic pressure on households has heightened social tensions across the country, less than six months away from the country's presidential elections — amid a highly fragmented political landscape.

According to a poll by public polling firm Ifop, carried out between 25 and 29 September, the far-right National Rally party's Marine Le Pen (35%) is currently leading for the first round, followed by Edouard Philippe (15%) and Jean-Luc Mélenchon (14%). Under these projections, the second round would see a Le Pen-Philippe face off. Other projections have predicted a Le Pen vs Mélenchon scenario for the second round.

A movement which shows no sign of abating

Despite Education Minister Édouard Geffray's announcement on Thursday that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed nationwide to schools facing teacher shortages, public anger shows little sign of abating. Geffray said the measure would likely cost “tens of millions of euros” for 2026.

Unions have criticised the plan as a short-term fix, warning that available substitute teachers may not match schools' needs in terms of specialisms or location. In cases where no replacement is available, classes may still go uncovered, while substitute teachers may be assigned support duties until a matching vacancy arises.

“We need to look at the details, because we have to be careful with this figure that has been thrown around," Jean-Rémi Girard, a teacher and president of the national union of schools and higher education (SNALC) told Euronews.

Students stand in front of a blockaded high school as they protest against under-resourced schools, in Paris, 9 October 2026. AP Photo

From the onset, students have been supported by teaching unions, as Girard pointed to a system in "crisis."

"We are increasingly struggling to replace teacher absences, French classrooms are among the most crowded in Europe, classrooms aren't properly equipped during heat waves. These are things we already know."

"The starting point is that the school system is in crisis, and it has been for a long time."

Major trade union federations in France have also rallied alongside students. Following Thursday's protests, the CGT, one of the country's largest trade unions, highlighted a range of demonstrations, some of which were unrelated to the student movement, declaring: "The struggles are multiplying, and the balance of power is shifting!"

Parallels with past student protests in France

Paolo Stuppia, professor of sociology and politics at Sciences Po Paris, drew parallels between the current demonstrations and past social movements in France, citing a range of movements including May 1968.

"It’s not new for students from the suburbs to rally around demands that are specific to them, and then for those demands to be taken up by other secondary schools located closer to the city centre."

For Stuppia, the fact that students from private schools have also participated in blockades marks a new departure for student protest movements. Many observers were also surprised that students from the Université Paris-Panthéon-Assas, which is viewed as having a conservative student body, staged a blockade on Thursday.

Nevertheless, Stuppia warned that the movement's momentum could be impacted by upcoming school half-term holidays in France.

"When there’s a two-week school break, it becomes harder to get a movement going again afterwards, because everything has been on hold."

A movement which has expanded in response to police violence

While many demonstrations have been peaceful, others have been marred by sideline riots and clashes with law enforcement authorities. According to figures shared by France's Ministry of Justice on Friday, there have been 6,877 arrests since the beginning of the movement, with 86% involving minors.

The scale of arrests is striking compared with those made in the initial weeks of the yellow vest movement in 2018, which saw 4,596 people placed in police custody during its first month.

Rights groups have condemned police brutality following a wave of shocking injuries to students.

Students face police officers in front of the Helene Boucher high School during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Paris, 8 October 2026. AP Photo

Outrage has grown over cases including a 15-year-old schoolboy who lost his left hand to a police stun grenade, a 16-year-old partially blinded by a rubber bullet, and a 14-year-old who suffered a shattered jaw and lost multiple teeth after being struck by a tear gas canister. The incidents are under internal investigation, with a total of 24 currently being conducted by the French police disciplinary body.

A United Nations spokesperson declared on Friday that the organisation was concerned about the situation in France, calling for demonstrations to remain peaceful and for the use of force to be proportionate.

Meanwhile, according to authorities, 761police officers and gendarmes have been injured since the beginning of the protests. Across the country, several schools have been damaged, burned or ransacked. In some cases, rioters have infiltrated the demonstrations.

Students face police officers in front of the Helene Boucher high School during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Paris, 8 October 2026. AP Photo

For Stuppia, the level of police repression in recent weeks was "unprecedented" since May 1968 protests.

Meanwhile, Valérie Becquet, a sociologist at CY Cergy Paris University and co-author with Paolo Stuppia of "Geopolitics of Youth: Engagement and (e)Mobilisation", said police brutality has helped draw adults into the movement.

"Adults [trade unions and parents] have been marching alongside students, but have also intervened through contacting lawyers and magistrates, in response to violence and possible human rights violations."

However, she said that there was also a portion of the adult population which viewed the protests with "disdain" and "dismissed or discredited" them.

Increasingly politicised protests

In a TV address on Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu lamented the “violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalised, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults.”

He took aim at “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles.” France goes to the polls for a presidential election in April. “We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth,” Lecornu said.

The government, joined by right-wing and far-right opposition parties, has accused Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party of exploiting and manipulating young people for political gain. Mélenchon has maintained that while his party supports the movement, it is not organising the protests and wants them to remain peaceful.

Students stand in front of a blockaded high school as they protest against under-resourced schools in Paris, October 2026. AP Photo

Ahead of the protests which took place on 5 October, the hard-left France Unbowed party hailed the fact that “student, secondary school, trade union and professional organisations" were "converging across the country."

For Becquet, although certain political leaders have been accused of “instrumentalising” student protests, secondary school students are on the whole able to distinguish between genuine political support and attempts to exploit the movement.

"There are people who have no particular interest in the movement, as you can see. Some are on the left, while others think 'well, this could be useful to us.'"

Students protest against under-resourced schools in Paris, 8 October. Aurelien Morissard/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

"Because of the way things work, and the way young people are treated — how they are dismissed and criticised — it ultimately creates opportunities for political intermediaries."

She warned that the protests could evolve into a broader social movement, given that frustration over school conditions reflect deeper anger about inequality across French society.

"There are inequalities at all levels, with gaps widening between different social groups."

"Given the rising cost of living, and the fact that working-class people already face numerous daily challenges, such as long working hours and commuting distances, in terms of social inequality, we are at a critical point."

Students share protests 'firsthand' on social media

Student demonstrations have spread rapidly across the country in part because footage of the initial demonstrations staged in the Paris suburbs went viral on social media.

According to Olivier Ertzscheid, senior lecturer in Information and Communication Sciences at the University of Nantes, social media allows students to organise themselves, but also to document protests firsthand from the ground.

"Social media allows them to document reality, to provide firsthand accounts of what is happening, both when things go well and when, unfortunately, they do not. Police investigations are now open, and social media images can be used as evidence, or at least play a part in the legal process."

Ertzscheid said that social media is also actively fostering a sense of connection and shared identity among protesters, which drives momentum.

A teenager looks at her mobile phone in London, June 15, 2026. AP Photo

"It is a way of building a sense of group identity and expressing one’s social connections, including their political awareness or at least civic engagement. This notion of young people's sense of belonging and social interaction is at play here, and these are very important in an age where the use of social media is so widespread."

Given that a large proportion of young people in France and across the world rely on social media as their main news source, the medium has also played a role in informing their perception of the protests, as well as the government's response.

Ertzscheid said there are no "hard and fast rules" governing how protests might evolve in coming weeks.

"Whatever happens next with this movement, we know that the media and social networks will act as echo chambers. By itself, no social media platform — however powerful it may be — is strong enough to trigger a movement. But these platforms are certainly helping with visibility and allowing students to get organised very quickly."

He described several different "converging" agendas ahead of upcoming protests in France, stating that "it is possible, that all these different starting points for anger or discontent could eventually converge. But equally, it is entirely possible that the student movement will fizzle out.”

World.title: Farming and solar power are competing for land. Can agrivoltaics solve the problem?
World.content:
As the sun moves westward across the sky in Murcia, Spain, solar panels capture its rays while sheltering diverse crops, from bell peppers to wine grapes and dragon fruit.

 

Known for its agriculture and abundant sunshine, this southeastern region is exploring whether, rather than competing for land, farming and solar energy can coexist peacefully.

“Agrivoltaics is the integration of food production with renewable energy production,” explains Silvia Tomasi, Senior Researcher at Eurac Research. This entails installing photovoltaic panels above, in between or at the margins of agricultural production, she adds.

A 2023 study estimated that Europe has the potential to generate 25 times its current electricity demand via agrivoltaics, also known as agri-PV.

Yet solar power is fraught with its own environmental and social costs. Requiring more land than other energy sources to generate the same amount of electricity, it has sparked conflicts over land use, especially in rural areas.

“Agrivoltaics has great potential: both economic benefits and environmental ones,” Tomasi says. “But then it’s always a matter of how the technology is implemented and who really benefits.”

Governments and Big Tech turn to agrivoltaics

The idea of turning southern Europe into a solar powerhouse received a high-profile endorsement in January, when Elon Musk said sparsely populated areas of Spain and Sicily could theoretically generate enough solar power for all of Europe.

Big Tech has already caught on. In southern Italy, Amazon and Apple have signed contracts to purchase power from large-scale agrivoltaic projects with a combined capacity of over 150 megawatts – enough to meet the yearly needs of roughly 100,000 Italian households.

Europe is also funding the shift. The EU-funded AGRISOL project intends to invest €1.9 million in agrivoltaics projects, including in Italy and Spain, while Italy alone has secured €1.7 billion in state aid for the initiative.

“For now, [agrivoltaics] is just a minimal contribution,” says Angelo Gentili, national secretary of Legambiente, Italy’s largest environmental organisation. “But if it expands, it will represent a big impulse for decarbonisation goals.”

Managing the impact on crops and land

EU and national rules increasingly require agriculture to remain a meaningful part of land where solar panels are installed. In France, projects must maintain at least 90 per cent of crop production compared to locally determined reference yields. In Italy, at least 70 per cent of the area must remain dedicated to agriculture.

Experts say not just any combination of solar and agriculture should qualify. “More than a definition, what we really need is a classification,” says Pilar Flores, who coordinates an EU-funded agrivoltaics project at the Murcian Institute for Agricultural and Environmental Research and Development (IMIDA). She says protecting agriculture should drive all classifications: “The key is to ensure there’s minimal loss [of arable land].”

Why use farmland rather than empty or abandoned land in the first place? Flores says the requirements are similar: relatively flat and near the grid. Unused land may also hold ecological value. “It’s not just a simple calculation of how much free land is left,” she says.

How agrivoltaics can benefit farmers

In some cases, agrivoltaics have been found to improve water-use efficiency, protect crops from extreme weather and increase the productivity of land. Solar installations can also help farmers face climate change. “Excessive rainfall and heat have heavily damaged agricultural fields, pushing farmers to abandon farmland,” says Gentili. “Agrivoltaics represent a great instrument to avoid land abandonment and profit gaps for farmers.”

Panels cast shade that can reduce evaporation, help soil retain moisture and offer relief to farmworkers and grazing animals. They can also protect crops from hail. Farmers can use the energy to power their own operations and sell any excess to the grid, or rent the space above their fields to energy producers.

But the benefits are not guaranteed, Flores warns. “All these opportunities are sometimes discussed as if they always happened, but it depends on the agrivoltaic system used and the specific characteristics of the site.” In Murcia, her team found that water-stressed peppers grew better under solar panels than well-watered ones. “You have to analyse each case and each location,” she says.

Special mounted solar panels are installed over a biological apple fruit tree plantation at an Agrivoltaics research project in Gelsdorf, western Germany, Aug. 30, 2022. AP Photo/Martin Meissner

But who really benefits from agrivoltaics?

Not all farmers are convinced. To Fabrizio Garbarino, president of the Italian farmers’ union Associazione Rurale Italiana, agrivoltaics fail to address the root problems farmers face. “Agrivoltaics are taking advantage of the farming sector crisis in Italy while we should actually focus on real solutions for preventing farmland abandonment,” he says. “To me, this just sounds like a shortcut.”

Startups representing larger companies, including data centre developers, are hounding farmers for their land, he says. “Even if the energy produced is good, we’re taking away [farmers’] land to support businesses that require a lot of energy.”

Big Tech firms say agrivoltaic power-purchase agreements help them reach net-zero targets. But a PPA does not necessarily mean that the electricity from a particular solar farm physically supplies a particular company facility, and the exact carbon footprints of AI data centres remain opaque.

A 2025 study co-authored by Tomasi, based on expert interviews across four European regions, found that the benefits of agrivoltaics can favour large-scale farmers, landowners and investors over smaller farmers and local communities. It also found that excluding residents and ecosystems from decision-making can deepen existing power imbalances.

High upfront costs and grid connection queues mean large projects backed by multinationals tend to dominate the sector. A 2025 review by the Italian newspaper Today.it found that about 86 per cent of the roughly €775 million in government funds for agrivoltaic projects went to large-scale projects, including ones owned by foreign multinationals.

In September, a new agrivoltaics project financed by an Israeli company in Tuscany sparked widespread outrage and raised concerns over who gets to profit.

Tomasi says local communities must have a voice to ensure a just transition. “Big investors going into places they really don’t know anything about, with a top-down approach… and getting the economic benefits from the renewable energy generation side of agrivoltaics… shouldn’t be labelled as agrivoltaics, from my point of view.”

‘Agriculture should not be a secondary concern’

Flores says administrations can help by offering farmers funding and giving agrivoltaic systems priority access to the grid.

There is also the question of what kind of agriculture the income supports. To live up to the environmental promise, one study has noted, “the type of agriculture funded by the rental income from agrivoltaics should not be a secondary concern”. Instead, the author argues, this rent could subsidise agroecological practices or help farmers transition away from industrial farming.

Agrivoltaics has the potential to be mutually beneficial to farmers and the renewable energy sector. It can help protect farmland, support farmers facing climate change and contribute to Europe’s decarbonisation goals. But it also risks becoming a greenwashing opportunity, a crutch for unsustainable farming practices, or a way of meeting growing corporate energy demand on arable land. On its own, it is not a silver bullet. Much depends on how the systems are designed, who owns them and, ultimately, who benefits.

“The goal of agrivoltaics is to protect farmland and the entire ecosystem; that’s the philosophy,” says Flores. “We have to be able to distinguish that from other interests.”

Reporting for this story was made possible by the Magma Environmental Reporting Fellowship.

World.title: Europe's best Christmas markets to visit in 2026, according to travellers
World.content:
As we get deeper into autumn, it feels as if we’ll blink and Christmas will be upon us.

 

With the festive season comes new opportunities to book a winter trip away, and a favourite must-do for many travellers is to visit a Christmas market.

There are more than 1,500 in Europe alone, and this year more than 800,000 travellers have voted for their favourites via the European Best Destinations platform.

A total of 20 were included in the final ranking, and we’re taking a closer look at the top five to give you some inspiration on where to go to shop, drink gleuwein and get into the festive spirit in 2026.

European Christmas markets: The top picks by travellers

Craiova, Romania

You might never have heard of Craiova, but the Romanian city has pipped far more famous Christmas markets to the top spot.

It’s an absolutely huge space, with more than 280,000 square meters transformed into a festive wonderland each year.

The theme in 2026 is The Nutcracker, and visitors will be able to see giant ornaments and toy-shaped sculptures along with countless sparkling lights.

The market, which runs from mid-November to early January, will also boast Eastern Europe’s highest-flying Santa sleigh, as well as an ice rink, a Ferris wheel, and traditional hand-painted chalets.

Visitors to the Craiova market also sing the praises of the food on offer here, which celebrates the flavours of Eastern Europe and beyond, serving dishes from the likes of Armenia, Georgia, Greece, Bulgaria and Serbia.

Zurich, Switzerland

Zurich may be better known for its chocolate and banking than Christmas markets, but the Swiss city has made a name for itself as one of Europe’s top festive destinations.

The main attraction is Wienachtsdorf at Sechseläutenplatz, between the Opera House and Lake Zurich. The market is filled with wooden chalets, twinkling lights and a huge Christmas tree, combining traditional Alpine touches with the city’s more polished feel.

There’s plenty more to discover beyond the main market, which was also voted as the most beautiful Christmas market in Europe. Weihnachtsallee near the main station is now in its third year, with around 80 rotating stalls selling international food, design-led crafts and, of course, plenty of fondue.

There’s even a dome dedicated to mulled wine, making it a popular spot for locals and visitors looking to warm up.

Zurich also puts its own artistic spin on the festive season with the Illuminarium at the Swiss National Museum. The courtyard is transformed with lights, music and immersive displays, adding something a little different to the city’s Christmas celebrations.

Zurich’s Christmas market offers festive cheer coupled with traditional Swiss refinement Seraina Larissa/Unsplash

Riga, Latvia

Riga may not have the same name recognition as some of Europe’s bigger Christmas destinations, but Latvia’s capital puts on a seriously atmospheric festive display each winter.

The main market takes over Doma Square in the heart of the UNESCO-listed Old Town, with wooden chalets selling Latvian crafts, cosy knitwear and local treats.

From late November to early January, the square fills with the smells of mulled wine, roasted almonds and cinnamon, while choirs and folk performers add a distinctly Baltic feel.

But Riga’s Christmas appeal goes well beyond the market itself. The city is known for its spectacular lights, with parks, squares and canals transformed into a glowing winter wonderland.

Head to places including Opera Square, Bastejkalns and Kronvalda Park to see installations inspired by Latvian fairy tales, with light, music and storytelling bringing the festive season to life.

Lisbon, Portugal

Lisbon offers a slightly different take on the Christmas market, swapping snowy streets for mild temperatures and winter sunshine.

Wonderland Lisboa takes over Parque Eduardo VII from late November to early January, with the Portuguese capital’s biggest Christmas market returning for its 11th edition in 2026.

This year’s theme, “The Roots of Christmas”, brings together nature, art, food and entertainment, with local artisans, live performances and plenty of family-friendly attractions.

There’s also a Ferris wheel offering views across the city, alongside a traditional carousel and plenty of opportunities for Christmas shopping.

Food is a big part of the experience too, with the Wonderland Lisboa Food Court serving Portuguese festive favourites, regional specialities and seasonal sweets.

More than 1.2 million people visited in 2025, making it a popular choice for anyone who wants their Christmas market with a side of sunshine.

Debrecen, Hungary

Hungary’s second-largest city may be less famous than the capital Budapest, but it certainly knows how to do Christmas properly.

In the winter, Debrecen’s main squares and pedestrian streets are transformed with glowing installations and wooden stalls selling handmade crafts, toys, decorations and Christmas ornaments.

There’s plenty of food to enjoy too, with classic festive treats including mulled wine, roasted chestnuts and kürtőskalács, the sweet Hungarian chimney cake.

More than 100 cultural events are held throughout the season, featuring more than 200 performers, while families can make the most of an ice rink and the Fairytale Town attraction.

There are also plenty of special events, including traditional advent candle-lighting ceremonies and a St Nicholas weekend complete with a carriage arrival, concerts and a mini train.

World.title: ESA director general reveals €10bn plan to get to space without NASA
World.content:
The European Space Agency received record budget commitments of more than €22 billion from member states at its ministerial council meeting in 2025, a 32% increase on 2022.

 

Member states also gave ESA a historic mandate to use space technology for non-aggressive security and defence, including technologies to monitor external borders.

With that backing, ESA director general Josef Aschbacher wants Europe to take its next big step: developing the ability to launch its own astronauts into space.

In the latest episode of The Big Question, Josef sat down with Hannah Brown to discuss Europe’s independent future in space.

‘Why don’t we do it ourselves?’

Since its founding in 1975 (and its first astronaut mission in 1983), the European Space Agency has relied on international partners, including NASA and Russia, for astronaut launches.

And while this arrangement has worked for all this time, geopolitical tensions are pushing Europe to seek an alternative.

Only the US, China and Russia have the capability to launch astronauts into space. But political tensions with China and Russia leave ESA reliant on the US.

And in recent years, NASA has partnered with SpaceX to launch astronauts into space. One way or another, today, ESA astronauts travel to space aboard a US spacecraft.

“SpaceX has already announced that they want to decommission Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon (the crew vehicles that bring the astronauts to space) probably around 2029,” Josef explained.

“That means in a few years, we will not have at least this capability available anymore. There may be others coming up, which we do not know today.”

This leaves Europe facing uncertainty over how to get its astronauts into space in the future.

To ensure reliable access and support investment in European industry, Josef is developing a plan for Europe to strengthen its position as a global space power by gaining the ability to launch its own astronauts.

ESA director general Josef Aschbacher sat down with Hannah Brown on The Big Question Euronews

Is space autonomy good for the European economy?

Of course, this won’t happen overnight and it needs political approval from ESA’s member states to secure funding.

Here’s how it might work.

Europe isn’t starting completely from scratch. It already has strong technological capabilities and world-leading programmes like Copernicus (Earth observation) and Galileo (satellite navigation constellation), as well as a talented workforce.

But Europe lacks its own crew vehicle and recovery system, in other words the means to get astronauts up there and bring them safely back to Earth.

Josef estimated that with a budget of around €10 billion, ESA could develop these independent capabilities in the next 10 years.

And yes, €10 billion is an enormous amount of money, but what’s the alternative?

ESA is facing the prospect of spending billions of euros in the coming years either way. The question is how to turn that spending into an investment in Europe’s space industry rather than simply a cost.

The International Space Station is essentially a floating laboratory where ESA does much of its vital science. After its decommission in 2032, this is likely to be replaced by a commercial space station.

Without its independent access to space, Europe will have to continue to rely on buying seats aboard US spacecraft with uncertain availability and then rent facilities aboard commercial space stations for research. Josef estimated that this would come at a cost of around €5 billion over the next 10 years.

“But the money is lost, or lost in the sense it's being spent not in Europe. So I'd rather invest this funding in Europe, strengthen our industry, increase the autonomy of Europe in this domain,” Josef explained.

But he stressed this would not mean an end to international collaboration for Europe.

“[We could] even offer a seat maybe to our friends and colleagues from Japan or Australia or some other countries, and I think this is also something that Europe could consider to build up its own strength, its autonomy, not to isolate, not at all - the opposite, but to be a strong partner internationally to other countries and other agencies.”

World.title: Trump says Ukraine needs new president after Zelenskyy condemns Russia fuel deal
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, claiming his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not tried sufficiently to bring an end to Russia's invasion.

 

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump told reporters at the White House before departing for Tennessee on Saturday.

The statement was welcomed by Russian President Vladimir Putin's top economic negotiator, who called Trump's remarks as "iconic and historic".

"President Trump joins the many who believe that Ukraine needs leadership actually focused on peace, not Zelensky's warmongering," Kirill Dmitriev, the Kremlin's special envoy on economic cooperation, said in a post on X.

Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine's foreign minister, said Zelenskyy "has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide."

"Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support," he added in a social media post on Saturday.

Trump's statement comes after Zelenskyy denounced Washington's deal with Moscow to buy Russian diesel in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.

European officials expressed dismay over the deal, warning it would help finance Russia's war efforts.

"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 tons during the month of November," Trump said following talks with Putin.

Zelenskyy called the move a "gift to Putin" that would "not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis," he added.

Diesel prices in the US have surged since the US and Israel launched a joint attack on Iran on February 28. Both the wars in Iran and Ukraine have both contributed to a global energy crisis, yet Trump places the blame for soaring US diesel prices solely on Zelenskyy.

He has previously urged the Ukrainian leader to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other critical infrastructure, saying the attacks are causing the global shortage.

“He (Zelenskyy) wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel,” Trump said on Saturday.

"And we told him, 'do whatever you want, but don't hit the diesel fuel, because there's a big problem.' And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel," he added.

Trump's approval rating has significantly dropped over the course of his second term. According to an Associated Press-NORC Centre for Public Affairs Research poll conducted last month, 71% of American adults disapprove of how Trump is handling Iran.

Europe backs Kyiv

It came as the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, on Saturday said suspending sanctions on Russian diesel would only provide Moscow with more revenues to fuel its war.

"This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t," she wrote on X.

"On Monday, EU Foreign Ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war," she added.

Zelenskyy also touted a series of conversations with European allies on Saturday, including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron.

Zelenskyy said he had held a "very good and timely conversation" with Burnham as he thanked him for his continued support.

According to Downing Street, Burnham used the opportunity to reiterate his "complete solidarity" with Ukraine and pledged to continue to strengthen UK sanctions on Russia.

Zelenskyy said he had also spoken with Macron about the "challenges posed by the easing of sanctions on oil products" and said Kyiv and Paris were preparing further meetings.

World.title: Lee Claims World Gold as Tasoev Secures His Third World Title in Baku
World.content:
Today closes out the individual competition at the Baku World Judo Championships and it's time for the heavyweights to take centre stage in Azerbaijan.

 

Before the finals, the traditional flag-passing ceremony was held to commemorate the closing of the event, as Azerbaijan passed the IJF flag to Kazakhstan - with Astana set to host the World Championships in 2027.

At +78kg, 19 year old Hyeonji LEE was on fire enroute to the final, with ippon in every contest. With a World bronze from last year, she would be feeling confident that this was her moment to claim the red backpatch.

Facing her was Romane DICKO, a former World Champion and no stranger to the podium. DICKO would be looking to regain the mantle and become a two time World Champion. Displaying a groundwork masterclass today, could she repeat her former success?

In the final, LEE continued her dominant run and bested DICKO with a waza-ari that transitioned into a hold down. The Korean had written her name into history. A composed finish to a remarkable day that sealed the biggest title of her career.

I’m so grateful that I was able to repay everyone who was cheering for me. It’s been a really special day Hyeonji Lee

IOC Member Ms Yael ARAD awarded the medals.

In the +100kg category, reigning double World Champion Inal TASOEV had come to Baku to earn his third title and looked in complete control on his route through the draw. Powerful and assured throughout the day, he arrived in the final with another World gold firmly within reach.

His opponent was Azerbaijan’s own Ushangi KOKAURI. With the crowd behind him, he had the chance to turn their energy into the biggest victory of his career. Every roar from the stands added pressure, but also belief that a home World title was possible.

In the +100kg final, TASOEV delivered a moment of pure judo feeling to score ippon, and achieve an incredible third World title. TASOEV will wear the red backpatch for another year. A commanding finish underlined his status as the man to beat.

I don’t really like the phrase “three time World Champion” I’ve simply become World Champion once again and I experienced those emotions again Inal Tasoev

Azerbaijan Minister of Youth and Sport Mr Farid GAYIBOV awarded the medals.

World.title: Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff
World.content:
The escalating clash between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia now threatens to ignite the already tense rivalry between Israel and Turkey in the Horn of Africa. This week, Turkey threw its military weight behind Saudi Arabia, while Somaliland – a self-declared state recognised only by Israel – is urgently seeking Israeli military support.

Advertising

Somaliland, a breakaway state from Somalia, is calling on Israel to provide military hardware. “We need air defence systems,” Mohamed Osman Fadal, a senior foreign affairs adviser to Somaliland’s president, said in a Middle East Eye interview this month.

Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi made a similar request last month for Israeli military support.

Last December, Israel became the first nation to recognise Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991. Because of its close ties to Israel, Somaliland now fears it could become a target for the Houthis, who operate from Yemen just across the Gulf of Aden and have previously targeted Israel.

“The Houthi threat is growing; it’s a major issue,” said Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

“Access to the Red Sea and Somaliland’s location just across from Yemen are very important, and I think this is where Israel recognises that it’s difficult to deal with the threat only from afar, and it’s important to have allies in the Horn of Africa,” she added.

Israel, which is in the midst of an election campaign ahead of the 27 October vote, has not commented on the request. But Lindenstrauss predicts a favourable response. “Obviously, if you look at the location, there should be some military support," she said.

Turkey’s backing for Somalia

Yet Somaliland’s call for military aid is fuelled by more than just anxiety over the Houthis. Somalia’s government is still intent on reclaiming Somaliland, branding it a rogue state. At the same time, Turkey has stepped up its military support for Somalia, deploying F-16s and advanced drones in January, and running its largest overseas military base to train Somali troops.

Somaliland president makes 'historic' visit to Israel

“Turkey has strong defence cooperation with Somalia; Somaliland sees that as an issue for them. It sees them as a potential future threat down the road. And so that’s why they’re calling for Israeli security support,” explained Horn of Africa analyst Omar Mahmood of the International Crisis Group.

“I think what’s happening is both sides, Somalia and Somaliland, are drawing external actors into their local dispute,” added Mahmood. “So it’s elevating what has been an unresolved but a local dispute for quite some time into something broader, something more regional.”

Tensions between Turkey and Israel have also been mounting, fuelled by Israel’s ongoing wars in Gaza and Lebanon and Ankara’s vocal support for Hamas. Both nations now see each other as an increasing threat.

“There is a security dilemma evolving between Turkey and Israel,” warns Lindenstrauss. “What Turkey does for its security, Israel sees as threatening. What Israel does for its defences in [Syria] is seen as threatening.”

Soli Ozel, an expert on Turkey at the Institut Montaigne in France, warns that because Somalia holds such strategic value for Turkey, any Israeli military involvement in Somaliland could dangerously escalate the situation.

“They may consider the deployment of Israeli missiles in Somaliland another destabilising factor,” said Ozel. “But I don’t think that the F-16s or the drones would be used against Somaliland, honestly; at least for the moment, I wouldn’t expect that to happen.”

Lebanon becomes latest battleground in Turkish-Israeli tensions

Containment, not conflict

Ozel argues that while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan are trading increasingly bellicose rhetoric, both countries are engaged in a high-stakes battle of containment rather than conflict.

“The theatrics and the realities of Turkish-Israeli relations may not be exactly the same,” explained Ozel. “I don’t think they will fight, but they are both showing their colours, right? Israel sent missiles to Somaliland; the Turks send F-16s and drones in order to set limits to what the other party will do.”

Turkey is preparing to expand its military footprint in the region. This week, Turkey and Pakistan pledged armed support to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August, a pact binding the three nations to mutual defence.

While the specifics remain unclear, Lindenstrauss notes that despite rising friction between Turkey and Israel, both countries may still find common cause in confronting the Houthis.

“I think the recognition that the Houthis are not something that is seen as only Israel’s problem, and it’s not just a minor proxy of Iran, but it’s a major problem that many states have to join together to deal with. I think that’s actually good news,” said Lindenstrauss.

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Yet Mahmood cautions that as clashes in the Red Sea escalate, Israel’s possible deployment of military hardware to Somaliland points to a worrying new trend.

“Horn actors need to realise that while they’re inviting external actors in to support their own ambitions locally, to get one step over their political adversaries, they risk turning their theatre into a wider proxy battleground. And so certainly, I think there’s a risk that those types of tensions can spill over,” he warned.

World.title: Podcast: AI in France, translators fight back, musicians' mentor
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is everywhere in France but who's using it, and how? We also look at its impact on translators and how they're striving to keep humans at the helm. And Nadia Boulanger – the pioneering French composer and conductor who taught generations of musical greats.

Advertising

AI is widely used in France, despite many peoples' misgivings. Tech consultant Frederic Cavazza says adoption is being driven by individuals, rather than a coherent or systemic approach. That results in a paradox: the technology is everywhere, but guidance and confidence in it is lacking. (Listen @2'40'')

One field that is heavily impacted by generative AI in France – and the non-English-language world – is translation. Low-cost translation agencies are increasingly using machines to deliver first drafts and relying on humans for ungratifying, poorly paid "post-editing". But translators are fighting back. The En chair et en os collective and the recently-launched STEF union for translators in publishing marked last week's World Translation Day with symbolic strike action. They gathered to find collective ways of keeping humans at the heart of the translation process, including an initiative to "sabotage" the post-editing system. (Listen @17'50'')

The story of French musician Nadia Boulanger, a talented composer and the first woman to conduct some of the world's top orchestras. Today she is best remembered for teaching an extraordinary number of the 20th century's most famous musicians, from Aaron Copland to Philip Glass, Burt Bacharach and Quincy Jones. (Listen @10'30'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

World.title: Demographic change: Germany's population is declining, but not everywhere
World.content:
By 2045, Germany will have more older people, fewer workers, and a smaller population overall. Yet some regions will defy this trend. Their success depends on how much they have to offer.

Germany's population is expected to decline from 83.5 million in 2025 to around 81.8 million by 2045, according to a new study from the Berlin Institute for Population and Development (Berlin-Institut für Bevölkerung und Entwicklung ), in collaboration with the Wüstenrot Foundation , a non-profit that supports research on housing, urban development, and social change.

The decline in population alone is not the central challenge. More significant is the continuing rise in the number of retirees alongside a steadily shrinking workforce. Across Germany, the working-age population is projected to decrease by 4.7% by 2045.

"The baby boomer generation is retiring, while significantly smaller cohorts are following. Birth rates are falling, and immigration is not sufficient to offset the growing surplus of deaths over births," said Institute President Catherina Hinz when presenting the study in Berlin.

The term "baby boomers" refers to those born in the 1960s, when annual births exceeded one million. Thereafter, the birth rate fell sharply, effectively halving.

The economy matters

Germany's population may be shrinking, but according to the study, this trend is far from uniform across the country. In the years ahead, a region's economic attractiveness, and the financial strength that comes with it, will become even more important than it is today.

"Some regions will lose substantial numbers of residents and workers in the years ahead, while others continue to grow. Even within eastern Germany, southern Germany, and rural areas, the demographic and economic divide is widening," said Hinz.

"Demographic change is unfolding before our very eyes, and its effects are being felt across the country," Hinz added. "Its consequences can still be mitigated, but they can no longer be avoided. And the longer we wait, the narrower our scope for action will become."

Hinz's warning is echoed by Frederick Sixtus of the Berlin Institute. Almost every region now records more deaths than births, he notes, a consequence of decades of low birth rates. The implication is clear: Migration, both inward and outward, now shapes a region's demographic trajectory. Over recent decades, immigration from abroad has repeatedly helped stabilize population trends. Yet migration alone is no longer enough to halt the aging of society.

According to the study, several factors are critical if a region is to remain attractive to people relocating from abroad or from other parts of Germany: High-quality jobs offering good pay and working conditions, a sufficient supply of skilled workers for local businesses, financially robust municipalities, reliable childcare, and efficient transport and mobility infrastructure.

Berlin leads the way

Many major cities are expected to continue to grow in the years ahead, according to Manuel Slupina of the Wüstenrot Foundation. The study projects that Berlin will lead the way, with the capital's population increasing by almost 10% by 2045. Other cities expected to attract people include Hamburg, Frankfurt am Main, Munich, and Düsseldorf in western Germany, as well as Leipzig, Dresden, and Potsdam in the east.

The study's authors argue that the familiar distinction between urban and rural areas does not hold true everywhere. The hinterlands of many major cities are also expected to grow. While young people are increasingly drawn to metropolitan centers, families with children tend to settle in the surrounding areas. Among the places likely to lose population are several large cities in western Germany, including Bremen, Duisburg, Dortmund, and Kaiserslautern, whose economic appeal has gradually diminished. At the bottom of the ranking are many sparsely populated regions, a large number of them in eastern Germany.

Competition for talent

Twelve of the 20 districts and independent cities with the weakest overall ratings are now located in eastern Germany, up from five in the previous assessment in 2019. According to the study, these regions are also expected to see the steepest declines in their working-age populations, with losses of up to 18% by 2045. The authors conclude that competition for workers is therefore set to become one of the key demographic challenges of the decades ahead.

In this competition, the southern German states of Bavariaand Baden-Württemberg are regarded as having the strongest prospects. Bavaria ranks particularly highly thanks to its robust economy, which is thriving across much of the state, and its strong labor market. Women, older people, and people without German citizenship are also more likely to be employed in Bavaria than elsewhere. The ranking shows that economically successful regions are more effective at integrating different population groups into the labor market than weaker ones.

Why Germans want children but are having fewer babies To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Policymakers must find local solutions

Under Germany's constitution, the country is committed to ensuring that people enjoy comparable opportunities, and with them the prospect of a good life, regardless of where they live.

The researchers offer clear recommendations to policymakers. They argue that the focus must be on addressing structural challenges and regional disparities. "What may be the right response for a growing major city is not necessarily the right one for a shrinking rural district," says Slupina. Tailor-made solutions are needed, but they require the right framework conditions. "There needs to be less rigid regulation, more scope for local initiative, and greater financial resources, especially for municipalities and those actively engaged at the local level." Slupina's message is clear: Regions should be trusted to shape their own futures.

Local authorities would no doubt welcome that. For years, mayors and district administrators have been calling for greater financial autonomy. They are currently seeking a larger share of overall tax revenues for municipalities. The federal government and the states, however, argue that they face budgetary constraints of their own. Yet both sides recognize that, sooner or later, Germany will have little choice but to reform its system of fiscal federalism.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Ukrainian prisoners of war and defectors have been gathered into a Russian battalion to face Ukrainian forces — why? And how?
World.content:
Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.

Pavlo Oliynyk, 25, says he joined enemy forces to escape Russian captivity. Before his capture in the Donbas region in 2024, he was a senior lieutenant for Ukraine's armed forces.

As a prisoner of war (POW), he says he was electrocuted, beaten, and psychologically tortured. So when he received the offer to join the Maksym Kryvonis battalion — named after a famous 17th-century Cossack commander — he accepted.

Oliynyk says he wanted to use this opportunity to reach the front lines, so he could escape to Ukrainian-controlled territory. DW was able to contact Oliynyk through his lawyer.

'Ukrainian volunteers' consist mostly of POWs

Reports of Russian combat units consisting of Ukrainian prisoners of war and former servicemembers of Ukraine's armed forces began emerging in late 2022. Several detachments were initially formed and in August 2026, they were merged into the so-called "Ukrainian Volunteer Special Forces Brigade."

Of the individual units, the Maksym Kryvonis battalion has perhaps drawn the most public attention for having evidently taken part in combat. Its true size is unknown — Russian media reports claim about 200 fighters while available footage only suggests several dozen.

An investigative team of the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne has identified over 30 members and confirmed they are all former Ukrainian servicemen, captured by Russian forces between 2023 and 2024.

Pavlo Oliynyk says he defected to Russian forces in order to escape captivity Image: Privatarchiv

An 'imitation' of Russian legions fighting for Ukraine

Pavel Luzin, an expert for Russian foreign policy and defense at the Center for European Policy Analysis, believes these units are an "imitation" of the Russian Volunteer Corps and the Freedom of Russia Legion — units in the Ukrainian armed forces, consisting of Russian citizens — and an attempt by Moscow to distract from the fact that these units exist in the first place. Ukrainian intelligence services tend to agree.

"It bothers them that Russians would fight on Ukraine's side, but Ukrainians won't fight on Russia's side," Yevhen Shybalov, author and veteran of the war in Ukraine, tells DW. He adds that Russian troops have never tried to hide the fact that Russian volunteer units in Ukrainian ranks were the main reason Russian forces wanted to create Ukrainian units for their owns ranks.

Just how voluntary are these combat units?

In 2025, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) reported that 95% of the released Ukrainian POWs interviewed reported torture or ill-treatment during Russian captivity.

Bill Wiley, executive director of the NGO Commission for International Justice and Accountability (CIJA), says that the physical and psychological state of the returned combatants raises serious doubts that their recruitment was voluntary. Mykhailo Savva of the Center for Civil Liberties, a Kyiv-based human rights organization, points to the criminal procedures running against several of the battalion members, which he says indicates that these suggest the combatants had switched sides voluntarily.

But where to draw the line between voluntary and involuntary recruitment? The war veteran and human rights activist Maksym Butkevych, who spent 28 months as a prisoner of war, says the conditions in Russian captivity make that line hard to distinguish. On the one hand, he says, there is a constant atmosphere of pressure, and on the other hand, it's not implausible that some prisoners defected out of ideological proximity.

How were Ukrainian prisoners made to join Russian forces?

Butkevych tells DW that between 2022 and 2023, all Ukrainian prisoners of war had received offers, "more or less persistently," to join the Russian army. In his case, he recounts, it was after he had been severely mistreated. "They showed us they could do anything they wanted to us," the veteran explains, "which was why we should agree to everything."

The veteran Shybalov reports similar experiences. He speaks of attempts to force confessions of war crimes, or to recruit members for Russia's intelligence services, and tells DW all prisoners were first interrogated and then made certain propositions under duress.

"You can torture people to get them to confess, but there comes the difficult moment when you need to give them a weapon," he says. "That's why it's more about psychological pressure, and forcing voluntary compliance."

Butkevych confirms these accounts with his own tales. But neither veteran has ever met someone willing to join Russian units, they say.

What happens after conscription?

Oliynyk, from the Maksym Kryvonis battalion, says he initially turned down multiple bids to join Russian forces. He says he only accepted the fourth offer so he could flee.

He claims he didn't sign official Defense Ministry paperwork, but a private contract with an individual offering military services. Afterwards, he says, he was brought to a room where he heard lectures and saw videos and photos he was later asked to retell.

Putin's foreign fighters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Control and mistreatment

He says fellow servicemembers in the Maksym Kryvonis battalion consisted both of those who had switched sides of their own volition, and those who had been forced.

In a video circulating online that appears to be of a trial in Ukraine, he also says that former Ukrainian POWs in the unit were followed and guarded by mercenaries of the private military company Redut. In the same video, he also speaks of beatings and torture, and receiving monthly wages in envelopes handed out by a member of Russia's military intelligence.

He tells DW he had been given a phone, but that he was too scared to call anyone in Ukraine because it was under constant surveillance. He denies having fought against Ukrainians, as he fled in March 2025 before his first deployment in the Donetsk province. After running across a field, he says he spent two days hiding from drones in basements and houses before making contact with Ukrainian fighters.

Now, Oliynyk has been in detention in Ukraine for nearly two years while authorities investigate possible treason. He has yet to be formally charged.

Sergey Nikitin contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Ukrainian.

World.title: US: Justice Department probes Trump's press pool boycott for antitrust violation
World.content:
The Department of Justice is investigating whether the five news organizations violated antitrust laws when they suspended their coverage of Trump in protest. The networks under probe are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.

The US Department of Justice announced on Saturday that it is investigating whether the White House press pool's decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month, violated the nation's anti trust law.

Group boycotts among business competitors might violate US law, spokesperson Emily Covington said.

"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws," she said.

The networks under the scrutiny are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.

Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists' regional director of the Americas, criticized the administration's decision to investigate.

"The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access," Zamora said on X. "The public's right to know depends on that access."

Under pressure — Trump's fractured America To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why is Trump's press pool under investigation?

On September 21, a pool of five broadcasters ceased presidential coverage after the Trump administration barred news networks CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, saying covering the president was a "privilege, not a right."

Trump bans media outlets from White House To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As a result, the five television networks suspended coverage in protest and refused to provide replacement program.

The news outlets also sued the administration, accusing it of violating free speech and free press rights under the First Amendment of the US Constitution and pursuing retaliation over their coverage.

On September 24, the White House reinstated their press credentials after a US district Judge ordered the administration to "immediately return, reinstate and restore" their access.

The president has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" and clashed with reporters during interviews.

The White House press pool is a roating group of news outlets which cover the president and accompany him on official duties.

CNN is one of the five news organizations, along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBS, that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the cost of covering the president and take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.

The White House press pool has now become a proxy for a fight over press freedom.

World.title: Shooter kills 8 people and himself in Pennsylvania — police
World.content:
The 45-year-old shooter, who is yet to be identified, carried out the killings at his home in Erie. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro offered support as the lakeside city grieves.

A man killed eight people and himself during a mass shooting at a house in Erie, Pennsylvania, local police said Saturday.

What do we know so far?

Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said seven of the eight victims were related to the shooter, with the eighth person being a family friend. The shooter had died of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound before authorities arrived at the scene.

Among the victims was a 1-year-old girl and 5-year-old boy, with a pregnant woman also dead in the shooting.

"Some scenes stay with you long after you leave them. This is one of those tragic scenes," Lorah said, describing an "eerie silence" when police arrived at the home.

The Erie SWAT team was also present at the scene of the shooting Image: Matt Barnum/WJET/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

The identity of the 45-year-old shooter has not yet been revealed by authorities. The motive for the massacre is also still unclear, with police pursuing an investigation.

At a press conference, Erie Mayor Daria Devlin addressed the families of the victims.

"I am so deeply sorry. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier," she said. "But you do need to know that our entire community is with you, we're grieving with you. And we are here to support you."

Pennsylvania Governor Shapiro offers support after 'tragic mass shooting'

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro spoke with Devlin by phone and offered his support to Erie.

"I've spoken with Mayor Devlin and offered my administration's full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night — killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians," Shapiro said in a statement post on X.

Shapiro said his "heart breaks for this family" and added that he and his wife Lori Shapiro "are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community."

Shapiro, a Democrat, has pushed for gun control bills in his state and signed an executive order in 2024 to reestablish the Pennsylvania Office of Gun Violence Prevention.

World.title: Storm Isaias leaves 4 dead as it moves across southern US
World.content:
The storm, which is now a post-tropical cyclone, had made landfall near Destin, Florida on Friday evening. The storm brings heavy rainfall and powerful winds and has caused mass power outages in Florida and Alabama.

Storm Isaias has left four people dead as it moves across the southern United States, officials said Saturday.

What's the latest on the storm?

Two of the deaths were in Florida, while the other two were in Alabama.

The storm originally made landfall on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida. It is the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.

Florida, Alabama and Georgia have all declared states of emergency due to the storm. According to PowerOutage.com, over 500,000 customers are without power in Florida and Alabama.

The Florida Division of Emergency Management said approximately 5,000 Florida National Guard soldiers and airmen have been "activated to support impacted communities."

A woman was killed in Florida after a tree fell on her home Image: Joe Raedle/Getty Images/AFP

The storm brings heavy rainfall and powerfall winds, bringing the risks of flooding and tornadoes. It has ripped the roofs off buildings and downed trees in its wake.

Storm moving into West Virginia

The storm has weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and is moving over the southern US states of Tennessee and Kentucky into West Virginia, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).

In its latest update, the NHC warned of possible flash and urban flooding and said "landslides are possible across the Southern Appalachians." It also warned of wind gusts along with additional power outages and downed trees.

In addition, swells from Isaias will continue to impact much of the Gulf coasts of the US, Mexico and western Cuba, and are "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions." NHC said a couple of tornadoes are also possible across eastern Georgia and the Carolinas.

Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon has hit Category 4 strength as it barrels towards Mexico's Pacific coast, where it is expected to make landfall on Sunday. The storm is expected to impact Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for American tourists.

World.title: Palestinian president postpones elections until late 2027
World.content:
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas previously committed to holding legislative elections in November 2026. He said that due to "obstacles ⁠posed by Israeli measures" the vote would be pushed back until late next year.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas has postponed legislative elections for almost another year, according to a decree issued on Friday.

Abbas had previously scheduled legislative elections for November 28, and presidential elections for early next year. Now both elections have been pushed back to September 11, 2027.

They would be the first Palestinian elections in more than 20 years.

Why are Palestinian elections postponed?

In his decree, Abbas cited "obstacles ⁠posed by Israeli measures" as the reason for the postponement of "free, fair and inclusive elections."

He pointed to Israeli settler violence, military attacks and restrictions of movent in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, as well as Israel's continued withholding of tax revenue.

Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Gaza, where Israeli strikes continue after three years of war, the decree cited "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions," the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces and a lack of progress towards reconstruction, among other issues.

Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded to the news on X, calling the decree "yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability."

A commitment to hold elections

Abbas had committed in writing to French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that elections would be held as part of France's recognition of the State of Palestine last year.

The delay comes just weeks after Abbas reaffirmed this commitment to hold elections in November when he delivered a video address to the UN General Assembly.

Abbas has governed by decree since his presidential mandate expired in 2009.

World.title: Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh airport attack
World.content:
A Saudi-led coalition has vowed a "decisive" response after the deadliest strike on Saudi soil in over a decade. Officials have pinned the attack on Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen.

At least 12 people were killed and hundreds were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday.

"King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in an initial statement.

Hours later, the authority announced that 12 people had been killed, including four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese national.

At least 309 others were injured in the attack, the aviation authority said, adding that "all injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals."

Operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen also announced that "a projectile" had also landed near King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam.

Coalition vows to respond

On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government accused the Houthis of carrying out the deadly attack on Riyadh's international airport. The coalition vowed to respond "decisively."

In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki described the attack as a "war crime" and vowed the coalition "will respond decisively to this terrorist attack."

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump called the attack on Riyadh's international airport "not acceptable."

He also told reporters that he will speak with Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

When asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio ‌said that ​the United States ​strongly condemns recent ​attacks ‌on ‌Saudi Arabia, confirming that ​an American citizen was killed ​in the strikes.

"These reprehensible ⁠attacks ​demonstrate ​a blatant ​disregard for innocent ‌civilian life. ​They ⁠must stop now," ⁠Rubio ​wrote on X.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by the Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport.

"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law," Guterres said. "These attacks must cease immediately."

What do we know about the Riyadh attack?

A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal.

The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh."

Ambulances were seen outside the passenger terminal Image: Social Media/REUTERS

Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport.

The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity."

What did the Houthis say?

The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack.

However, after the attack, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree retweeted his own post from a day earlier in which he said that only pre-approved humanitarian flights would be allowed to land at Riyadh airport.

In the retweet on Saturday night, Saree wrote: "A reminder."

When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly."

Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Strikes hit Riyadh airport earlier this week

Fighting has intensified between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.

The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes.

Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their ​respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday.

King Khalid Airport was hit earlier this week in an attack claimed by Yemen-based Houthi rebels Image: Social Media/REUTERS

Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains.

The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July.

The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.
