World.title: Nepal urges villagers to evacuate after landslide triggers flood
World.content:
Nepali authorities urged villagers on Sunday to move to safer ground after a flash flood swept away several houses.

A dry landslide in Chumnubri village in Gorkha district, about 100km west of Kathmandu, blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, leading to downstream flooding, authorities said.

There were no immediate reports of casualties.

Videos on social media show houses and sheds being swept away by the swollen river flowing between mountains.

The river merges into the Trishuli River, where a glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing.

"We have asked villagers living along the river banks downstream to evacuate and remain safe," said Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, Gorkha district's most senior bureaucrat.

The Budhi Gandaki River in north-central Nepal on Sunday. (AP: Supplied)

Mr Mishra said about a dozen houses and two suspension bridges had been swept away, and a hydro-electric project camp was damaged by the flood.

Residents rescued

The flooded river is rising and has washed away a highway bridge connecting two districts, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.

The army rescued six people from Jagat who were facing the risk of a landslide, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a social media post.

Another 18 workers at the hydro-electric project, whose camp was damaged, escaped to safety, said Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

Nepal ends search and rescue after flood Nepal has ended the search-and-rescue operation for the more than 5,000 people still missing after the devastating August flood.

National disaster authorities alerted people living along the river in the Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flood.

"Please help ensure that people in at-risk areas are moved to safe locations in time and assist search and rescue operations as needed," the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said in a social media post.

Officials said army and police rescue personnel had reached the area and were also monitoring the situation from a helicopter.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Owners fear rare lamb worth up to $25K stolen
World.content:
A rare lamb worth up to $25,000 has gone missing from an Adelaide Hills property, with its heartbroken owners urging the community to keep an eye out for the distinctive breed.

Vet and hobby farm owner Madeleine Babos recently started breeding Swiss Valais Blacknose sheep after a decade-long interest in the unique-looking animals.

Originating in the icy Swiss Alps, Valais blacknose sheep are renowned for their fluffy white coats, dark faces, spiral horns and dog-like personalities.

Valais blacknose sheep are renowned for their fluffy white coats, dark faces, spiral horns and dog-like personalities. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

Ms Babos said the ewe was only born last week and went missing several days after its arrival.

"I noticed the mama sheep of the lamb was over there sniffing... pacing back and forth looking a bit frantic," she said.

" I realised our initial singleton was gone, which was quite stressful at the time just knowing that she'd been fine several hours before. "

Ms Barbos said the breed has a "loving personality" and were like the "dogs of the sheep world". (ABC News: Steve Opie)

The vet said she suspected the disappearance, which occurred in the afternoon, wasn't likely due to a predator.

"Just given the time of the day... the way the mother is and the fact we had some other tiny vulnerable lambs there in the paddock, I was less worried about predation," Ms Babos said.

"Whether she was close to the fence, whether someone's just seen her and said, 'Oh that's really cute, I'll just take her home as a pet'."

Ms Babos said she and her partner Alasdair Rodgers decided to invest in the costly breeding project in the hope of making a return in a few years.

The rare breed first arrived in Australia via Victoria in 2020, and has since spread to Tasmania, South Australia, and New South Wales.

The couple's first purchase for $25,000 was the lost lamb's mother, 'Sugar'.

They didn't expect Mr Rodgers would have to stop work for over a year to care for their middle daughter who had health complications after her birth.

"These sheep have kind of been a little bit of an investment for us to help us get back on our feet," he said.

" Disappointing to have something vanish that's the next stage in your life that you've been working towards. "

Alasdair Rodgers said the previous investment in the breed was in the hope of a profitable return in a few years. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

Ms Barbos said the police told her livestock theft was common.

"She does have some very distinct markings, she's a pure ewe lamb," the vet said.

"Please reach out to us...reach out to police."



Anyone with information is urged to phone Crime Stoppers SA on 1800 333 000.

World.title: Missing Melbourne hiker Jordan Yap has died in Peru, authorities confirm
World.content:
A Melbourne man who went missing in a mountainous region of Peru has been found dead, weeks after he failed to return from a remote solo hike.

Family and friends of Jordan Yap launched a search mission after the 30-year-old failed to return from a hike in South America last month.

Mr Yap's friends shared the sad news on a social media page launched to help with search efforts.

"With a heavy heart we are so sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive," the social media statement said.

" Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people's lives. "

The ABC understands friends and family of Mr Yap were notified by local authorities that his body had been found in the Mitucocha Lagoon area.

Mitucocha Lagoon, or Lake Mitococha, is a high-altitude (4,270 metres) lake in central Peru around 200 kilometres north of the capital, Lima.

The Department of Foreign Affairs confirmed it was assisting the family of an Australian who died in Peru.

"We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time," a spokesperson said.

Mr Yap had attempted to complete a hike in the remote Huayhuash region, which was expected to take about 10 days.

He left his hostel in the town of Huaraz on September 14 and was due to check into a hotel on the 23rd before catching a flight from Lima to Cusco the following day.

His family raised concern after Mr Yap failed to check into his hotel and missed his flight.

They reported him missing and engaged a local private mountain rescue team to help search for their son.

His father, Vinh Dao, had previously told the ABC that Mr Yap was an experienced hiker, but the trip to Peru was one of his first solo trips.

World.title: The Aussie guy who gave away his kidney and 10pc of his income for life
World.content:
Early on a Tuesday morning, Hu Pennington found himself being prepped for surgery that he had hesitated to tell his family about.

As his stomach was painted with an orange antiseptic, the thought crossed his mind: "It'd be really embarrassing if I died."

Hu is one of the few Australians who volunteered to donate a kidney to a stranger.

"As they were preparing me for surgery … I saw the cooler bag that the kidney was going into," Hu told triple j hack.

"[It] was inside someone … by the end of the day."

Hu says he was released from hospital three days after donating his kidney to a stranger. (Supplied)

'This century's biggest idea'

"Effective altruism" is what inspired Hu to donate his kidney and 10 per cent of his income for life.

He is on the board of Effective Altruism Australia and says the movement encourages people to do the most good they possibly can.

"To try to do good in your life, in the world, with your time, with your money," he says.

The concept of effective altruism originated in Oxford lecture halls and has been championed by Australian philosopher Peter Singer.

The movement was recently described as "this century's biggest idea" by British publication The Economist.

Loading...

It has also been criticised for oversimplifying morality and focusing on increasingly "stranger" causes. Some in the Trump administration have called it "dystopian" and "dangerous".

But Hu says, while there are some strange ideas, the Effective Altruism Movement is committed to helping the global poor, "helping kids who don't really have a chance to get past the age of five".

Having seen the impacts of malaria on a friend, he focuses some of his giving on malaria bed nets.

Giving well

Every year, Hu sets aside 10 per cent of his income to support global health and development causes.

He says the financial pledge gives him agency when modern life can make it feel as though there is little: "whether it is politicians that make decisions about your life, or an algorithm that shows you what it wants".

"This sort of a pledge isn't something you make on a whim, it is a really lifelong commitment," he says.

Hu is on the board of Effective Altruism Australia and has pledged to give away 10 per cent of his income for the rest of his life. (triple j hack: Jason Katsaras)

When asked whether he worries he won't be able to keep the pledge as the cost of living rises, he admits it's something he thinks about.

"There certainly are a lot of pressures to living, even in Australia. But at the same time, I think as Australians, many of us are much more affluent than other people in the world."

Why Hu chose to donate a kidney

Loading Instagram content

The giving hasn't always come easily. When Hu first pursued kidney donation, his GP told him to come back in "20 years", and a psychiatrist asked about his childhood and relationship with his parents.

Hu admits he was nervous about telling his friends and family about the decision.

"I was sort of worried about how people might feel about it, how people may respond, but it was overwhelmingly positive," he says.

" Almost everyone I talked to was really supportive. There was one person who asked if I was crazy. "

What's life like with one kidney?

Between 2022 and 2025, only 15 people altruistically donated a kidney through the Australian and New Zealand Kidney Exchange program, according to Donate Life.

"Basically, I learnt two things: one, living without a kidney is really, really tough, and the other thing I learnt is that living with just one kidney is just fine," Hu says.

"Once I knew those two things, it became pretty obvious what the right thing to do was."

Hu recovered quickly, but doctors warned him to steer clear of combat sports, horse riding and dirt biking for life to avoid damaging his remaining kidney.

"My MMA skills were not up to scratch anyway," Hu joked.

People with one kidney live healthy lives, said Organ, Tissue and Transplant Authority deputy chair Carol Pollock, who is also chair of Kidney Health Australia.

"Provided there's no other health issues."

A polaroid photo of Hu recovering in hospital after donating his kidney. (Supplied)

She says it poses limited risk for the individual but makes a big difference.

"I recognise a lot of people wouldn't just want to donate to a complete stranger," she says.

"I think people should consider donating to people that they may not even know remotely because it changes lives and transforms families," she says.

Altruistic donations account for less than 2 per cent of donations but can set off chains where multiple people get a lifesaving transplant.

Hu's donation created a chain of seven transplants. He doesn't know any of the recipients but received an anonymous letter from one telling him their life had changed dramatically.

Hu says the idea of effective altruism is to do as much good as you can with what you have. (Supplied)

"One of the challenges of trying to do the most good is it can be really hard to take stock and feel like you've accomplished that, like you always feel like, you can do more," he says.

"This does give me something that I can fall back on and think, 'Well, look, maybe this year hasn't gone that great for me. At least I've done this one really good thing, and I can be proud of that'.

"That kind of backstop is pretty priceless and has helped me at a number of times in my life where things have been pretty tough."

World.title: 'Incredibly difficult': Business reports robbery after crash injures five
World.content:
A Canberra massage parlour was robbed after a car crashed into its shopfront on Friday, the business says.

Authorities say five people were injured in the crash in Weston at about 11:45am, including three workers who became trapped and the vehicle's driver.

For some time, the car remained deep inside the building, which houses Harmony Tree Therapeutic Massage and Day Spa, and sits across from Cooleman Court shopping centre off Brierly Street.

Five people were taken to the Canberra Hospital, two in a serious but stable condition, one in a stable condition, and another two with minor injuries.

Police said the driver, an 84-year-old woman, was assisting with enquiries.

The business at Cooleman Court in Canberra's south says it was robbed after the crash. (ABC News: Robert Baird)

'Incredibly difficult and stressful'

On Sunday, the massage parlour claimed on social media it had been burgled.

"Unfortunately, after the serious accident at our shop on Friday, when a vehicle crashed into our premises and caused significant damage, we experienced another distressing incident later that same night," the post said.

"Someone broke into our shop and stole a staff member's mobile phone, car keys, house keys, and ATM card, which was used without permission.

"We had tried to retrieve our belongings earlier that day, but unfortunately, they were still locked inside the shop."

Emergency services were called after the crash in Weston on Friday morning. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

The business said it was an "incredibly difficult and stressful time for us and our staff".

" We are doing our best to deal with the damage and get through these challenging circumstances. "

ACT Policing confirmed a burglary at the business had been reported to police earlier on Sunday, and it was looking into it.

"As for the collision, that investigation is still underway," a statement from police said.

World.title: Children of shark victim call for return to the ocean at his memorial
World.content:
More than a thousand people, many dressed in blue, gathered on Perth's Sorrento beach today to pay tribute to Greg O'Neill, who was killed by a shark just off the shore a few weeks ago.

Son Keelan O'Neill urged the crowd to return to the water and "keep doing the things that you love", adding that his father would have wanted everyone to "embrace life to the fullest".

Mr O'Neill's family urged the crowds to go back into the water and "embrace life". (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

The 63-year-old was swimming close to the shoreline in September when he was attacked and killed by a large great white.

He was the third person killed by a shark in Western Australia so far this year.

"He'd wish for you all to keep exercising … keep swimming, keep paddling, keep doing the things that you love as dad would have done, and the things that bring you happiness," Keelan O'Neill said.

Third person killed by sharks in WA this year The often-heated debate over how to protect beachgoers from sharks is likely to get hotter after the death of a third person this year.

Mr O'Neill's daughter, Bianca, thanked the crowd, saying: "The love, support and kindness we have received from this community is beyond belief.

" The water was Dad's happy healing place; he wouldn't want anyone to feel unsafe because of what happened. "

The family was the first among the crowd to throw a handful of sand into the surf in memory of the beloved father, husband, brother and friend who frequented the beach.

More than a thousand people attended the memorial event. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

The Squids back in the water

Mr O'Neill's swimming group, the Sorrento Squids, were back in the water on Sunday, including, for the first time, the friend who was swimming with him on the day he was killed.

The Sorrento Squids were among those who went into the ocean today. (Supplied)

The group has kept swimming and supporting each other in the weeks since Mr O'Neill's death, but have spent time in the Scarborough Pool instead of the ocean.

Tom Webster, another member of the group, said today's tribute ceremony was another step towards helping the group — and the broader community — come to terms with their loss.

"As a group, this is going to help heal us, bring us together and move forward," said Mr Webster.

"Individually, we have all struggled a little bit. I know I have."

He said he believed Mr O'Neill was "splashing about" in the ocean today with the crowds.

"It was great to see so many people jumping in today. They have got over that fear of Sorrento being a sad place or a scary place. We are reclaiming it," he added.

Shark safety this summer

Greg O'Neill was a regular at Sorrento Beach. (Supplied)

Mr O'Neill's death was the third fatal shark attack in Western Australia this year and has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe.

AI-powered drones on cards for WA shark monitoring Western Australia's shark-tagging program will be expanded and the use of AI-powered drones investigated as new funding is announced.

A 'catch-and-kill' order was issued for the great white shark in September, but it was called off when the shark was not located.

Head of the Sorrento Surf Life Saving Club, Robert Doherty, said a shark barrier at the beach in Perth's north would ease concerns.

"Would I be supportive? Yes," he said.

"I think something small, in an area of the beach, that doesn't affect the whole beach."

Surf lifesavers, including those who witnessed the attack, took part in the tribute. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Many from the surf lifesaving club have been left shaken by the fatal attack, including members who witnessed the horror unfold firsthand.

"We gathered about 20-odd members that were directly involved that day and had a [counselling] session," Mr Doherty said.

" We thought it was really appropriate that the community does come together today to share a moment, dip your feet in the water. "

Those who entered the surf on Sunday did so under the watchful eye of Water Police, Marine Rescue Surf Life Savers and two shark-spotting drones.

World.title: Missing Melbourne hiker Jordan Yap found dead in Peru
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMissing person Missing Melbourne hiker Jordan Yap found dead in Peru Shelby Brooks October 11, 2026 — 6:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The family of Melbourne hiker Jordan Yap has confirmed that the 30-year-old, who went missing in Peru last month, has been found dead. “With a heavy heart, we are sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive,” the family wrote on social media. Jordan Yap (right) with his partner Anita. “We want to thank everyone who has helped; friends and family, the contributors, the search teams, the police, the many groups we engaged with who gave their time and effort, everyone who helped to share on social media. We are appreciative of all of you. “Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives.”



Yap, an intrepid adventurer, embarked on a solo hike through the remote Huayhuash mountain range on September 14, telling friends and family he would be off the grid for 10 days to complete the high-altitude trek. Related Article Missing person Jordan went off-grid for a 10-day hike in Peru. No one has seen him since day three The alarm was raised by his partner, Anita, when he failed to check in at his hotel and missed a scheduled flight several days later. The Huayhuash circuit is known for its steep, rugged terrain and is considered one of Peru’s most challenging mountain routes. Jordan’s family said he was an experienced traveller who had previously solo hiked across Australia, China, Turkey and Jordan.



“He’s an avid outdoor person. In winter time, he will spend most weekends on the snow field, even though he didn’t have a lot of luck with the weather, he loves hiking,” Yap’s father, Vinh Dao, said last month. Yap’s family launched a desperate search with local mountain rescue organisation Socorro Andino Peruano after struggling to get in touch with Peruvian authorities. Jordan (right) pictured with a friend. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said they were providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian who died in Peru. Peruvian media reported that Jordan’s body was found on Friday near the remote village of Machaycancha, located in the northern section of the world-famous mountain range.



Loved ones have remembered Jordan as a giving and kind man “I’ll think of you every time I pitch a tent, cook a particularly extravagant meal or have a boogie on the dance floor,” one mourner wrote in tribute. World.title: The world needs a new president – but not in Ukraine
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Every day over the past two years, one has repeatedly woken up and turned on the news, only to have the first words be “US President Donald Trump ...” You are immediately bracing in dread. What has he done now? What foundation of the house of post-WWII stability and relative peace has he kicked out this time? Often it becomes apparent in a couple of milliseconds that this has been done to either play to his domestic supporters, and/or his vain ego, and/or his nefarious and bizarre siding with Russia. Often all three. Today he said that Ukraine needs a new president after buying oil from the aggressor, Russia (“‘Time for a new president’: Trump calls on Zelensky to go amid diesel stoush”, smh.com.au. October 11). It is like we are in some episode of The Twilight Zone with Franklin Roosevelt saying that Winston Churchill should resign so that the UK can make peace with Nazi Germany. My father dropped bombs on fascist supply lines in northern Italy during WWII, and his generation would be turning in their graves at how their sacrifices and lifetime efforts to ensure a lasting peace in the West (that we have all enjoyed) are being deliberately and methodically dismantled in the name of one man’s enormously inflated ego. We do need a change in president, but in the USA – and right now, before he precipitates World War III. Geoff Holmes, Woonona Illustration by Badiucao Scratching my head here; isn’t Russia an ally of Iran, helping with its targeting of US assets in the Middle East? Sue Walsh, Woollahra Two articles sickened me: “Trump strikes diesel deal with Putin” and “New US sanctions aimed at crippling the ICC” (smh.com.au, October 11). The naked self-interest in President Trump’s newly established plutocracy was never more self-evident. Morality has been trampled in the interests of the dollar in both cases. First, Trump is enabling Putin to continue his aggression against Ukraine by buying Russian diesel, and second, Trump is thumbing his nose at the international community by seeking to weaken the power of the International Criminal Court. So much for democracy as the US changes its role as the leader of democratic nations into an enabler of dictatorships and a domestic agenda that swamps the lower classes with legislation that enables the rich to become richer. Let’s hope that Australians see through Gina Rinehart’s manipulations of Pauline Hanson’s agenda to avoid the same happening here. Larry Woldenberg, Forest Lodge So relieved that our government is not supporting Trump in his latest idiotic endeavour to finance his friend Putin. This major misstep should convince the world to disassociate from him. Trump has evolved from incompetence to megalomania to evil. Hopefully, the voting American public will finally recognise this. Ashley Berry, Toolijooa Public executions: is this the Stone Age? We need a new leader of the US. The petty, childish and dangerous behaviour of the current holder of the office has outraged the world. Sanctioning the International Criminal Court because he failed to gain the Nobel Peace Prize is one example. His support of the ruthless dictator Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine, a denial of the title of leadership of the “free world”, is another. And the sickness of American society under this president is surely indicated by the touted decision to reintroduce public executions, an example of medieval barbarity (“Trump says decision on streaming killer’s execution still pending”, smh.com.au, October 11). A new president is badly needed. Derrick Mason, Boorowa



I was horrified to read that the United States plans to livestream a firing squad execution (“US to livestream military execution”, October 10). This sort of public display belongs to the darkest chapters of human history, when people were executed in town squares for crowds to watch. Are we really drifting back to the Stone Age? One cannot ignore the impact such a spectacle will have on young people and children who may see it on television or on social media. At a time when we are trying to teach them empathy, restraint and respect for human life, broadcasting a killing as if it were a form of public theatre sends exactly the opposite message. What troubles me even more is that this move seems to be designed to appeal to people such as Donald Trump, who enjoy dramatic TV spectacles. But where is America heading if death itself becomes entertainment? Vijay Khandelwal, Winston Hills US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution by firing squad would be public, before the White House clarified saying it would be livestreamed. The plan is now under review. Bloomberg When ISIS streamed pre-recorded beheadings they were condemned as barbaric, yet here we are with the United States, the supposed leader of the free world, supposedly planning to stream a live execution. The method may be different, but I fail to see what this will achieve. Streaming it live for the world to see is just as barbaric as an ISIS delayed stream. Atrocities committed in the Middle East do not deter the US or its allies from taking up arms, so if the Trump administration thinks this will make people think twice about becoming a terrorist, then it is sadly wrong. Peter Miniutti, Ashbury Bob Dylan’s classic Desolation Row (1965) begins with the horrifically prescient: “They’re selling postcards of the hanging”. Should I be surprised if the ever-transactional Donald Trump sees a buck to be made from the unspeakable savagery of the livestreamed execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan? John Campbell, South Golden Beach The USA is going to livestream the execution, by firing squad, of a wheelchair bound, paraplegic man who wants to be a martyr. What could possibly go wrong? Margaret Broadbent, Dunbogan Nobel Committee makes noble choice Trump has missed out on the Nobel Peace Prize once again (“Former UN human rights chief Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay wins the Nobel Peace Prize”, smh.com.au, October 9). He decided to take revenge on the winner by sanctioning the International Criminal Court, where she worked (“New US sanctions aimed at crippling the ICC”, smh.com.au, October 11). I think he should declare war on Norway, only to discover that the Norwegian government has no control over the decision, as it is made by the independent Nobel Committee. Mokhles Sidden, South Strathfield



Former UN human rights chief Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. AP Chris Sidoti is reported elsewhere describing Judge Navi Pillay as modest, unassuming, lovely and funny, as well as entirely focused on the law and never running a political agenda. If those are some of the qualities of a Nobel Peace Prize winner, Donald Trump will never stand a chance. Ross Duncan, Potts Point Guns don’t equal security I respect and appreciate the difficult work our police do, but I also support the concerns raised by your correspondent Paul Pearce (Letters, October 10). Having lived in Europe and seen heavily armed police in public spaces, I have never wanted Australia to go down that path. Nor do I believe arming private groups is the answer. Once firearms become accepted in the hands of private organisations, pressure to extend that privilege will only grow. We do not need an armed vigilante culture. Of course, police must be equipped to respond to genuine threats. But the proliferation of weapons, especially long-arm rifles, does not guarantee public safety or prevent a determined terrorist from acting. Australia must not mistake more guns for more security.

Vivien Clark-Ferraino, Duckmaloi Town Hall square has history The fate of Town Hall Square still seems up in the air (“State seizes control of square plan”, October 10). The square plan has history. In 1959, Sydney lord mayor Harry Jensen had a plan for a civic square and an underground carpark by demolishing the Queen Victoria Building. Architect Harry Seidler strongly advocated the plan, describing the QVB as an “architectural monstrosity”. Various municipal leaders and a Labor Party mayoral candidate continued pushing for demolition. But happily, the QVB was retained to become a grand shopping destination and an architectural treasure, while the civic square was put on the back burner. The seven buildings now planned for demolition may not be architectural wonders, but tearing them down in our enlightened times would be environmentally wasteful, and it would ignore the City of Sydney’s current strategy, which says: “Imagine a Sydney where nothing is wasted. In a circular economy, everything you own can either be reused, repaired or recycled as much as possible, not thrown away.” Ian Ferrier, Paddington



Artist’s impressions of the proposed Town Hall square in central Sydney. City of Sydney From my observation, large public squares in cities in Europe hark back to a time when buildings and homes were crammed into narrow streets – London, Paris, Prague, Budapest, Vienna. A public square was an open space where citizens could enjoy the tepid sunshine of the northern summer. Now that summers in Europe have become so hot, people don’t congregate in big open squares but seek shade wherever they can. Here, people would rather sit in the shade during summer. The latest proposal for a public square doesn’t seem to cater for any trees at all. Even in “winter”, Sydney gets temperatures of 25 to 30 degrees. A large square without shade would be shunned. This may be Clover Moore’s pet project that she wants to leave as a legacy, but maybe she could find something else – a park, perhaps? Judith Rostron, Killarney Heights While I will miss Woolworths at the Town Hall and its cafeteria, as it is one of the few buildings in the city I can remember from childhood, I am all for a Town Hall square (“Moore’s Town Hall Square would long outlast the small-minded fools who are trying to kill it”, October 10). And I am with Bevan Shields, it is the city council that has the impressive plan. The state government needs to keep its parochial fingers off the project. Genevieve Milton, Dulwich Hill Fix voting IT One of the things we can be most proud of is our electoral system. I was therefore disturbed to read that the NSW system is facing “intolerable risk ... of cyberattack, external interference and challenges to its validity” because of a lack of funding for urgently needed systems upgrades (“‘Polls face intolerable risk’, says watchdog”, October 10). When we compare our systems to those of the United States, few things could be more important than this. I therefore urge the NSW government to provide the necessary funding without delay. Andrew Macintosh, Cromer Chris Minns voting at a booth in Carlton in his electorate of Kogarah on March 25, 2023. Nikki Short The NSW Electoral Commission has told the government that its antiquated IT systems have led to “an intolerable level of risk of election failure at future polls”, including March 2027. This warning was first issued in 2019. So, essentially, this is a bipartisan disregard for the protection of the democratic process. Thanks, Gladys Berejiklian (premier 2017-21), Dominic Perrottet (premier 2021-23) and Chris Minns (2023-?). Not good enough. Jennifer Raines, Newtown



All talk, no action So true, Peter Hartcher (“Hanson blame game fixes nothing”, October 10). Hanson loves to play the blame game but offers no “fixes” for the “cause of anxiety and despair” felt by so many as living standards decline. Immigration cutbacks will not solve the economic problems. We need healthy economic growth at the risk of fuelling inflation. As Hartcher says, we need “more solutions, less blame”, but I can’t now see any party offering solutions as they brawl with each other for popular votes concerning the immigration chaos. Sadly, lots of negativity but not much hope from any of them.

Denis Suttling, Newport Beach Matt Canavan, Pauline Hanson and Karl Stefanovic at the CPAC in Brisbane on Saturday. AAPIMAGE It’s time for a brief summary of the immigration issue. Pauline Hanson initiated the recent political push towards minimising immigration – far too many Asians and Muslims in this country. Her solution? Very simple – don’t bring any more in and deport as many as possible. This became One Nation’s migration policy, and it attracted a great many people to that party. Then there’s the Coalition. Angus Taylor, wanting to get back some of the support lost to One Nation, announces the Coalition migration policy, very similar to the One Nation policy, except that he promises “to make the biggest reduction to immigration in Australia’s history”. Pathetic, really. Immigration has made this country great, given us the living standards we now enjoy and a wonderful multicultural society. It needs to continue, with the level adjusted from time to time to suit circumstances, but essentially determined as it always has been, and definitely without any hint or suggestion of racism. Ken Butler, Mount Colah Make banks cover cost of fee ban When the surcharges were banned starting October 1, I was under the impression that the government had been successful in forcing financial institutions to cancel these charges (“Labor unrest after ban on credit card fees backfires”, October 10). But looking at the ATO, the reason for refusing to accept credit card payments is because the ATO can’t absorb the cost. So it appears the government perhaps made a law to ban the surcharges without thinking who is going to pay. If the ATO can’t absorb the cost, why would small business absorb it? No wonder my morning coffee went up by 50 cents from October 1. It’s not just coffee, it’s just about everything for which I pay by credit or debit card. Why can’t the financial institutions making billions of dollars in profit absorb these costs? Ariyur Rangarajan, Baulkham Hills Credit where it’s due? Coffee and baked cheesecake go down well though prices are rising. Chris Hopkins

World.title: Voters cool on Hanson as Albanese wears the blame for cost of living
World.content:
PoliticsFederalResolve Political Monitor Voters cool on Hanson as Albanese wears the blame for cost of living James Massola October 11, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Voter support for One Nation has fallen from its high point in June, with the party’s primary vote down by 2 percentage points in the past month and 4 points since the middle of the year, while leader Pauline Hanson’s likeability and performance ratings have also taken a dive. But the government is being blamed for the cost-of-living crunch: 46 per cent of people are sheeting home primary responsibility to federal Labor, a rise of 6 percentage points since March. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s popularity flagged in the past month while there was not a lot of movement for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Aresna Villanueva This is 1.7 times as many voters faulting Labor for economic pain as the 26 per cent who now blame global factors including the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Those blaming global factors rose 9 percentage points since March, while just 4 per cent blamed the Reserve Bank, despite the bank’s decision at the end of September to raise the cash rate for the fourth time this year. Resolve Political Monitor pollster Jim Reed said that although housing costs were hurting less,“high fuel prices, rate increase and credit card fees are all stoking renewed cost-of-living concerns. Voters appreciate there are global pressures in some of this, but government is seen to be hindering rather than helping”.



Support for the major parties in the latest Resolve poll was relatively steady. Labor’s primary vote edged up 1 point to 29 per cent and support for the Coalition dipped 1 point to 23 per cent – though the Coalition was still trailing One Nation, which was on 25 per cent. In the first full poll since David Shoebridge became federal leader, the Greens were up 1 percentage point to 12 per cent over the past month, though a majority of the 2250 voters Resolve Political Monitor surveyed from Tuesday to Saturday of last week were not even aware the party had a new leader. All of these movements were within the poll’s margin of error of plus or minus 2.1 per cent. Just 36 per cent of Greens voters were aware the party had chosen Shoebridge after former leader Larissa Waters stepped down for health reasons, compared with 42 per cent of Labor voters and 44 per cent of One Nation and Coalition voters. The figure was 40 per cent for all voters.



The poll recorded a significant movement in people’s expectations of who will win the next election. The percentage of voters expecting One Nation to win fell by 8 percentage points to 20 per cent. The number of people expecting Labor to win fell by 1 point to 32 per cent, while 20 per cent said they expected the Coalition to win, up 2 percentage points in a month. Amid growing concern within Labor that Anthony Albanese has become a drag on the party’s primary vote, the prime minister increased his lead as preferred leader by 3 points to 32 per cent – comfortably ahead of his political opponents. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor edged up 1 point to 22 per cent and Hanson gained 1 point to 26 per cent. Hanson outscored Albanese and Taylor on the leaders’ performance ratings, with 45 per cent rating her performance as good or very good, down 2 points, while 41 per cent rated her performance as poor or very poor, up 4 percentage points in a month. The net movement of a 6 percentage point drop is statistically significant and outside the margin of error.



Similarly, Hanson’s net likeability rating fell from 7 points to zero, while Taylor’s rating fell 2 points to 8 per cent and Albanese’s improved by 1 point to minus 15 per cent. Hanson’s slide could be down to a week out of the headlines, Reed suggested, noting that One Nation thrived on controversy and attention “and we simply haven’t seen them as much lately”. “If we think about the political spectrum in terms of the two centrist parties now being flanked by the Greens and One Nation, it’s remarkable how similar the extremes are. Both grew from wealthy donors, both have evolved from single-issue parties into broader ideological movements, both care about identity. “The major difference seems to be that One Nation thrives on media attention because people see themselves and like what they see, whereas scrutiny either damages the Greens or only appeals to their base.”



Just over a third of surveyed voters, 36 per cent, rated Albanese’s performance as good or very good, up 1 point on last month, while 54 per cent said the prime minister’s performance was poor or very poor, also a 1 point rise on last month. The proportion of undecided voters was just 9 per cent, suggesting views of the prime minister’s performance are firmly set. Taylor’s performance rating improved by 2 percentage points to 41 per cent, but the percentage of people who rated his performance as either poor or very poor rose 4 points to 34 per cent, with 25 per cent of people undecided. Ahead of parliament returning on Monday, both Hanson and Taylor spoke at the Conservative Political Action Conference in Brisbane to set out their competing visions. Hanson criticised Taylor during a speech on Saturday for being a “smarmy management consultant” but said her party would work with the Coalition to boot Labor from office at the next election. On Sunday, she claimed to News24 (formerly Sky News) that one attendee had told her he was quitting the Liberal Party after Taylor’s speech. In his speech at CPAC, Taylor acknowledged what he saw as mistakes made under the Morrison government including COVID-era spending, signing up to net zero and “allowing immigration numbers to creep up, especially student and bridging visas”.



The change in Greens leader made no difference to 70 per cent of voters, while 13 per cent said they were more likely to vote for the environmental party and 17 per cent said they were less likely. Larissa Waters’ net likeability score was plus 5 percentage points, well ahead of Shoebridge on minus 3 points, but Shoebridge was better known than Waters. The new leader was familiar to 55 per cent of voters and unfamiliar to 45 per cent, whereas 50 per cent of people were unfamiliar with Waters even after she had spent nearly 18 months as leader. World.title: ‘Never-on-time airline’: Aussie golf great Greg Norman takes swing at Qantas
World.content:
NationalNSWCBD Opinion ‘Never-on-time airline’: Aussie golf great Greg Norman takes swing at Qantas Anthony Segaert Parramatta bureau chief October 11, 2026 — 5:50pm

October 11, 2026 — 5:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Fiona Byrne, The Age’s CBD columnist, writes that Australian golf legend Greg Norman has taken a very public swing at Qantas, calling it the “never on-time” airline and describing it as outdated and unreliable. Norman, who was a high-profile celebrity ambassador for Qantas for decades, teed off at the airline’s management on Sunday, challenging them to get the service back up to his expected standard, adding the hashtag #alottodo to make his point. Australian golfing great Greg Norman has teed off at Qantas after his flight was delayed. Getty He also questioned whether profit had been put above “customer caring, reputation and service” and said it used to be one of the world’s top three airlines but “alas no more”. Known as the Great White Shark since the early ’80s, Norman took a fair bite out of Qantas, blasting it on his 244,000-strong Instagram account and saying he was looking for another airline to travel with. Among other things, the lack of Wi-Fi on the long haul seems to have been part of what riled him.



US-based Norman recently attended the NRL grand final in Sydney and was travelling from Sydney to Dallas on a Qantas A380 over the weekend. A delay in leaving appears to have been the trigger for his epic spray. “I have always tried to support my national airline @Qantas. Sadly, their reputation of the ‘never on-time’ airline (or the ones I am on – this time Syd-Dallas circa 3 hrs late departing) + an hour to get one bag in Dallas now has me looking elsewhere,” Norman fumed online. “Maybe @emirates longer but reliable, Wi-Fi, comfort caring. “Too bad, as @Qantas was once one of the top 3 in the world for a great travel experience. “Alas no more #whathappened Profit before customer caring, reputation and service!?



Greg Norman (left) was among the guests of the NRL, along with US ambassador David Brat (orange tie) and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (foreground) at the 2026 NRL grand final in Sydney last week. ”And not to have Wi-Fi in this day and age with the cost/ticket - #insane #dated. Ground staff excellent - Qantas admin get to work and bring back the pride in - “The Spirit of Australia” and be a world leader in your industry again!! #alottodo” Not surprisingly, Qantas was well aware of Norman’s dummy-spit when CBD called on Sunday. “Unfortunately, our flight from Sydney to Dallas Fort Worth on Saturday was delayed departing Sydney while our engineers fixed a fuelling issue,” a Qantas spokesperson told us, with no mention of Norman’s other gripes. No doubt someone will let Norman know Wi-Fi is in the process of being rolled out on Qantas’s A380 fleet, and is available on its 787s and A330 planes.



It might be too little too late, as it sounds like Norman will have swapped his boarding pass allegiances before that rollout is complete. Julie Bishop’s accidental ‘false flag’ This was a change to the programming: Julie Bishop, who normally uses her Instagram page to share highlights of European trips and designer dresses, last week reposted a conspiracy-laden video describing the flydubai incident as a “false flag” for Israel. The former foreign minister, who led Australia’s overseas efforts from 2013 to 2018 (and more recently became infamous for her role in the Australian National University’s prolonged crisis when she was chancellor) reshared a video from the Daily Rumble, a vague Instagram account that promised “100% independent news on the Middle East”. “This is not the story they’re telling us,” announced its presenter, before launching into some generally debunked conspiracies about how the incident unfolded – all to gain more than seven million viewers.



So did our former foreign minister really believe the video she’d reshared with her 110,000 followers? “It was an accident,” she told us. “I deleted it as soon as I realised it had been done.” We’ve all been there. An even slower news day Don’t get mad, get even. We brought news last week that Sydney’s favourite tech villain and a regular of this column, Richard White, had sent his staff at the beleaguered WiseTech a surprise email with a “gift”: an AI jingle made by one of his children. “The song and video is so good and the song is so catchy that I think we share the love and give it to you all to see if your children love it as much as we do,” he wrote.



But Jazzy Learns, the AI character White had shared with staff, called us out on Instagram for how “a proud, supportive dad moment of his teenage daughter [was] usurped and demonised by the media”. We were accused of picking up a “cheap headline on a slow news day” without referencing the actual work. A cheap headline? We’d do nothing of the sort! But we are fans of the (slightly) good-natured response. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: Kostecki wins unforgettable Bathurst 1000 after De Pasquale runs out of fuel on last lap
World.content:
Breaking SportMotorsportSupercars Kostecki wins unforgettable Bathurst 1000 after De Pasquale runs out of fuel on last lap Frances Howe Updated October 11, 2026 — 5:37pm ,first published 12:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

5.35pm: Brodie Kostecki has won the 61st Bathurst 1000 after Anton De Pasquale ran out of fuel in the final lap. It almost looked like it would be the first Bathurst 1000 since 1991 without a safety car. Then, with six laps to go, Chaz Mostert crashed in the same part of the track as his teammate Ryan Wood on Friday. Brodie Kostecki and Todd Hazelwood win the 2026 Bathurst 1000. Fox Queue the safety car with Anton De Pasquale running out of fuel and now able to preserve it, Zach Bates gaining on him in second and Brodie Kostecki regaining third place after a dramatic showdown with his podcast co-host Will Brown. The race restarted with three laps to go and De Pasquale, who pitted early to get the lead, ran out of fuel. Kostecki flew past him to the front in his Ford Mustang and went on to claim his second Bathurst 1000 win.



4.45pm: Anton De Pasquale made what could be the defining move of the Bathurst 1000 when he pitted ahead of Zach Bates on the 139th lap. When Bates stopped on the next lap, and despite only changing tires and adding fuel, it seemed to drag on, and he returned to the circuit 11 seconds behind De Pasquale. Late race leader Anton De Pasquale. Getty Images The rookie was then a second faster than the race leader – who was saving his tyres and fuel – but with 19 laps to go, Bates was warned not to push too hard. Elsewhere, Ryan Wood hit the wall to continue a run of bad luck at Bathurst, including crashing on Friday and having to sit out qualifying. The Walkinshaw TWG Racing Team needed to repair the car and return it to the track in order for Wood to qualify for the Supercars championship finals series.



4pm: When the Bathurst 1000 entered the final 40 laps, Brodie Kostecki had such a comfortable lead that it seemed only a safety car or some other catastrophe could deny him and co-driver Todd Hazlewood a second Bathurst victory. The race’s entertainment was being supplied by Anton De Pasquale and Will Brown jostling for second place, while Kostecki extended his lead. De Pasquale and Brown came and went for their pit stops with Kostecki staying out for another lap. Brodie Kostecki dropped to fifth after a slow pitstop late in the Bathurst 1000. Fox Sports Then catastrophe did strike Kostecki. A brake change went wrong and the 2024 Bathurst winner lost a stack of time, dropping him down the order. He came out of the pit lane behind Bates, behind De Pasquale and behind Brown. Now, he’ll have to try to crawl his way back up Mount Panorama from fifth. Rookie Zach Bates, who stole podium position off Kostecki a day earlier and prevented him from becoming the first driver in 61 years to claim four successive pole positions, was back in the lead for the first time in three hours.



3.15pm: Things are heating up at the back of the Bathurst 1000 pack as 2025 Supercars champion Chaz Mostert spends several laps trying to overtake Cameron Waters. Todd Hazelwood, who has led the race for more than an hour, completes his 77 laps and more than two hours of the race as he swaps with Brodie Kostecki on lap 99. A crowd cheers on the drivers of the Bathurst 1000. Getty Images Kostecki returns to the circuit ahead of Zach Bates and Will Brown follows in third. 2.30pm: Last year’s winner Matt Payne has copped a penalty at the Bathurst 1000 due to an out-of-control tyre in the pit lane as the race passes the halfway mark.



Payne’s teammate, Will Davison, was forced to serve a pit-lane drive-through penalty, where he had to drive the length of pit lane at its 40km/h speed limit. That’s several times slower than the cars on the actual track to his right. Matt Payne has copped a second infringement in the Bathurst 1000. Getty Images The pit-lane infringement occurred when a spare wheel rolled out of control behind Payne’s Ford Mustang. The situation was worsened when a team member of Grove Racing ran behind the car to stop it. That exceeded the number of people on the team allowed to cross the safety line in the pit lane. He was also not wearing a mandated fire suit. It’s the second infringement for Payne after serving a five-second penalty for running another driver, David Reynolds, off the track earlier in the race. Grove Racing chief executive Brenton Grove told Kayo Sport, “We’re doing a pretty good job of throwing this race away at the moment.”



Meanwhile, there’s been no change in the top three after the first pit stop as the drivers reach the 81st lap and the halfway point of the race. Dick Johnson Racing remains in the lead with Todd Hazelwood driving while Aaron Seton is behind him with care Triple Eight in third. 1.50pm: Dick Johnson Racing is in the lead for the first time in the race after the cars completed their second pit stops and are being forced to contend with tyre blistering as the track temperature reaches 40 degrees Celsius. Todd Hazelwood is driving for Dick Johnson after teammate Brodie Kostecki was jumped by Triple Eight’s Will Brown, who moved from fifth to first position after the first round of pit stops. Nathan Herne takes in action during the Bathurst 1000 on Sunday. Getty Images



By lap 63, Matt Stone Racing has moved into second with Aaron Seton back in the driver’s seat, while the Triple Eight car has dropped back to third. Macualey Jones spun out his Toyota GR Supra and had to complete a three-point turn to again be moving in the right direction. The incident did not trigger a safety car, but there were delays for the rest of the field. As the temperature on the course heats up, teams are contending with shortened lifespan for their tyres. 1.15pm: The first leadership change of the 61st Bathurst 1000 has Triple Eight Race Engineering in the lead after Will Brown jumped from fifth to first in the first round of pit stops. With 26 cars starting the 161 laps of the Mount Panorama circuit, Matt Stone Racing held the early advantage in the race for the Peter Brock Trophy after driver Zach Bates secured pole position for the team on Saturday – the first time a rookie had done so since 2001.



Aaron Seton started in pole position for Matt Stone Racing. Getty Images His co-driver, Aaron Seton, maintained the lead before coming in for a pit stop on lap 25, one ahead of Dick Johnson Racing in second and Triple Eight in fifth. But after the first stops, Bates dropped to third and Brodie Kostecki, who took over for DJR, was jumped by Brown on the way out. Further down the field, full-time Supercars driver Kai Allen got off to a strong start for Grove Racing against the co-drivers, recording the fastest lap and gaining five spots on his starting position, from 11th to sixth. Last year’s Bathurst winner Matt Payne was given a five-second penalty for forcing David Reynolds off the track while overtaking him. Reynolds subsequently called Payne “not the sharpest tool in the shed”.



Zach Bates prepares on Sunday morning for the Bathurst 1000. He is the first rookie since 2001 to start in pole position. Getty Images By the 40th lap, Bates was holding on to third position despite glancing a wall. He shocked spectators on Friday when he completed the fastest lap of the circuit in the current generation of car, and becoming the first driver to break the two-minute and four-second barrier when claiming provisional pole position. Related Article Supercars Rookie claims Bathurst 1000 pole position in a Shootout shock He backed up that performance in Saturday’s top-10 shoot-out, upsetting Kostecki, who was attempting to become the first driver to start four successive Bathurst 1000s from pole position. Instead, the 22-year-old Bates turned his provisional pole into the real thing.



He is the first rookie since Marcos Ambrose in 2001 to start from No.1 on the grid, and just the third in history to do so. Payne began the race in 10th position after finishing last in the top 10 shootout, while defending Supercars champion, Chaz Mostert, started from 16th. A tribute to Brock, the nine-time Bathurst winner who died 20 years ago, took place before the race, which included a rendition of John Williamson’s True Blue. The anniversary year has attracted more spectators than usual to the mountain; many waited more than a week in their campsites at the summit of the mountain to watch the Gen3 Supercars flash past them. When the race started at 11.30am, the temperature on Mount Panorama was a warm 25 degrees with clear skies.

A teenage boy has been arrested after allegedly driving a stolen car through Melbourne’s city centre on Sunday morning and hitting a pedestrian outside Flinders Street Station. Havoc erupted about 10.30am when the 16-year-old allegedly drove a stolen white Ford Escape through the CBD and struck a woman in her 50s, several parked cars and street signage. A teenager has been arrested after allegedly driving a stolen car through the CBD. Nine News It is understood the SUV travelled along tram tracks on Elizabeth Street before it mounted the footpath and hit the Southbank woman, who had been standing at the busy intersection, before turning left onto Flinders Street. Witnesses reported seeing police draw their weapons as the vehicle travelled towards the intersection of Flinders and Swanston streets, which was blocked off as part of the Melbourne Marathon route.



The driver then did a U-turn before speeding back along Flinders Street. Barista Kirk Pearson was working at his Flinders Street cafe when he heard a car “screaming from Elizabeth Street”. Kirk Pearson, a barista at Zero Coffee on Flinders St, said bystanders scrambled to help the injured woman. Luis Enrique Ascui As the car sped away from police, Pearson said, bystanders scrambled to help the injured woman off the road so she wouldn’t be hit again. The car then continued speeding towards Southern Cross Station with police in pursuit, he said.



Ambulance Victoria confirmed on Sunday afternoon that the woman was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries to her upper body. Police said the Dandenong boy was later arrested on Beaconsfield Parade, Albert Park, and would soon be interviewed. Debris on Elizabeth Street at the intersection with Flinders Street after the incident. Victoria Malek Investigators have ruled out the incident as an act of terrorism or a targeted attack. One witness, who works at Walker’s Doughnuts on Elizabeth Street and asked not to be named, said panicked bystanders began crying immediately after the incident.



“Incidents happen every day,” he said. “But this is the most intense thing I’ve seen in the past three, four years.” The vehicle is alleged to have been stolen from a business in Cranbourne South about 2am. Though the Melbourne Marathon starting gun went off at 6.15am for those undertaking the full 42-kilometre course, thousands of runners participating in the half-marathon were still racing when the incident occurred – having set off at 9.45am. Starting on Batman Avenue, 20,000 participants travelled west along Flinders Street and past the station before turning onto St Kilda Road. Runners then travelled to Albert Park Lake, and for full marathon participants a lap of Beaconsfield Parade followed, before they doubled back along St Kilda Road and Flinders Street Station to eventually finish inside the MCG. World.title: ‘What they’re doing isn’t working’: Opposition hits back at premier over poverty report
World.content:
NationalWACost of living ‘What they’re doing isn’t working’: Opposition hits back at premier over poverty report Michael Philipps October 11, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

WA Premier Roger Cook has defended the state’s efforts to relieve cost-of-living pressures for Western Australians, but says it requires governments at all levels to work together to ensure people aren’t falling through the cracks. Leader of the opposition of Western Australia, Basil Zempilas. AAPIMAGE His comments follow a new report that estimates that 456,000 Western Australians, including almost 99,000 children, are living in poverty in 2026 as rising housing costs and inadequate household incomes push more people below the poverty line. The Bankwest Curtin Economics Centre’s 2026 Poverty Snapshot: The changing face of poverty in Western Australia found 15.1 per cent of Western Australians are now living in poverty, up from 11.8 per cent in 2021. Speaking at a press conference at Dumas House on Sunday, Premier Roger Cook acknowledged that Western Australians are doing it tough.



″I remember when I stood in this place and I was elected in June 2023. I said I’d do two things. I said I’d keep the economy strong and to help those that are doing it tough,” he said. “We acknowledge that there are Western Australians at the moment that are doing it tough, and that’s one of the reasons why we’ve provided a billion dollars in this budget alone of cost-of-living relief for Western Australians. “We know that there’s a whole range of circumstances that lead to that, and that’s why our cost-of-living measures go across a range of different areas around public transport, around school costs, around fuel costs, and we’ll continue to look at what we could do to help West Aussies.” WA Premier Roger Cook. Matt Jelonek Cook said there are a range of targeted measures to make sure the government is supporting those on the poverty line.



“It requires governments at all levels to work together to ensure that people aren’t falling through the cracks,that there are people who get supported when they’re not enjoying the best of economic times,” he said. WA opposition leader Basil Zempilas said if 15 per cent of Western Australians are living on or below the poverty line, then what the state government is doing to support the public is not working. “Western Australians are concerned about housing, they’re concerned about health, they’re concerned about police resources, and they are very clearly concerned about the cost of living that is getting beyond them and their families,” he said. “That’s where the people of Western Australia want this state government to focus.” Zempilas said announcements and big sums of money don’t get the job done.



“If 15 per cent of West Australians are living on or below the poverty line, what do you think they think when they hear the state government talk about the most prosperous state in the nation?” he said. “It’s not for them. It’s not for ordinary West Australians who are suffering like this.” BCEC director Professor Alan Duncan said while the number of Western Australians living in poverty had increased substantially, we also need to understand how deeply people are experiencing poverty. “Poverty is not just about how many people fall below a particular income threshold. It’s also about how far their incomes fall short of what they need to maintain a basic standard of living,” he said. “The evidence points to two fundamental issues that need to be addressed together – the incomes available to households and the cost of essential expenses, particularly housing.”



The report recommends making affordable housing a poverty-reduction priority. This includes expanding access to social and affordable housing, supporting households experiencing rental stress and ensuring incomes keep pace with the cost of living. Anglicare WA chief executive Mark Glasson said the findings should be a wake-up call for WA. “Hundreds of thousands of Western Australians are struggling to afford the basics, and the pressure is getting worse,” he said. “Housing is a huge part of this story. Perth rents have more than doubled since 2020, and more than one in four private renters in WA are now living in poverty. “We need to make sure people can afford a safe and secure home without sacrificing food, electricity or other essentials.”

The family of Melbourne hiker Jordan Yap has confirmed that the 30-year-old, who went missing in Peru last month, has been found dead. “With a heavy heart, we are sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive,” the family wrote on social media. Jordan Yap (right) with his partner Anita. “We want to thank everyone who has helped; friends and family, the contributors, the search teams, the police, the many groups we engaged with who gave their time and effort, everyone who helped to share on social media. We are appreciative of all of you. “Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives.”



Yap, an intrepid adventurer, embarked on a solo hike through the remote Huayhuash mountain range on September 14, telling friends and family he would be off the grid for 10 days to complete the high-altitude trek. Related Article Missing person Jordan went off-grid for a 10-day hike in Peru. No one has seen him since day three The alarm was raised by his partner, Anita, when he failed to check in at his hotel and missed a scheduled flight several days later. The Huayhuash circuit is known for its steep, rugged terrain and is considered one of Peru’s most challenging mountain routes. Jordan’s family said he was an experienced traveller who had previously solo hiked across Australia, China, Turkey and Jordan.



“He’s an avid outdoor person. In winter time, he will spend most weekends on the snow field, even though he didn’t have a lot of luck with the weather, he loves hiking,” Yap’s father, Vinh Dao, said last month. Yap’s family launched a desperate search with local mountain rescue organisation Socorro Andino Peruano after struggling to get in touch with Peruvian authorities. Jordan (right) pictured with a friend. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said they were providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian who died in Peru. Peruvian media reported that Jordan’s body was found on Friday near the remote village of Machaycancha, located in the northern section of the world-famous mountain range.



Loved ones have remembered Jordan as a giving and kind man “I’ll think of you every time I pitch a tent, cook a particularly extravagant meal or have a boogie on the dance floor,” one mourner wrote in tribute. World.title: Voters cool on Hanson as Albanese wears the blame for cost of living
World.content:
PoliticsFederalResolve Political Monitor Voters cool on Hanson as Albanese wears the blame for cost of living James Massola October 11, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Voter support for One Nation has fallen from its high point in June, with the party’s primary vote down by 2 percentage points in the past month and 4 points since the middle of the year, while leader Pauline Hanson’s likeability and performance ratings have also taken a dive. But the government is being blamed for the cost-of-living crunch: 46 per cent of people are sheeting home primary responsibility to federal Labor, a rise of 6 percentage points since March. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s popularity flagged in the past month while there was not a lot of movement for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Aresna Villanueva This is 1.7 times as many voters faulting Labor for economic pain as the 26 per cent who now blame global factors including the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Those blaming global factors rose 9 percentage points since March, while just 4 per cent blamed the Reserve Bank, despite the bank’s decision at the end of September to raise the cash rate for the fourth time this year. Resolve Political Monitor pollster Jim Reed said that although housing costs were hurting less,“high fuel prices, rate increase and credit card fees are all stoking renewed cost-of-living concerns. Voters appreciate there are global pressures in some of this, but government is seen to be hindering rather than helping”.



Support for the major parties in the latest Resolve poll was relatively steady. Labor’s primary vote edged up 1 point to 29 per cent and support for the Coalition dipped 1 point to 23 per cent – though the Coalition was still trailing One Nation, which was on 25 per cent. In the first full poll since David Shoebridge became federal leader, the Greens were up 1 percentage point to 12 per cent over the past month, though a majority of the 2250 voters Resolve Political Monitor surveyed from Tuesday to Saturday of last week were not even aware the party had a new leader. All of these movements were within the poll’s margin of error of plus or minus 2.1 per cent. Just 36 per cent of Greens voters were aware the party had chosen Shoebridge after former leader Larissa Waters stepped down for health reasons, compared with 42 per cent of Labor voters and 44 per cent of One Nation and Coalition voters. The figure was 40 per cent for all voters.



The poll recorded a significant movement in people’s expectations of who will win the next election. The percentage of voters expecting One Nation to win fell by 8 percentage points to 20 per cent. The number of people expecting Labor to win fell by 1 point to 32 per cent, while 20 per cent said they expected the Coalition to win, up 2 percentage points in a month. Amid growing concern within Labor that Anthony Albanese has become a drag on the party’s primary vote, the prime minister increased his lead as preferred leader by 3 points to 32 per cent – comfortably ahead of his political opponents. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor edged up 1 point to 22 per cent and Hanson gained 1 point to 26 per cent. Hanson outscored Albanese and Taylor on the leaders’ performance ratings, with 45 per cent rating her performance as good or very good, down 2 points, while 41 per cent rated her performance as poor or very poor, up 4 percentage points in a month. The net movement of a 6 percentage point drop is statistically significant and outside the margin of error.



Similarly, Hanson’s net likeability rating fell from 7 points to zero, while Taylor’s rating fell 2 points to 8 per cent and Albanese’s improved by 1 point to minus 15 per cent. Hanson’s slide could be down to a week out of the headlines, Reed suggested, noting that One Nation thrived on controversy and attention “and we simply haven’t seen them as much lately”. “If we think about the political spectrum in terms of the two centrist parties now being flanked by the Greens and One Nation, it’s remarkable how similar the extremes are. Both grew from wealthy donors, both have evolved from single-issue parties into broader ideological movements, both care about identity. “The major difference seems to be that One Nation thrives on media attention because people see themselves and like what they see, whereas scrutiny either damages the Greens or only appeals to their base.”



Just over a third of surveyed voters, 36 per cent, rated Albanese’s performance as good or very good, up 1 point on last month, while 54 per cent said the prime minister’s performance was poor or very poor, also a 1 point rise on last month. The proportion of undecided voters was just 9 per cent, suggesting views of the prime minister’s performance are firmly set. Taylor’s performance rating improved by 2 percentage points to 41 per cent, but the percentage of people who rated his performance as either poor or very poor rose 4 points to 34 per cent, with 25 per cent of people undecided. Ahead of parliament returning on Monday, both Hanson and Taylor spoke at the Conservative Political Action Conference in Brisbane to set out their competing visions. Hanson criticised Taylor during a speech on Saturday for being a “smarmy management consultant” but said her party would work with the Coalition to boot Labor from office at the next election. On Sunday, she claimed to News24 (formerly Sky News) that one attendee had told her he was quitting the Liberal Party after Taylor’s speech. In his speech at CPAC, Taylor acknowledged what he saw as mistakes made under the Morrison government including COVID-era spending, signing up to net zero and “allowing immigration numbers to creep up, especially student and bridging visas”.



The change in Greens leader made no difference to 70 per cent of voters, while 13 per cent said they were more likely to vote for the environmental party and 17 per cent said they were less likely. Larissa Waters’ net likeability score was plus 5 percentage points, well ahead of Shoebridge on minus 3 points, but Shoebridge was better known than Waters. The new leader was familiar to 55 per cent of voters and unfamiliar to 45 per cent, whereas 50 per cent of people were unfamiliar with Waters even after she had spent nearly 18 months as leader. World.title: Kostecki wins unforgettable Bathurst 1000 after De Pasquale runs out of fuel on last lap
World.content:
Breaking SportMotorsportSupercars Kostecki wins unforgettable Bathurst 1000 after De Pasquale runs out of fuel on last lap Frances Howe Updated October 11, 2026 — 5:37pm ,first published 12:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
